overview.summary: A sturdy, compact medium-sized northern French scent hound of classic briquet build, prized for its cold-trailing nose on hare, roe deer, and wild boar, its nearly flat hanging ears, and its dark-fawn tricolour coat.
overview.description: The Artois Hound (Chien d'Artois, historically called the Picard or Briquet d'Artois) is a well-constructed, muscular, medium-sized French pack hound built for methodical stamina and scenting precision rather than sheer speed. Standing 53 to 58 cm at the withers (with a ±1 cm tolerance) and weighing 28 to 30 kg on average, it embodies the compact, nearly square 'briquet' format (withers height to body length between 10:10 and 10:11). Its broad, strong, rounded skull with a flattened top and accentuated stop is slightly longer than its straight muzzle (roughly a 10:8 skull-to-muzzle ratio), whose overhanging upper lips give the tip of the foreface a square profile. Unlike Anglo-French hounds with narrower skulls and lower-set curled ears, the Artois Hound is distinguished by wide-set round dark brown eyes with a gentle, melancholic expression and broad, fairly thick, almost flat ears set at eye level and reaching the base of the black nose. Its short, thick, flat coat is always dark-fawn tricolour with a hare- or badger-like shading, a mantle or large patches, and a fawn head sometimes overlaid with black. Renowned as a meticulous 'closer' (rapprocheur) capable of puzzling out cold trails up to six hours old and giving voice in a high-pitched, melodious cry, it is a peaceful, gregarious pack mate and an affectionate, calm companion off duty.
overview.history: Originating in the historic northern French provinces of Artois and Picardy as a smaller descendant of the black Saint-Hubert hound, hounds of Artois are recorded as early as 1394 and 1410 ('valets de chiens d'Artois') in the hunting accounts of the Dukes of Burgundy Philip the Bold and John the Fearless, and in a 1431 chronicle of King Henry VI of England's coronation entry into Paris. Highly prized during the reigns of Henry IV and Louis XIII (who hunted hare, fox, and wild boar with his 'petits chiens d'Artois' between 1608 and 1610, and whose father received a prized pack from Prince Charles-Alexandre de Croÿ in 1609), the breed—also known as the Chien Picard—was celebrated by Jean de Sacquépée, seigneur de Sélincourt, in Le Parfait Chasseur (1683) for trailing a hare that had passed an hour earlier in dry weather. In Manuel de Vénerie Française (1890), Count Jean-Emmanuel Le Couteulx de Canteleu noted that although pure specimens had grown scarce through crossbreeding with Norman and English hounds, the Artois remained one of the finest hare hounds and placed examples in the Paris Jardin d'Acclimatation. Around 1888, Picardy breeder Ernest Levoir at the Château du Plouy in Domqueur (Somme) founded the Rallye-Scardon pack (motto: 'Chasse droit, Briquet d'Artois') to restore the ancestral type without English or heavy Norman blood, while Auguste and Albert Mallart in Barly (Pas-de-Calais) bred a competing line until 1932. In 1930, French hunting authorities dropped the term 'Briquet' in favour of 'Chien d'Artois', and the breed received definitive international recognition on 18 October 1963. Nearly extinct after the Second World War, the breed was rescued in the early 1970s by farmer-hunter André Audréchy of Buigny-lès-Gamaches in the Somme ('du Parc à Biches' kennel), joined around 1975 by Joseph Mancini in the Var and breeder Josette Pilat in Oise ('La Meute Saint-Louis' kennel and 'Piqu'Artois Saint-Louis' pack), leading to the modern standard published in July–November 1996.

physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; weekly brushing removes dead hairs and field debris.
physical.droolingLevel: Low (despite well-developed upper lips that give the muzzle tip a square profile, the skin is only moderately loose with very little throat dewlap).
distinctiveFeatures: Compact, muscular, nearly square 'briquet' outline (withers height to body length between 10:10 and 10:11, and chest depth equal to half the withers height) built for steady endurance rather than high speed
Strong, broad, rather short skull rounded at the sides and flattened on top (skull width to head length ~5:9) with an inconspicuous occipital peak and an accentuated stop

Straight, moderately elongated muzzle slightly shorter than the skull (muzzle-to-skull ratio ~8:10), with overhanging upper lips giving the muzzle tip a distinct square profile, clean cheeks, a strong black nose with wide nostrils, and a square-set scissor bite
Round, dark brown eyes set well apart and level with the head surface with concealed lower-lid conjunctiva, conveying a soft, melancholic expression
Broad, somewhat thick, almost flat hanging ears set at eye level with rounded tips, reaching the beginning of the nose (a key hallmark distinguishing it from Anglo-French hounds)
Moderately long, powerful neck with very little dewlap, broad well-supported back, slightly arched loin, deep chest reaching the elbows with well-sprung ribs, and full flanks

Strong, fairly long tail carried sickle-fashion (never falling forward over the back) and furnished toward the tip with slightly longer, coarser off-standing hairs like ears of grain ('épiée' / 'espiée')
Strong, vertical, round-boned limbs ending in tight, slightly elongated 'cat-like' feet with tough, compact black pads, and an even, effortless gait

Withers height of 53 to 58 cm with a ±1 cm tolerance (52–59 cm; French breed commentary favours 52–56 cm in males and 48–53 cm in females to preserve true briquet proportions) and average adult weight of 28 to 30 kg across both sexes

traits: Vigorous, hardy, and tireless in the field across plains, woods, and thickets
Exceptionally fine nose ('rapprocheur') capable of unravelling cold trails up to six hours old
Gregarious, peaceful, and non-quarrelsome in a pack (entering the pack from 6 months of age and coexisting peacefully with same-sex hounds)
Balanced, gentle, and affectionate with its handler, actively seeking petting and cuddles
More biddable, cooperative, and easy to lead than many other scent hounds
High-pitched, melodious hunting voice audible from afar (often preceded by soft 'meowing' whimpers when working a cold trail), yet quiet and rarely a nuisance barker off duty
Dislikes being tied or chained and requires space and regular field or outdoor exercise
Never aggressive or timid (aggression or shyness is a disqualifying fault)

exercise.level: High. Bred as an all-terrain endurance hound, it needs long daily country walks or runs, spacious enclosed turnout, and regular scent-tracking or hunting work—and must never be kept tied up.
activities: Small-pack or shooting-party scent hunting (chasse à tir / petite vénerie) on hare, wild boar, or roe deer
Cold-trail tracking, blood trailing, and structured nose-work games
Long, brisk daily country walks or hikes (ideally twice daily) on a leash or long line
Free movement and social interaction with packmates in a spacious, securely fenced rural enclosure
Recall, horn/whistle conditioning, and handler-focus exercises

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice a week with a rubber hound mitt or soft bristle brush to remove dead hair, dust, and plant debris and keep the short, thick coat clean.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when dirty or malodorous using a mild, dog-safe shampoo, rinsing thoroughly and drying the coat and hanging ears completely afterward.
notes: Inspect the long, broad, nearly flat hanging ears systematically after every outing in woods or brambles to remove burrs, grass awns, or ticks and check for moisture, redness, or odour.
Examine the short coat, skin, and tough black paw pads after field work for thorns, cuts, or external parasites.
Trim the nails whenever natural wear does not keep them short.
Brush the teeth frequently with dog-specific toothpaste to prevent tartar accumulation.

training.difficulty: Moderate for experienced hound handlers. National breed guidance notes that the Artois Hound is intelligent, gentle, and more obedient and easier to lead than many other scent hounds, though dominant individuals require a 'firm hand in a velvet glove' and early recall training.
tips: Begin recall conditioning and basic obedience early in puppyhood, combining calm firmness with kindness ('an iron hand in a velvet glove') so the dog's natural willingness to please develops.
For working hounds, gentle scent-search initiation can begin at 4 to 5 months of age in a safely enclosed brushy paddock, and young hounds can integrate into an adult pack from 6 months of age.
Never tether or chain an Artois Hound, and always use a leash or secure fencing in open areas where a fresh game trail can override recall.
Provide structured olfactory enrichment—such as laid scent trails or tracking games—if the dog is not actively hunted.
training.socialization: Bred to live and hunt harmoniously in packs—including peacefully with hounds of the same sex—the Artois Hound is naturally dog-sociable. Introduce puppies early and positively to household routines, varied people, children, handling, and rural environments, while supervising around small non-canine pets due to its strong hunting instinct.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low when isolated alone. As a deeply gregarious pack hound that loves living with fellow hounds and stays closely attached to its owner, the Artois Hound thrives in a spacious rural enclosure with packmates or attentive human company and does poorly if isolated or tied up.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality commercial diet (or a veterinarian-supplemented home-prepared ration with added calcium and vitamins) tailored to life stage, body condition, and seasonal hunting workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Two substantial measured meals daily until the dog finishes growing at around 12 months of age.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete, balanced industrial diet suited to growth and adult maintenance—or, if feeding a traditional home-prepared ration, supplement with appropriate vitamins and calcium under veterinary guidance. Because the Artois Hound continues growing until about 12 months of age, provide two substantial measured meals per day throughout its first year. In adulthood, increase daily rations during active hunting seasons to match higher energy expenditure, then return to maintenance portions during the off-season so the dog stays lean and muscular around 28 to 30 kg. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Provide two substantial measured meals daily during the growth period up to 12 months of age.
If using a home-prepared (ménagère) diet rather than complete commercial food, add veterinary-recommended vitamin and calcium supplementation.
Increase energy intake during active hunting seasons and reduce portions in the off-season to prevent excess weight.
Allow rest before and after meals rather than feeding immediately before or after intense field runs.
Monitor body condition regularly so the flanks remain full without obesity.
nutrition.note: While two substantial meals daily during the first year of growth are recommended for puppies, adult and senior meal frequencies and exact calorie targets should be individualized with a veterinarian.

health.overview: A hardy, rustic, and solid working hound (with typical longevity estimates ranging from 10 to 13 or 12 to 14 years), the Artois Hound has no documented breed-specific hereditary disease prevalence profile or mandatory genetic testing panel. Conformation and breeding rules mandate that only functionally and clinically healthy dogs with breed-typical morphology be used for reproduction, and explicitly disqualify any dog exhibiting a detectable disabling hereditary defect, anatomical anomaly, frail limbs, overshot or undershot jaw (prognathism), very light eyes, or behavioural abnormality. As with other active, drop-eared pack hounds worked across fields, woods, and brambles, everyday veterinary care centres on post-outing ear canal hygiene, parasite and infectious-disease prevention, dental care, and field-injury checks.
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding stock is functionally and clinically healthy, free of disqualifying hereditary or anatomical defects, and has a normal scissor bite.
Inspect the long, broad hanging ears, short coat, and black paw pads after every outing in woods, fields, or thickets to remove ticks, grass awns, burrs, or thorns and prevent otitis externa.
Keep vaccinations, deworming, and external parasite prevention strictly up to date—especially for hounds living in packs or working in wildlife areas.
Maintain a lean, athletic body weight (typically 28–30 kg) by adjusting food intake between hunting and rest seasons.
Brush the teeth frequently with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule routine veterinary wellness and oral examinations.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth frequently with dog-specific toothpaste and have the mouth examined at routine veterinary visits. Conformation rules require a regular scissor bite with the upper incisors closely overlapping the lower incisors and set squarely in the jaws, while overshot or undershot jaws (prognathism) are disqualifying faults.
health.earCare: Inspect the broad, nearly flat hanging ears after every field outing and during weekly brushing for plant debris, parasites, excess wax, redness, or foul odour. Clean only as advised by a veterinarian and dry the ears thoroughly after wet weather.
health.skinCare: Examine the short, dense tricolour coat, fairly thick skin, and compact black paw pads during weekly brushing and after runs through brambles or forest cover for scratches, ticks, burrs, or interdigital foreign bodies.

idealFor: Hunters (including novice hare hunters as well as wild-boar and roe-deer hunters) seeking a steady, biddable, cold-trailing pack or shooting hound
Active rural households with a large, securely fenced garden or spacious enclosure
Scent-work and tracking enthusiasts who can provide long daily countryside outings
Multi-dog homes or pack-hound keepers seeking a peaceful, non-quarrelsome hound that gets along well with peers
notIdealFor: Urban or apartment dwellers—national breed guidance states that this country hunting hound is not made for city life or narrow quarters
Anyone who would tie or chain a dog or leave a single hound isolated without companionship or space
Sedentary households unable to provide long daily walks and scent-based outlets
Owners expecting reliable off-leash recall in unfenced wildlife areas without dedicated training

funFacts: Records of 'valets de chiens d'Artois' appear as early as 1394 and 1410 in the hunting accounts of the Dukes of Burgundy (Philip the Bold and John the Fearless), and in 1431 a live stag hunt with Artois hounds was staged along the streets of Paris during the coronation entry of young King Henry VI of England.

Formerly called the Picard or Chien Picard, the breed was a favourite of Kings Henry IV and Louis XIII; in 1683, royal huntsman Jean de Sacquépée, seigneur de Sélincourt, marvelled at seeing these hounds puzzle out the trail of a hare that had passed an hour earlier in dry weather.

Around 1888, Picardy breeder Ernest Levoir established the famous 'Rallye-Scardon' pack at the Château du Plouy in the Somme under the rhyming French motto 'Chasse droit, Briquet d'Artois' ('Hunt straight, Briquet of Artois').

Feared extinct after the Second World War, the breed was rescued in the 1970s by Somme farmer André Audréchy (in the very same Gamaches area where seventeenth-century authors had praised Picard hounds), joined by Joseph Mancini and Josette Pilat.

Renowned as a cold-trail specialist ('rapprocheur') able to pick up trails up to six hours old, an Artois Hound often emits high-pitched whimpers—humourously described by breeder Josette Pilat as 'meowing' ('miauler')—when working a cold scent before bursting into full, resonant voice once the trail is hot.

A matched pack of just six to eight tricolour Artois Hounds is traditionally considered sufficient to delight the most demanding huntmaster, and although bred for hare, roughly three-quarters of working Artois Hounds in France today are used on wild boar.

faq.question: Where does the Artois Hound come from, and what are its historical names?
faq.answer: The Artois Hound (officially the Chien d'Artois) originates from the Artois and Picardy regions of northern France. Historically, it was also known as the Picard, Chien Picard, and—until French hunting authorities dropped the term 'Briquet' in 1930—the Briquet d'Artois.

faq.question: What was the Artois Hound bred to do, and how is it used today?
faq.answer: It was bred as a medium-sized 'briquet' scent hound for hunting with the gun (chasse à tir) and in small packs (petite vénerie) of six to eight hounds. Prized for its fine nose and steady endurance as a cold-trail finder ('rapprocheur' capable of following trails up to six hours old), it outwits hare on open plains, drives roe deer through open woods, and flushes or holds wild boar in thickets. Today, roughly three-quarters of working Artois Hounds in France hunt wild boar, and the breed is also appreciated in Greece, Italy, and Spain for hare hunting.

faq.question: How large is an adult Artois Hound?
faq.answer: Conformation rules specify a withers height of 53 to 58 cm (with a ±1 cm tolerance, or 52 to 59 cm) and an average weight of 28 to 30 kg for both males and females. In France, an ideal working height of 52 to 56 cm for males and 48 to 53 cm for females is favoured to preserve the breed's compact, nearly square 'briquet' proportions.

faq.question: How can you tell an Artois Hound apart from an Anglo-Français de Petite Vénerie?
faq.answer: The Artois Hound is more compact and cobby, with a broader, rounded skull flattened on top, a muzzle slightly shorter than the skull (about an 8:10 ratio) squared off at the tip by overhanging upper lips, and broad, thick, almost flat ears set at eye level. By contrast, the Anglo-Français de Petite Vénerie has a narrower skull equal in length to the muzzle (1:1), drier lips, and lower-set, thinner, slightly curled ears.

faq.question: What coat colours are accepted in the Artois Hound?
faq.answer: The short, thick, flat coat must always be dark-fawn tricolour (fawn, black, and white) with a hare-toned or badger-toned shading, carried as a mantle or large patches, with a fawn head that is sometimes overlaid with black ('charbonnée'). Bicolour white-and-orange coats without black/badger hair are not accepted, and heavy ticking or mottling on the white areas is a disqualifying fault.

faq.question: Is the Artois Hound suitable for city or apartment living?
faq.answer: No. This country hunting hound is not suited to urban or apartment living, dislikes confined spaces, and must never be kept tied up. It needs a rural home with a large, securely fenced enclosure or kennel, ideally with canine companions, and long daily country outings.

faq.question: What is the Artois Hound's temperament like with people and other dogs?
faq.answer: Off the hunting field, the Artois Hound is calm, gentle, affectionate, and fond of cuddles, and barks very little at home. It is more obedient and easier to lead than many other scent hounds—making it popular even with novice hare hunters—and is exceptionally sociable and non-quarrelsome with other dogs, integrating into packs from 6 months of age and living peacefully with same-sex kennelmates.

faq.question: Does the Artois Hound have known hereditary diseases or a fixed lifespan?
faq.answer: A breed-specific list of hereditary diseases and a single definitive lifespan range have not been established (so those structured fields are kept empty or null), though typical longevity estimates in France range from 10 to 13 or 12 to 14 years. Breeding rules disqualify any dog with a detectable disabling hereditary defect, anatomical anomaly, or bite malocclusion, and routine care focuses on ear checks after field outings, dental hygiene, parasite prevention, and balanced nutrition.

overview.summary: The Australian Silky Terrier is a small, lively companion dog with a fine, glossy coat and an alert terrier expression. Its compact build should not be mistaken for a low-energy temperament: it enjoys exploring, playing, learning, and staying involved in household life.
overview.description: This Australian breed combines a neat, moderately low-set body with a straight, silky coat that is parted along the back. Its characteristic adult colouring is blue and tan, with clear boundaries between the colours. Although bred in a toy-sized format, it retains the curiosity, alertness, and confidence associated with terriers. Regular coat care, consistent reward-based training, and daily engagement are important parts of responsible ownership.
overview.history: The breed developed in Australia through the work of breeders who combined local terrier stock with Yorkshire Terriers to establish a distinctive silky coat and blue-and-tan appearance. The breed was also known historically as the Sydney Silky. A national standard was agreed in the mid-twentieth century, and the Australian Silky Terrier became established as a distinct breed.
overview.originalPurpose: A small terrier developed as a companion while retaining the ability and structure to hunt domestic rodents.
currentRoles: Household companion
Companion for owners who enjoy training and interactive play

physical.coatType: Straight, flat, fine, glossy hair with a silky texture, parted along the back.

Reward calm behaviour to help manage alert barking.
Introduce grooming, tooth brushing, nail care, and gentle handling gradually.
Teach loose-leash walking and reinforce attention around moving animals.

nutrition.guidelines: Use the food's feeding guide as a starting point and adjust portions according to body condition, activity, age, and veterinary advice. Keep fresh water available. Account for treats as part of the overall daily intake.

Monitor body condition and adjust portions when needed.

Make dietary changes gradually unless a veterinarian advises otherwise.

health.overview: Australian Silky Terriers should receive routine preventive veterinary care throughout life. Breed profiles report some concerns involving the knees and eyes, but such reports do not mean that every dog will develop these conditions or establish their prevalence. Ask breeders about the health of related dogs and discuss suitable screening with a veterinarian.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation, a condition in which the kneecap moves out of its normal position.
Eye disorders, including conditions for which veterinary eye assessment may be appropriate.
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, a hip condition reported among possible concerns in small breeds.
Juvenile cataracts, reported as a possible eye concern in breed information.

Discuss patellar and eye screening with a responsible breeder and veterinarian.
Maintain a healthy body condition through appropriate feeding and activity.
Brush the teeth regularly and seek veterinary advice for persistent bad breath, oral pain, or difficulty eating.

recommendedScreenings: Discuss patellar evaluation with the veterinarian or breeder.

health.dentalCare: Small dogs can develop plaque and periodontal disease. Regular tooth brushing with dog-specific toothpaste and veterinary dental checks can help maintain oral health.
health.earCare: Check the ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge, or persistent scratching. Ask a veterinarian for advice if signs of irritation or infection appear.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin during brushing, especially in areas where the coat tangles or equipment rubs. Seek veterinary advice for persistent itching, redness, sores, or hair loss.

The breed has also been known historically as the Sydney Silky.

faq.question: Is the Australian Silky Terrier suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: It can adapt to apartment life when its exercise, training, grooming, and companionship needs are met. Teaching a reliable quiet cue and rewarding calm behaviour can help manage alert barking.

faq.question: How much grooming does an Australian Silky Terrier need?
faq.answer: A long coat needs frequent brushing and combing, often daily, to prevent tangles and matting. The amount of work depends on coat length and the dog's routine.

faq.question: What is the Australian Silky Terrier's recognised height?
faq.answer: The breed standard gives a height of 23–26 cm for dogs. It says bitches can be slightly less but does not specify a separate numeric female range.

faq.question: What is the breed's expected lifespan?
faq.answer: A breed profile gives a broad lifespan range of 10–15 years. This is a general guide rather than a guarantee for an individual dog.

faq.question: Does the Australian Silky Terrier shed?
faq.answer: It is generally described as a relatively low shedder, but the long coat still needs regular grooming to prevent tangles and maintain its condition.

faq.question: Is the Australian Silky Terrier good with children?
faq.answer: It can be a family companion, but children should be taught gentle handling. Supervise interactions, particularly with young children, because a small dog can be injured by rough play or accidental falls.

faq.question: Which health concerns should owners discuss with a veterinarian?
faq.answer: Reported concerns include patellar luxation and eye disorders. Ask a veterinarian or responsible breeder about suitable screening and seek advice if you notice limping, repeated skipping, or changes in the eyes or vision.

overview.summary: A medium-sized Austrian farm-dog breed known for its lively, alert nature, close attachment to familiar people, and instinct to watch over its home.
overview.description: The Austrian Pinscher is a sturdy, short-coated dog with a compact build and an attentive expression. It was developed from traditional Austrian country dogs that worked around farms, and its character reflects that practical background: it is lively and playful with familiar people while tending to be wary of strangers. Its strong watchdog instincts make early socialisation, thoughtful introductions, secure boundaries, and consistent training important parts of everyday life. The breed's dense double coat is relatively straightforward to maintain, but its activity and alertness call for regular exercise and engagement.
overview.history: The breed descends from traditional Austrian country Pinschers that were widespread in rural areas during the second half of the nineteenth century. Systematic pure breeding began in 1921. National cynological recognition arrived in 1928 under the designation Austrian Shorthaired Pinscher, before the name was formally shortened to Austrian Pinscher in 2000.

faq.question: Where does the Austrian Pinscher come from?
faq.answer: The breed originated in Austria and descends from traditional country dogs used on farms.

faq.question: How tall is an Austrian Pinscher?
faq.answer: Males measure 44 to 50 cm at the withers, while females typically stand 42 to 48 cm.

faq.question: How much does an Austrian Pinscher weigh?
faq.answer: Official publications do not specify a mandatory adult weight range, focusing instead on balanced proportions and functional substance relative to height.

faq.question: What is the Austrian Pinscher's temperament like?
faq.answer: It is generally described as lively, alert, playful, and devoted to familiar people, while tending to be wary of strangers.

faq.question: Does the Austrian Pinscher need much grooming?
faq.answer: Its dense double coat is relatively easy to maintain. Regular brushing and routine checks of the coat, skin, ears, and nails are sensible.

faq.question: Is the Austrian Pinscher suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: There is no reliable universal yes-or-no answer. Suitability depends on the individual dog, exercise and enrichment, barking management, training, and the home's setup.

faq.question: Are there known breed-specific health conditions?
faq.answer: The sources reviewed did not establish a sufficiently reliable list of common breed-specific conditions or screening recommendations. A veterinarian and a responsible breeder can advise on health information relevant to an individual dog.

overview.summary: An exceptionally slim, elegant, and ancient West African sighthound from the Sahel desert, celebrated for its upright rectangular silhouette, prominent bone structure, explosive coursing speed, and fiercely loyal yet aloof temperament.
overview.description: The Azawakh is a tall, exquisitely lean, and aristocratic sighthound native to the arid Azawakh Valley of the sub-Saharan Sahel. Characterized by an upright, vertical rectangular silhouette where height at the withers exceeds body length, the dog embodies supreme functional adaptation to extreme desert heat. Its bone framework, ribs, and dry, flat musculature show distinctly beneath fine, parchment-thin skin. The coat is short and fine, thinning to near bareness on the belly, and occurs in shades from light sand to dark mahogany, with or without black brindling, complemented by white markings on the chest, tail tip, and all four feet. The head is long, lean, and chiseled with almond-shaped dark or amber eyes, high-set flat drop ears, and high-protruding hip bones that stand level with or slightly higher than the withers. Reserved, dignified, and fiercely protective of its home territory, it forms an intense, affectionate bond with its immediate family while remaining aloof with strangers.
overview.history: The Azawakh is an ancient indigenous hunting and camp guardian developed by the nomadic Tuareg, Fula, and Daoussahak pastoralists of the Sahelian borderlands between Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso. Rock engravings in the central Sahara dating back thousands of years depict sighthounds of identical slender morphology coursing game across what were once fertile plains. As desertification progressed, nomadic hunters migrated south along the seasonal waterways of the Azawakh Valley, relying on these dogs—locally known as Oska or Idi—to chase down swift dorcas gazelles, hares, and ostriches, as well as to defend desert encampments from hyenas, jackals, and leopards. The dogs traditionally rested on elevated straw-thatched platforms above the camp, providing a commanding vantage point. The first specimens arrived in Europe in the early 1970s through diplomatic exchanges, followed by selective preservation of the gene pool and formal international recognition in the 1980s.
overview.originalPurpose: Coursing and hunting swift desert game including gazelle, hare, and wild fowl, alongside guarding nomadic livestock and desert encampments against predators and intruders.
currentRoles: Devoted household companion for experienced sighthound owners
Lure coursing and open-field amateur coursing athlete
Alert home and property watchdog
Long-distance running and endurance hiking partner in warm climates

Divide the daily allowance into two meals, refrain from vigorous running for at least one hour before and after eating, and provide fresh, cool drinking water at all times.

health.overview: The Azawakh is an ancient landrace possessing exceptional natural hardiness and a typical lifespan of 12 to 15 years. Developed in harsh desert conditions, it is free from many common artificial genetic exaggerations. However, its specialized sighthound physiology—including extremely low body fat, minimal drug-binding plasma proteins, and reduced hepatic clearance of certain compounds—makes it uniquely sensitive to anesthesia and cold exposure. Documented health priorities include idiopathic epilepsy, autoimmune thyroiditis, gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat), cardiac murmurs, and orthopedic issues such as cervical spondylopathy.
commonConditions: Sighthound anesthetic sensitivity — lack of adipose tissue and atypical hepatic metabolism result in dangerously delayed recovery from thiobarbiturate anesthetics; modern protocols using propofol, isoflurane, or sevoflurane with careful temperature monitoring are essential
Idiopathic epilepsy — inherited seizure disorder reported in some bloodlines, monitored and managed through neurological evaluation and anticonvulsant therapy
Hypothyroidism / autoimmune thyroiditis — immune-mediated destruction of thyroid tissue causing lethargy, symmetrical alopecia, and weight changes, screenable via blood antibody panels
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — an acute, life-threatening twisting and distension of the stomach common in deep, narrow-chested sighthounds
Cardiac conditions — occasional reports of murmurs, dilated cardiomyopathy, or arrhythmias evaluated via echocardiography
Masticatory muscle myositis — an inflammatory autoimmune condition affecting the muscles of mastication, causing difficulty opening the jaw
Demodectic mange — localized or generalized proliferation of skin mites in puppies or young dogs with developing immune systems
Hypothermia — rapid loss of body heat in cool or wet environments due to minimal body fat and a fine, thin coat
preventiveCare: Ensure any attending veterinarian is experienced with sighthound anesthesia and avoids thiobarbiturates, maintaining active warming blankets during surgery.
Verify that breeding stock has completed certified screenings for thyroid function, cardiac health, eyes, and hips.
Provide thick, padded bedding indoors and dress the dog in insulated coats during cold or wet weather.
Feed two smaller meals daily and avoid strenuous running immediately before or after feeding to minimize bloat risk.
Inspect footpads, toes, and skin after high-speed runs over rough ground for cuts or abrasions.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine parasite control.
recommendedScreenings: Autoimmune thyroiditis blood profile (free T4, TSH, and autoantibodies) prior to breeding
Cardiac evaluation including auscultation and Doppler echocardiogram by a veterinary cardiologist prior to breeding
Comprehensive ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. Sighthounds have long, narrow jaws that benefit from early dental care to prevent tartar accumulation and gingivitis.
health.earCare: Inspect the thin drop ears weekly for dust, wax, or irritation, and clean gently with a veterinary-recommended cleanser; check ear margins in winter to prevent cracking in sub-freezing winds.
health.skinCare: Wipe the thin coat with a soft damp cloth weekly. Provide soft orthopedic dog beds to protect pressure points over hip bones and hocks from developing hygromas or skin calluses.

funFacts: The Azawakh is uniquely built taller than it is long: its vertical rectangular silhouette has a height-to-length ratio of ten to nine, creating an unmistakable, skyward elegance.

Unlike most classic sighthounds that are purely hunting coursers, the Azawakh has served for millennia as a fierce camp guardian, historically perching atop elevated straw roofs in Tuareg villages to survey the surrounding desert.
The breed's hip bones (the pin bones of the pelvis) naturally sit at the same level as or slightly higher than its withers, giving the topline a distinctive, proud poise.
In the Tuareg language, the breed is called 'Oska', while the French and international name 'Azawakh' derives from the Azawakh Valley, a dry wadi basin in the Sahel.
The breed's paper-thin skin and almost hairless belly are evolutionary adaptations that allow it to rapidly dump body heat while coursing game in desert temperatures exceeding 40°C.
Nomadic tribes historically regarded the Azawakh as a member of the family rather than livestock, sharing their tents and milk with their prized hunting companions.

faq.question: What is an Azawakh?
faq.answer: The Azawakh is an ancient, tall, and elegant sighthound native to the Sahel region of West Africa, renowned for its slender bone structure, high hip bones, explosive running speed, and protective devotion to its family.

faq.question: Where does the Azawakh originate?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the Azawakh Valley in the Sahelian borderlands of Mali, Niger, and northern Burkina Faso, where it was bred by nomadic Tuareg and Fula pastoralists.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an Azawakh?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 64 to 74 cm at the withers and weigh 20 to 25 kg, while adult females stand 60 to 70 cm and weigh 15 to 20 kg, presenting a light, upright, and muscular frame.

faq.question: Why does the Azawakh look so skinny?
faq.answer: The breed is naturally lean and flat-muscled, with paper-thin skin designed to dissipate heat in the extreme Sahel desert. Having three to five visible ribs, clearly defined hip bones, and a deep tuck-up is normal and healthy for this breed, not a sign of malnutrition.

faq.question: How long does an Azawakh live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, indoor care, and conscientious veterinary attention, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 12 to 15 years.

faq.question: How does the Azawakh behave with strangers?
faq.answer: By nature, the breed is aloof, reserved, and observant with strangers. It does not solicit attention from unfamiliar people and requires time to accept new acquaintances; early socialization helps ensure this wariness remains calm and composed.

faq.question: Can an Azawakh live in cold climates?
faq.answer: Yes, provided it lives indoors in a heated home. Because it has minimal body fat and a very fine coat with a bare belly, it must wear warm, insulated fleece coats or jackets during outdoor walks in cold or wet weather.

faq.question: Can an Azawakh live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. While it is quiet and cat-like indoors, its intense need for regular, high-speed sprinting in a secure, tall-fenced enclosure makes it best suited to a home with a large, safely fenced yard.

faq.question: Is the Azawakh good with children and other pets?
faq.answer: It is affectionate and gentle with familiar children in its family, but interactions should be calm and supervised. Its fierce prey drive makes it unsafe around small outdoor animals, cats, or pocket pets.

faq.question: How much exercise does an Azawakh need daily?
faq.answer: The breed requires 60 to 90 minutes of daily exercise, including brisk leashed walks and safe opportunities to sprint at full speed in an escape-proof fenced field of at least six feet in height.

faq.question: What health concerns are unique to the Azawakh?
faq.answer: Key considerations include extreme sensitivity to anesthesia (requiring sighthound-safe protocols), susceptibility to hypothermia in cold weather, autoimmune thyroiditis, idiopathic epilepsy, and bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus).

faq.question: How is an Azawakh groomed?
faq.answer: Grooming is very simple: wiping the coat weekly with a hound glove or soft brush and providing thick, soft bedding to protect its prominent bones from developing pressure calluses.

overview.summary: An ancient, medium-sized French water retriever distinguished by its dense, curly, water-repellent fleece coat, distinctive chin beard, webbed feet, and calm, affectionate, and cheerful working disposition.
overview.description: The Barbet is a rustic, medium-sized water dog built with balanced, sturdy substance, strong bone, and an athletic, slightly rectangular frame. Historically developed to locate, flush, and retrieve waterfowl from freezing marshes and coastal estuaries, the dog possesses a waterproof double coat composed of thick, natural woolly curls that cover the body from head to tail. Its facial furnishings feature prominent whiskers and an abundant chin beard—from which the French word 'barbe' and the breed name derive—framing round, dark hazel or dark brown eyes radiating gentle intelligence. The webbed paws and muscular thighs provide powerful swimming drive in muddy waters. In domestic life, the dog is calm, cheerful, and deeply affectionate with family members, adapting easily to active households while maintaining an enduring passion for swimming, retrieving, and outdoor exploration.
overview.history: The Barbet is one of Europe's most ancient waterfowl dogs, with historical and literary records across France dating back to the late sixteenth century. Mentions appear in King Henry IV's royal court chronicles as well as natural history treatises by Buffon, who described the rustic water dog as an ancestor of several modern gundog and companion breeds, notably the Poodle, Bichon types, and various European water spaniels. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, French market hunters and wildfowlers relied on these dogs to retrieve downed ducks, geese, and game from freezing bogs and marshes. The disruptions of the World Wars caused the rustic working landrace to decline sharply, prompting French cynologists and dedicated breeders in the mid-twentieth century to collect and preserve surviving bloodlines. Today, the breed is celebrated internationally as an authentic, historical sporting dog and versatile companion.

health.overview: The Barbet is a remarkably robust, rustic sporting dog with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years. Having been preserved through functional working lines with attention to genetic health, it has avoided many artificial conformational exaggerations. However, responsible health management requires screening for hereditary conditions seen across water retrievers, including hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, hereditary eye diseases (such as progressive retinal atrophy and cataracts), idiopathic epilepsy, and chronic otitis externa due to heavily coated drop ears.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the coxofemoral joints leading to osteoarthritis and hind-limb lameness, monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening
Elbow dysplasia — developmental abnormalities of the elbow joint causing forelimb lameness and joint stiffness
Progressive retinal atrophy (prcd-PRA) — an inherited neurodegenerative ocular condition causing progressive photoreceptor degeneration and eventual blindness, screenable via DNA testing
Hereditary cataracts and distichiasis — ocular conditions monitored through annual veterinary ophthalmologist examinations
Idiopathic epilepsy — inherited seizure disorder reported in some European lines, managed through pedigree evaluation and neurological care
Chronic otitis externa — bacterial and yeast ear infections promoted by heavy, hairy drop ears that restrict ventilation and trap moisture after swimming
Allergic dermatitis — occasional sensitivities to environmental allergens or fleas causing skin itching and secondary infections
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has certified radiographic clearances for hips and elbows, DNA clearance for prcd-PRA, and current ophthalmologist eye certifications.
Thoroughly dry the ears and wipe ear canals with a veterinary ear wash after every swim or bath.
Maintain a lean, athletic body condition to avoid placing excess mechanical wear on hips and elbows.
Brush and comb the curly fleece down to the skin multiple times weekly to prevent painful matting and skin hot spots.
Administer consistent year-round parasite prevention against fleas, ticks, and heartworms.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine dental cleanings.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accredited national screening program prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
DNA marker test for Progressive Retinal Atrophy (prcd-PRA) prior to breeding
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using dog-specific enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong, wide jaws with a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the long drop ears two to three times weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or foul odor. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear cleanser, drying the leather and canal opening thoroughly after swimming.
health.skinCare: Part the dense curly fleece weekly during line-combing to inspect the skin for external parasites, redness, or mats. Avoid blow-drying the coat straight, as natural air drying maintains healthy curl structure and skin aeration.

funFacts: The breed name Barbet comes directly from the French word 'barbe' (meaning beard), referring to the characteristic tuft of long, curly hair growing from its chin.
The popular French idiom 'crotté comme un barbet' (muddy as a barbet) originated centuries ago, affectionately describing someone soaked, disheveled, and covered in mud after an outdoor adventure.
Historical cynologists widely consider the Barbet to be the common ancestor of several European breeds, including the Poodle, the Portuguese Water Dog, the Spanish Water Dog, and the Bichon family.

King Henry IV of France was an avid hunter who kept Barbet water dogs, and historical letters recount his mistress jokingly complaining that the king brought his wet, muddy Barbets directly into royal bedchambers.
Unlike the sculpted, shaved show trims of poodles, the Barbet's breed standard strictly requires it to be presented in its natural rustic curls, with no clipping of the face or hindquarters.
The breed has fully webbed feet, functioning like natural flippers that give the dog remarkable propulsion and endurance when swimming in deep or muddy water.

faq.question: What is a Barbet?
faq.answer: The Barbet is an ancient French water dog known for its dense curly fleece coat, characteristic chin beard, webbed paws, and gentle, joyful personality.

faq.question: What is the difference between a Barbet and a Poodle?
faq.answer: While closely related historically, the Barbet is a distinct gundog with a broader head, slightly rectangular body, heavier bone, and a natural, unsculpted curly coat, whereas the Poodle has a longer muzzle, a square silhouette, lighter bone, and a tradition of styled coats.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Barbet?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 58 to 65 cm at the withers and weigh 20 to 28 kg, while adult females stand 53 to 61 cm and weigh 17 to 24 kg, with a height tolerance of plus or minus one centimetre.

faq.question: How long does a Barbet live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, regular exercise, and conscientious preventive veterinary care, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Do Barbets shed, and how is their coat groomed?
faq.answer: Barbets are low-shedding dogs because dead hairs catch in their dense curls rather than falling out. They require thorough line-combing two to three times a week down to the skin to prevent mats, along with an occasional uniform trim every couple of months; they should not be blown straight or shaved.

faq.question: Are Barbets good family pets and good with children?
faq.answer: Yes. They are famously gentle, patient, and affectionate with children, making wonderful family pets; they also get along very well with other dogs and domestic animals.

faq.question: Can a Barbet live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes. They adapt well to apartment living provided they receive daily physical exercise, walks, and human companionship, as they are calm and clean indoors.

faq.question: Are Barbets easy to train?
faq.answer: They are highly intelligent, eager to please, and food-motivated, responding enthusiastically to positive reinforcement, praise, and gentle guidance in obedience, agility, and retrieving.

faq.question: Do Barbets love water?
faq.answer: Yes. Swimming and retrieving from water are deep ancestral instincts for the breed; their webbed feet and waterproof double coat make them exceptional swimmers.

faq.question: What health tests are recommended for the Barbet?
faq.answer: Recommended pre-breeding screenings include radiographic evaluations for hip and elbow dysplasia, DNA testing for progressive retinal atrophy (prcd-PRA), and annual specialist eye examinations.

overview.summary: A rustic, low-slung French scenthound distinguished by its mottled slate-blue coat, long curling drop ears, deep resonant voice, exceptional tracking persistence, and gentle, calm companion temperament.
overview.description: The Basset Bleu de Gascogne is a substantial, low-to-the-ground hunting hound of ancient Gascon heritage, combining remarkable scenting endurance with a calm, aristocratic disposition. Bred down from the Grand Bleu de Gascogne, the dog presents an elongated, sturdy frame supported by heavy bone and strong limbs, allowing it to navigate dense brambles, thorny underbrush, and rugged ravines at an unhurried, persistent pace. Its short, dense coat exhibits an unmistakable slate-blue coloration created by fine black and white mottling, accented by dark head patches and warm tan markings above the eyes, on the muzzle, and on the lower legs. The head is noble and domed, framed by remarkably long, thin, cone-curling ears that fall well past the nose tip, paired with deep dark brown eyes radiating a calm, solemn expression. While passionate, loud-voiced, and tenacious on quarry trails, it settles into an exceptionally gentle, peaceful, and devoted presence in the home.
overview.history: The breed developed in southwestern France by crossing ancient Grand Bleu de Gascogne scenthounds with native short-legged basset mutations, producing a slower-paced tracker that mounted or walking hunters could easily follow through dense forest terrain. During the late nineteenth century, hunting with firearms gained widespread popularity, creating a high demand for deliberate, methodical hounds that did not outrun the guns. French hound enthusiast Alain Bourbon played a pivotal role in refining and preserving the breed during the early twentieth century, gathering surviving working strains from Gascon valleys. Although the disruptions of the World Wars reduced its population, dedicated southwestern French huntsmen revived the breed by the 1960s. Today, it remains an esteemed hunting pack dog in southern Europe and an increasingly valued, distinctive family companion.
overview.originalPurpose: Tracking and driving hare, rabbit, wild boar, and roe deer through dense woodland and rocky ravines using methodic scenting and resonant voice.
currentRoles: Traditional tracking and hunting pack hound for small and medium game
Blood tracking and wounded game search partner

Channel natural tracking instincts into structured scentwork games or search trails.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age, transitioning to two meals daily on a growth formula supporting steady development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support steady metabolism and minimize digestive discomfort.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic output, joint support, and lean muscle retention.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure food portions carefully using a digital kitchen scale or standard measuring cup, adjusting amounts to maintain a lean, athletic body condition where the ribs are easily felt. An elongated spine is vulnerable to excess weight; avoid overfeeding. Divide daily food into two distinct meals, restrict vigorous exercise immediately before and after eating, use narrow spaniel-style bowls to keep long ears clean, and provide cool, clean drinking water continuously.
considerations: Maintain a lean, muscular body condition; excess weight puts severe mechanical stress on the elongated spine and short limbs.
Account for training treats within the total daily caloric allowance to avoid creeping weight gain.
Use narrow bowls or ear snoods during feeding to prevent long ears from soaking in food and water.
Rest the dog before and after meals to mitigate the risk of bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus).
Avoid feeding high-fat table scraps that can trigger digestive upset or acute pancreatitis.
Transition between diet formulas gradually over five to seven days.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs vary significantly based on hunting activity, outdoor temperature, and daily exercise. Consult a veterinarian to establish tailored daily feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The Basset Bleu de Gascogne is a rustic, sturdy, and robust hunting hound with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years. Having been cultivated for practical field work in southwestern France, it enjoys good general constitutional vitality. Primary health priorities reflect its low-slung, chondrodysplastic conformation and long drop ears, including intervertebral disc disease (IVDD), chronic otitis externa, gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat), hip and elbow dysplasia, and eyelid conditions such as ectropion.
commonConditions: Intervertebral disc disease (IVDD) — spinal disc herniation or degeneration resulting from an elongated back, causing neck or back pain, nerve deficit, and hind-limb lameness, manageable by maintaining a lean weight and limiting furniture jumping
Chronic otitis externa — bacterial and yeast ear infections promoted by heavy, long drop ears that restrict ventilation and trap moisture in the ear canal
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — an acute, life-threatening twisting and distension of the stomach in deep-chested hounds, requiring emergency veterinary care
Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the coxofemoral joints leading to osteoarthritis and stiffness
Elbow dysplasia — developmental abnormalities of the elbow joints that can cause forelimb lameness and joint degeneration
Ectropion and entropion — eyelid margin abnormalities where loose facial skin causes the lower lid to sag outward or roll inward, predisposing to conjunctivitis
Traumatic outdoor injuries — skin scrapes, thorn punctures, or ear leather tears sustained while pushing through dense briars and brambles
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has certified radiographic clearances for hips and elbows, alongside certified specialist eye examinations.
Inspect and clean the long drop ears weekly, wiping canals with an approved veterinary cleanser and drying thoroughly.
Maintain a strictly controlled, lean body condition to avoid placing excess load on the elongated spine and joints.
Prevent high-impact jumping off beds, sofas, or vehicle tailgates to protect spinal discs.
Feed two smaller meals daily and avoid vigorous exercise immediately before or after eating to mitigate bloat risk.
Administer consistent year-round parasite prevention against fleas, ticks, and heartworms.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Regular veterinary spinal and musculoskeletal assessment
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong, wide jaws with a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the long pendulous drop ears two to three times weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or redness. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather thoroughly.
health.skinCare: Part the short coat weekly during brushing to inspect the skin for external parasites, redness, or scratches. Check and clean pendulous lip folds and ear margins regularly.

funFacts: The breed's distinctive 'blue' coloration is an optical illusion: it is actually created by a dense, fine mottling of black and white hairs intermingling across the coat, giving the impression of slate blue from a distance.
Bassets Bleus de Gascogne are famous among French hunters as 'hurleurs' (howlers) due to their deep, melodious, and ringing bay that can carry for kilometers across forested valleys.
Despite having short legs, the breed was historically used to track big game including wild boar and roe deer, as its deliberate, steady speed prevented driving game past hunters too quickly.

The breed's remarkably long ears are not just ornamental; as the hound runs with its nose to the ground, the sweeping ears stir up ground scent particles and funnel them directly toward the sensitive olfactory receptors in the nose.

In southwestern French folk tradition, the breed's prominent tan spots above the eyes are known as 'quatre-oeillères' (four-eyes), which folklore romantically claimed allowed the hound to see unseen forest spirits.
The breed is one of four distinct varieties in the Bleu de Gascogne hound family, sharing identical slate-blue coloration and heritage with the Grand, Petit, and Griffon Bleus de Gascogne.

faq.question: What is a Basset Bleu de Gascogne?
faq.answer: The Basset Bleu de Gascogne (Blue Gascony Basset) is a medium-sized, low-slung French scenthound known for its mottled slate-blue coat, long curling ears, melodious bay, and calm, affectionate personality.

faq.question: Why is the coat called 'blue'?
faq.answer: The blue appearance is created by an intricate mix of black and white hairs mottled closely together across the body, producing a striking slate-blue effect accented by black patches and warm tan points.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Basset Bleu de Gascogne?
faq.answer: Adult males and females stand 34 to 38 cm at the withers and typically weigh between 16 and 20 kg, presenting a sturdy, heavy-boned, and elongated frame.

faq.question: How long does a Basset Bleu de Gascogne live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, regular exercise, and conscientious preventive veterinary care, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Do Bassets Bleus de Gascogne shed a lot, and how are they groomed?
faq.answer: They shed low to moderate amounts year-round. Their short coat is low-maintenance, requiring only a weekly brushing with a rubber hound mitt, regular ear cleaning, and occasional nail trimming.

faq.question: Can a Basset Bleu de Gascogne live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Due to their deep, resonant baying voice and need for scent exploration, they are best suited to a house with a securely fenced yard in rural or suburban environments.

faq.question: Are Bassets Bleus de Gascogne good family pets and good with children?
faq.answer: Yes. Within the home, they are remarkably gentle, patient, and affectionate with children; they also get along exceptionally well with other dogs due to their pack-hunting background.

faq.question: Is the Basset Bleu de Gascogne easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent and gentle, but possess an independent hound nature. When an interesting scent captures their attention, they can be single-minded; training requires patience, food rewards, and positive reinforcement.

faq.question: Why are ear care and spine health important for this breed?
faq.answer: Their long, pendulous ears trap moisture and require regular weekly cleaning to prevent infections, while their elongated spine is susceptible to intervertebral disc disease (IVDD), making weight management and avoiding steep jumping essential.

overview.summary: A cheerful, low-slung French scenthound originating in the bramble-covered terrain of the Vendée, the Petit Basset Griffon Vendéen was bred to trail rabbits and hares by scent through rocky undergrowth. Compact, sturdy, and cloaked in a naturally tousled rough coat, this extroverted hound pairs tireless tracking persistence with a merry, sociable disposition.
overview.description: Affectionately known as the PBGV, this hardy little hound is built slightly longer than tall with strong bone, a deep chest, and a weather-resistant double coat that shields the skin from thorns and brush. Its expressive face is framed by bushy eyebrows, a full mustache and beard, and narrow, supple ears set below the eye line, while a medium-length saber tail is carried proudly aloft like a flag in dense cover. Exceptionally outgoing and pack-oriented, the breed thrives on lively family interaction and gets along wonderfully with other canines. However, its powerful scenting instincts, resonant voice, and independent problem-solving habits demand secure fencing, dedicated nose-work enrichment, and patient, reward-based training.
overview.history: Developed from the sixteenth century onward along the rocky, thicket-filled Atlantic coast of western France's Vendée department, the breed descended from the larger Grand Griffon Vendéen to serve hunters pursuing rabbits and small game on foot. Its descriptive French name translates directly to its key attributes: 'Petit' (small), 'Basset' (low to the ground), 'Griffon' (wire- or rough-coated), and 'Vendéen' (from the Vendée). For generations, the smaller Petit and taller Grand Basset varieties were interbred and judged under shared specifications until distinct structural standards separated them completely in the mid-twentieth century.
overview.originalPurpose: Trailing and flushing rabbits, hares, and small game by scent across rocky, bramble-choked coastal terrain.
currentRoles: Active family companion
Scent work, nosework, and tracking competitor
Small-game hunting hound
Agility, rally, and obedience participant
Conformation show dog

physical.coatType: Harsh, rough, weather-resistant double coat featuring a coarse, unexaggerated outer jacket over a thick, insulating underlayer, naturally tousled and casual in outline.
physical.coatLength: Medium-length rough coat over the body, complemented by prominent facial furnishings including long eyebrows, beard, and mustache.
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; regular shedding managed through weekly brushing and combing to clear dead hair from the rough coat.
physical.droolingLevel: Low; dry lips and beard retain water after drinking but do not produce heavy drool.
distinctiveFeatures: Sturdy, low-set rectangular body somewhat longer from shoulder to buttocks than tall at the withers
Rough, tousled, weatherproof double coat worn in a casual, untrimmed state
Expressive dark eyes surmounted by long, tousled eyebrows that do not obscure vision
Full beard and mustache framing a well-developed black nose with wide nostrils
Narrow, fine, inward-folding ears set below the eye line and covered in long hair
Medium-length, high-set tail tapering like a saber blade and carried proudly upright

traits: Cheerful, extroverted, and perpetually upbeat
Sociable and harmonious with other dogs due to pack-hunting origins
Inquisitive, bold, and intensely scent-driven
Independent-minded and tenacious when locked onto a trail
Affectionate, playful, and engaged with family members
Vocal with a resonant, musical bay and ready alert bark
Responsive to upbeat, reward-based training but easily distracted by ground scents

exercise.level: High. Bred for a full day's work in tough terrain, this energetic hound requires substantial daily physical activity paired with dedicated scenting enrichment.
activities: Brisk daily leashed walks with ample time allotted for sniffing and scent investigation
Structured nosework, scent discrimination games, and tracking trails
Vigorous play and romping in a securely fenced, dig-proof yard
Agility, rally obedience, and barn hunt competitions
Interactive food-dispensing puzzles and hide-and-seek games

grooming.level: Moderate. The rough double coat repels dirt well, requiring weekly combing to prevent mats while preserving its natural, unclipped appearance.
grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly once or twice weekly using a slicker brush and metal hound comb, paying special attention to the longer hair on the beard, ears, legs, and belly.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when necessary using a mild canine shampoo that does not soften the harsh outer coat texture, drying the ear canals thoroughly afterward.
notes: Inspect the coat, paws, and ear fringes after outdoor walks to remove burrs, twigs, and grass awns.
Maintain the breed's casual, tousled look; never clip or sculpt the body coat.
Clean and dry the beard regularly after meals to prevent trapped moisture and skin irritation.
Check the long, folded ear canals weekly for wax buildup, redness, or yeast odor.
Trim strong toenails every two to three weeks and brush teeth regularly with enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging. Bright and eager to please when motivated, yet independent and quick to prioritize a compelling scent over handler commands.
tips: Use positive reinforcement featuring high-value aromatic treats, play rewards, and enthusiastic praise.
Keep training sessions short, varied, and engaging to prevent boredom.
Practice recall on a long training line, and never allow off-leash roaming in unfenced areas.
Incorporate scent-finding games directly into obedience routines as a functional reward.
Establish calm household boundaries early to manage vocal baying and counter-surfing.
training.socialization: Introduce puppies positively to diverse people, children, household noises, and novel settings. While naturally friendly with other dogs and strangers, early supervised exposure around smaller household pets is important due to innate rabbit-chasing instincts.

climates: Thrives in temperate and cool climates where its rough double coat provides ideal protection.
Adapts to warm weather when provided shaded rest areas, air-conditioning, fresh water, and early-morning exercise.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. As a pack-bred scenthound, prolonged solitary confinement can trigger loneliness, vocal baying, and digging.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced commercial or veterinary-formulated canine diet appropriate for active small-to-medium hounds across their specific life stages.
nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily meals accurately to maintain a lean, athletic working weight where ribs can be felt easily beneath the rough coat. Excess weight places harmful mechanical strain on the low-set spine, shoulders, and stifles. Deduct training treats from the daily ration and keep clean drinking water available.
considerations: Account for high-value training treats used during nosework and obedience sessions within the daily calorie budget.
Monitor body condition score regularly, as thick coat hair can mask gradual weight gain.
Clean and dry facial furnishings after wet or raw meals to maintain skin hygiene.
Introduce any dietary transitions gradually over 7 to 10 days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs vary by individual age, metabolism, neuter status, and daily exercise workload.

health.overview: Generally a hardy and long-lived scenthound with a typical life expectancy of 14 to 16 years. Parent-club health programs focus primarily on inherited ocular conditions—particularly primary open-angle glaucoma—alongside routine monitoring for orthopaedic, endocrine, and neurological disorders.
commonConditions: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), an autosomal recessive ocular disorder caused by an ADAMTS17 gene mutation leading to elevated intraocular pressure and lens subluxation
Persistent pupillary membranes (PPM), retinal dysplasia/folds, and juvenile cataracts
Otitis externa, involving bacterial or yeast ear infections promoted by pendulous, hair-covered pinnae
Hip dysplasia and medial patellar luxation, affecting hindlimb joint stability
Autoimmune thyroiditis and hypothyroidism
Idiopathic epilepsy, causing recurrent seizure episodes
Intervertebral disc disease (IVDD) and neck pain associated with a longer-backed build
preventiveCare: Verify parentage DNA test status for the ADAMTS17 mutation responsible for primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG).
Schedule periodic ophthalmic evaluations with a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist throughout adulthood.
Inspect and gently clean the folded ear canals weekly, keeping them dry after baths or wet walks.
Maintain a lean body weight and avoid encouraging repetitive jumping from high furniture.
Seek prompt veterinary attention for ocular redness, squinting, cloudy corneas, sudden lameness, or seizure activity.
Maintain routine dental cleanings, vaccinations, and year-round parasite prevention.
recommendedScreenings: DNA genetic test for primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG / ADAMTS17 mutation) prior to breeding
Annual clinical eye examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Radiographic hip evaluation and clinical patellar examination to assess joint conformation
Comprehensive thyroid panel to screen for autoimmune thyroiditis when indicated by lineage
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule professional veterinary dental cleanings as advised to prevent periodontal disease.
health.earCare: Check the long, inward-folded ears weekly for trapped moisture, grass seeds, dark wax, or odor. Clean gently with a veterinary-approved ear solution, drying the canal entrance thoroughly.
health.skinCare: Part the coarse coat during weekly brushing to inspect the skin for ticks, burrs, scratches from brushy cover, or localized dermatitis beneath the beard.

idealFor: Active families and outdoor enthusiasts who enjoy daily brisk walks, hiking, and scent-based games
Multi-dog households seeking a cheerful, pack-friendly companion
Handlers interested in canine nosework, tracking, barn hunt, or agility sports
Homes with a securely fenced, dig-proof yard and tolerance for occasional hound vocalisation
notIdealFor: Apartment dwellers or close-quarter urban homes sensitive to resonant baying and barking
Owners expecting instant, off-leash obedience in open, unfenced areas around wildlife
Sedentary households unable to provide 60 to 90 minutes of daily exercise and mental enrichment
Homes with free-roaming small pets such as rabbits or ferrets that trigger hunting instincts

funFacts: Every word in the breed's name describes a key trait: 'Petit' (small), 'Basset' (low-set), 'Griffon' (rough-coated), and 'Vendéen' (from the Vendée region of France).
Its proud, saber-curved tail is tipped in white so hunters on foot can spot the hound moving through tall, dense brambles.
Often nicknamed the 'happy breed', these extroverted hounds are famous for their constantly wagging tails and cheerful, musical voices.
Until the mid-twentieth century, the Petit and Grand Basset Griffon Vendéen were considered size varieties from the exact same litters rather than separate breeds.

faq.question: What does the name Petit Basset Griffon Vendéen mean?
faq.answer: The French name translates directly to 'small, low-set, rough-coated hound from the Vendée', describing its compact size, short legs, wire-like jacket, and native region in western France.

faq.question: How big does a Petit Basset Griffon Vendéen get?
faq.answer: Adults stand 34 to 38 cm tall at the withers and typically weigh between 25 and 40 pounds, possessing a sturdy, muscular build.

faq.question: What is the typical life expectancy of a PBGV?
faq.answer: They are a remarkably long-lived hound breed, with a typical lifespan of 14 to 16 years when given attentive preventive healthcare and weight management.

faq.question: Can a PBGV be trusted off leash in unfenced areas?
faq.answer: Generally no. Because they were bred for centuries to follow game trails independently, a compelling scent can easily override recall training. They should be exercised on a leash or within a securely fenced area.

faq.question: How much grooming does the rough coat require?
faq.answer: Grooming is moderate. Weekly brushing and combing removes dead hair and prevents mats in the beard, ears, and leg furnishings, while preserving the breed's natural, untrimmed, tousled look.

faq.question: What health screenings are most important for this breed?
faq.answer: The primary genetic test is a DNA screening for primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), paired with annual eye examinations by a veterinary ophthalmologist, as well as hip and patellar evaluations.

overview.summary: A short-legged, heavy-boned scenthound of French heritage developed in Great Britain, renowned for its low-slung rectangular frame, loose elastic skin, soulful brown eyes, long velvety ears, and remarkable trailing scenting power second only to the Bloodhound.
overview.description: The Basset Hound is a remarkably heavy-boned, low-slung scent hound possessing an elongated, rectangular silhouette that holds an extraordinary amount of substance in a dwarf stature. Characterized by short, stout legs with substantial bone density and a deep chest that clears the ground with deliberate balance, the hound is built for slow, methodical endurance tracking rather than speed. Its smooth, dense coat is smooth and weather-resistant, traditionally appearing in tricolour or lemon-and-white patterns over loose, pliable skin that forms gentle folds along the forehead, muzzle, and ankles. The head is large, domed, and noble with a prominent occiput, deep pendulous flews, long velvety drop ears that extend well past the nose, and sunken dark eyes that convey a dignified, mournful expression. Placid, calm, and deeply affectionate in the home, it transforms on the trail into a tenacious, unyielding tracker possessing a booming, melodious bay.
overview.history: The ancestry of the Basset Hound traces back to the ancient St. Hubert hounds of monastic France, where dwarfed, low-set hunting hounds ('bassets', from the French 'bas' meaning low) were selectively bred to trail game through dense brush at a pace easily followed by hunters on foot. In the 1860s and 1870s, French aristocrats gifted breeding pairs of Basset d'Artois and Basset Artésien Normand to British nobility, including Lord Galway and Sir Everett Millais. Working in England, Millais and fellow breeders crossed these French lines with Bloodhounds to increase bone substance, enhance head type, and strengthen scenting capacity, establishing a heavier, distinctive hound. Formal registration was achieved in England in 1880, followed by American recognition in 1885. Throughout the twentieth century, the breed attained worldwide fame as an iconic companion, pop-culture symbol, and formidable tracking competitor.
