funFacts: The Berger Picard is one of France's traditional sheepdog breeds.
Dogs of this type were shown alongside Beaucerons and Briards in 1863.
An early breed standard was drafted in 1922, and the breed received definitive recognition in France in 1925.
Its rough eyebrows, beard, and moustache are important parts of its characteristic rustic expression.
The FCI standard describes a coat that is harsh and semi-long, with a fine, dense undercoat.
The breed's name refers to its traditional association with the Picardy region, although its exact historical origin is uncertain.

faq.question: Where does the Berger Picard come from?
faq.answer: The Berger Picard comes from France and is traditionally associated with the Picardy region in the north. Its precise historical origin is uncertain because similar rough-coated sheepdogs were found across north-western Europe.

faq.question: What was the Berger Picard bred for?
faq.answer: It was developed as a working sheepdog used to drive and protect flocks. It also served as a farm and home guardian.

faq.question: How tall is a Berger Picard?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 60–65 cm for males and 55–60 cm for females, with a stated tolerance of 1 cm.

faq.question: How much does a Berger Picard weigh?
faq.answer: The FCI standard used for this record does not specify a weight range, so a breed-standard weight is not recorded.

faq.question: What colours does a Berger Picard come in?
faq.answer: The FCI standard lists fawn, fawn with a dark overlay, fawn brindle, and grey that generally remains dark. Large white patches are not accepted under the standard.

faq.question: How long does a Berger Picard live?
faq.answer: A commonly reported life expectancy is 12–13 years. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, diet, and care.

faq.question: Does the Berger Picard need a lot of exercise?
faq.answer: Yes. It is an active working sheepdog with good stamina. Most healthy adults benefit from daily walks, structured activity, and mental enrichment. The right amount depends on age, health, and fitness.

faq.question: Is the Berger Picard easy to groom?
faq.answer: Its rough double coat is relatively low-maintenance compared with many long-coated breeds. Regular brushing is useful, with more frequent attention during seasonal shedding.

faq.question: Is the Berger Picard good with children?
faq.answer: The breed standard describes the Picard as a family dog that enjoys close contact with children. As with any dog, interactions should be supervised, children should be taught safe handling, and suitability depends on the individual dog's temperament and upbringing.

faq.question: What health tests should Berger Picard breeders consider?
faq.answer: Breed-club guidance recommends hip evaluation and an ophthalmologist examination. It also discusses cardiac evaluation and additional elbow or thyroid testing. Ask breeders for documented results and discuss the appropriate checks with a veterinarian.

faq.question: Can a Berger Picard live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Living arrangements depend on the individual dog and the owner's ability to provide sufficient exercise, training, and companionship. The breed's high activity needs make daily engagement essential, regardless of home size.

overview.summary: A sturdy, heavy-boned Swiss farm and draft dog distinguished by a lustrous tricolour double coat of jet black, rich rust, and crisp white, combining a composed, affectionate household demeanour with cold-weather working strength.
overview.description: The Bernese Mountain Dog is a large, substantial working dog native to the agricultural midlands and pre-Alpine valleys of the Canton of Bern in Switzerland, and is the sole long-coated member among the four traditional Swiss Sennenhund breeds. Built slightly longer than tall in an approximate 9:10 height-to-length ratio with a chest depth equal to half the withers height, the breed combines heavy bone and broad musculature with surprising agility and a ground-covering slow trot. Its weather-resistant double coat always features a jet-black ground colour paired with symmetrical rust-red markings above the eyes, across the cheeks, on the sides of the chest, and on all four legs, complemented by a white facial blaze, muzzle band, chest cross, feet, and tail tip. Self-assured, attentive, and deeply attached to its family, the breed is patient and gentle indoors while remaining composed and dignified around unfamiliar visitors. Because of its large adult frame, heavy seasonal coat shedding, sensitivity to heat, and comparatively short 7 to 10 year life expectancy linked to hereditary cancers and orthopaedic conditions, prospective owners must prioritize health-screened breeding lines, climate-conscious management, and reward-based early training.
overview.history: Rooted in ancient Alpine farm and droving dogs shaped after Roman military mastiff-type dogs crossed the Swiss Alps more than two millennia ago, the Bernese Mountain Dog evolved as an all-round homestead guardian, dairy-cattle drover, and cart-pulling draft dog across the fertile valleys surrounding Bern. For generations the breed was called the Dürrbächler after the hamlet and country inn of Dürrbach near Riggisberg, where these long-haired tricolour farm dogs were especially concentrated and valued for hauling woven baskets of milk and cheese to local dairies. By the late nineteenth century, industrialization and foreign dog breeds had reduced native populations until Swiss fancier Franz Schertenleib began systematically locating surviving rural stock in 1892. Dogs from these lines were exhibited at shows in 1902, 1904, and 1907, prompting breeders around Burgdorf to establish the Schweizerischer Dürrbach-Klub in November 1907 and codify the breed's defining traits. With guidance from Swiss cynologist Professor Albert Heim, the breed was renamed Berner Sennenhund to group it alongside the other Swiss mountain and cattle dogs, and by the 1910 Burgdorf exhibition local farmers presented 107 dogs. The breed subsequently gained national registration in the United States in 1937 and definitive international recognition on 26 July 1954.
overview.originalPurpose: All-purpose Alpine homestead work in the Canton of Bern, including guarding farmyards, driving dairy cattle to mountain pastures, and pulling loaded milk and cheese carts.
currentRoles: Devoted family and household companion
Recreational and competitive carting and draft work
Obedience, rally, and canine good citizen competition
Tracking, nosework, and search-and-rescue support
Herding trials and outdoor hiking or backpacking companion
Therapy and community-visitation work for calm, well-trained adults

physical.coatType: Thick, weather-resistant double coat consisting of a moderately long, lustrous outer coat and a dense, woolly undercoat.
physical.coatLength: Long, straight to slightly wavy with a bright natural sheen; never distinctly curly or short-coated.
coatColors: Jet-black ground coat covering the head, neck, back, flanks, tail, and upper limbs

Rich rust-red (tan) markings positioned above each eye, on the cheeks reaching to the corners of the mouth, on both sides of the chest, on all four legs between the black upper limb and the feet, and beneath the tail

Clean, symmetrical white markings forming a facial blaze that widens into a muzzle band, an unbroken white throat and chest patch (often shaped like an inverted cross), and preferred white feet (not extending above the pasterns) and white tail tip
physical.sheddingLevel: High year-round shedding, with heavy twice-yearly seasonal coat blows.
physical.droolingLevel: Low to moderate; the breed is dry-mouthed with close-fitting black lips and only slightly developed flews, so heavy drooling is uncommon compared with loose-lipped giant breeds.
distinctiveFeatures: Sturdy, heavy-boned working frame built in a compact 9:10 height-to-body-length ratio rather than an elongated silhouette
Deep, broad chest reaching to the elbows, ideally measuring half of the dog's height at the withers (2:1 ratio)
Striking tricolour coat with a mandatory jet-black ground colour, rich rust-red points, and symmetrical crisp white markings
Distinctive rust spots above each dark brown, almond-shaped eye and a white chest marking that frequently forms an inverted cross
Broad, slightly rounded skull with a gentle frontal furrow, a well-defined but unexaggerated stop, and a straight, strong muzzle
Close-fitting, dry-mouthed black lips with minimal flew development and a complete, strong scissor bite
Medium-sized, high-set triangular ears with gently rounded tips that lie flat against the cheeks in repose and pivot forward when alert
Heavily furred, bushy tail reaching at least to the hock joint, carried hanging straight down at rest and level with or slightly above the back in motion

traits: Self-confident, steady, and fearless in everyday surroundings
Deeply affectionate, loyal, and people-oriented with family members
Patient and gentle around children when properly socialized and supervised
Alert and watchful around the home without unprovoked sharpness
Placid, composed, and often dignified or aloof toward unfamiliar people
Biddable and eager to please during reward-based training
Sensitive to harsh verbal or physical corrections
Sociable and generally tolerant alongside other household dogs

exercise.level: Moderate. Adult dogs thrive on at least 30 to 60 minutes of steady daily outdoor activity paired with family interaction, while juvenile dogs require carefully moderated, low-impact movement until their growth plates close.
activities: Brisk daily neighbourhood or woodland walks during cool hours
Recreational carting and draft pulling once skeletal maturity is complete
Day hikes and camping trips in cool or temperate weather
Scent-tracking, nosework games, and outdoor exploration
Reward-based obedience, rally, and low-impact agility exercises
Controlled off-leash romps in securely fenced areas

grooming.level: High shedding maintenance with routine weekly coat care.
grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly with a slicker brush and long-toothed metal comb at least once or twice weekly—and daily during spring and autumn coat blows—focusing on the dense feathering behind the ears, under the elbows, along the breeches, and in the tail.
grooming.bathing: Bathe every 6 to 8 weeks or when soiled using a gentle canine shampoo, rinsing completely and drying the thick undercoat down to the skin to prevent trapped moisture and hot spots.
notes: Plan for substantial household hair year-round and heavy tufts of undercoat during twice-yearly seasonal moults.
Never shave the double coat, which insulates the skin and regulates body temperature; keep the dog in its natural coat with only neatening around the feet if needed.
Inspect the skin carefully while brushing for mats, ticks, localized moisture dermatitis, or subcutaneous masses.
Keep nails trimmed short so the round, compact feet maintain proper posture and traction.
Check and gently clean the interior of the pendant ears weekly to prevent wax accumulation or otitis.
Brush the teeth several times weekly with enzymatic canine toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Because individuals are intelligent and eager to please their handlers yet emotionally sensitive and physically powerful as adults, early, gentle, reward-based guidance is essential.
tips: Begin puppy kindergarten, loose-leash walking, and impulse-control exercises early before the dog reaches 80 to 115 lb.
Rely on positive reinforcement—food rewards, praise, and play—because sensitive individuals shut down under harsh corrections.
Teach polite four-on-the-floor greetings early so an enthusiastic adolescent does not accidentally knock over children or visitors.
Practice cooperative husbandry handling from puppyhood, including table brushing, paw inspection, ear cleaning, and nail trimming.
Channel the breed's natural working heritage into structured tasks such as carrying a light pack, carting, rally, or scent games.
Build gradual independence with calm crate or mat-settle routines to prevent isolation distress.
training.socialization: Provide calm, well-structured exposure during puppyhood to varied people, friendly dogs, household noises, grooming equipment, and veterinary clinics. Because mature adults naturally remain somewhat aloof or reserved toward strangers, steady positive experiences help ensure confident, relaxed composure in public.

climates: Well adapted to cold, snowy, and temperate mountain or northern climates thanks to its heavy double coat.
Poorly suited to prolonged high heat and humidity; in warm weather, restrict walks to dawn or dusk and provide air-conditioned indoor quarters.
Always supply shade, cool drinking water, and breathable resting surfaces, and watch closely for heavy panting or heat exhaustion.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Deeply bonded to its human household, the breed thrives when living indoors with its family and can develop boredom or separation distress if regularly left isolated for long workdays.

nutrition.dietType: A complete, balanced canine diet formulated for large-breed life stages, with controlled energy, calcium, and phosphorus levels during puppyhood to support steady skeletal development.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a large-breed puppy formula divided into 3 measured meals daily up to 6 months of age, then transition to 2 meals daily while keeping growth steady and lean.
feedingFrequency.adult: Serve 2 measured meals per day rather than one large meal to support digestive comfort and help reduce gastric dilatation-volvulus risk.
feedingFrequency.senior: Provide 2 measured daily meals tailored to senior energy requirements, joint mobility, and kidney or metabolic health under veterinary supervision.

nutrition.guidelines: Weigh or measure daily rations to keep the dog lean and protect the hips, elbows, and stifles from excess mechanical load. Avoid high-calorie diets or unprescribed calcium supplements in growing puppies, which accelerate growth and increase developmental joint risk. Withhold vigorous running or rough play for at least 1 hour before and after meals, and discourage rapid gulping of food or large volumes of water. Because food sensitivities and inflammatory bowel conditions occur in some family lines, transition between diets gradually over 7 to 10 days.
considerations: Deduct training treats from the daily calorie allowance to prevent gradual weight gain.
Monitor body condition score monthly—the ribs should be palpable beneath the thick coat without a heavy fat layer, and the waist should remain visible from above.
Discuss specialized diets or elimination trials with a veterinarian if chronic soft stools, ear irritation, or skin itching develop.
Keep fresh water accessible at all times and store human foods toxic to dogs—such as chocolate, grapes, raisins, xylitol, and onions—securely out of reach.
nutrition.note: General nutritional guidance only; consult a veterinarian for individualized calorie targets, growth curves, or therapeutic diets.

health.overview: The Bernese Mountain Dog has a comparatively short average lifespan of 7 to 10 years, shaped primarily by a strong hereditary predisposition to aggressive cancers—most notably histiocytic sarcoma—as well as orthopaedic disorders and degenerative myelopathy. Historical breed-wide mortality surveys have attributed roughly two-thirds of deaths in the breed to cancer. Responsible breeders participate in open-registry health tracking across full litters and screen breeding stock for hip and elbow dysplasia, inherited eye and heart conditions, both known SOD1 degenerative myelopathy mutations, von Willebrand disease, thyroid function, and polygenic histiocytic sarcoma risk.
commonConditions: Histiocytic sarcoma (malignant histiocytosis, the most prevalent hereditary cancer in the breed) as well as mast cell tumours, lymphoma, and hemangiosarcoma
Hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia (including fragmented coronoid process, ununited anconeal process, and osteochondritis dissecans)
Degenerative myelopathy associated with two distinct SOD1 mutations: the common Exon 2 variant (c.118G>A) and a breed-specific Exon 1 variant (c.52A>T)
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), a sudden, life-threatening stomach torsion emergency in deep-chested dogs
Hereditary eye disorders including progressive retinal atrophy (PRA), cataracts, entropion, and ectropion
Sub-aortic stenosis (SAS) and other congenital or acquired cardiac disorders
Von Willebrand disease Type I (an autosomal recessive bleeding disorder)
Autoimmune hypothyroidism, steroid-responsive aseptic meningitis in juvenile dogs (typically 3 to 12 months old), panosteitis in growing dogs, and food allergies or inflammatory bowel disease
preventiveCare: Select puppies from breeders who openly record complete vertical-pedigree health results—including littermates—for hips, elbows, eyes, heart, degenerative myelopathy, and longevity.
Maintain a lean body weight and avoid forced running, jumping, or repetitive stair climbing until skeletal growth plates close.
Learn the warning signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus—distended abdomen, unproductive retching, pacing, salivation, and pale gums—and discuss prophylactic gastropexy with a veterinarian.
Perform regular hands-on checks during grooming for cutaneous or subcutaneous lumps, swollen lymph nodes, pale mucous membranes, unexplained weight loss, or lethargy.
Assess clotting status or verify von Willebrand disease DNA test status prior to surgical procedures.
Schedule biannual or annual veterinary physical examinations, routine dental care, and year-round parasite prevention.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip evaluation for hip dysplasia
Radiographic elbow evaluation for elbow dysplasia
Board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination (first exam by 12 months of age, with periodic re-evaluation)
Veterinary cardiology evaluation for sub-aortic stenosis and other heart conditions
DNA testing for both canine degenerative myelopathy variants (SOD1 Exon 2 c.118G>A and the Bernese-specific Exon 1 c.52A>T mutation)
Additional targeted screening such as von Willebrand disease Type I DNA testing, autoimmune thyroid profiling, or polygenic histiocytic sarcoma risk testing
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times per week with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule professional veterinary dental assessments to prevent periodontal disease.
health.earCare: Inspect the triangular hanging ears weekly for redness, waxy build-up, odour, or head shaking, and dry the ear flaps thoroughly after swimming or bathing.
health.skinCare: Part the dense double coat regularly to check the skin for hot spots, allergic irritation, external parasites, or nodular mast-cell and histiocytic masses.

idealFor: Families and households in cool or temperate climates seeking a devoted, gentle indoor-outdoor companion
Owners who enjoy daily walks, hiking, camping, or recreational carting and draft activities
People willing to commit to frequent brushing, heavy seasonal shedding cleanup, and proactive veterinary care
Handlers who use patient, reward-based training and include their dog closely in everyday family life
notIdealFor: Residents of small apartments or homes without convenient outdoor access for a large 80 to 115 lb dog
Households in hot, humid climates unable to provide reliable air conditioning and careful heat management
People who dislike loose dog hair in the home or want a low-maintenance coat
Owners who are away from home for long workdays and cannot provide regular companionship
Prospective buyers unprepared for the emotional and financial realities of a 7 to 10 year average lifespan and elevated cancer risk

funFacts: Before being renamed to match the other Swiss mountain breeds, the dog was locally called the Dürrbächler after a hamlet and country inn near Riggisberg in the Canton of Bern.
Among the four traditional Swiss Sennenhund breeds—the Greater Swiss Mountain Dog, Appenzeller Sennenhund, Entlebucher Mountain Dog, and Bernese Mountain Dog—it is the only variety with a long coat.
Swiss dairy farmers historically hitched these dogs in pairs or singles to small carts to haul heavy milk churns and wheels of cheese from Alpine pastures to village creameries.
The distinct rust-red spots above each dark brown eye gave rise to traditional Swiss folklore describing these dogs as having 'four eyes' that allowed them to spot intruders even in the dark.
At a milestone specialty show held in Burgdorf, Switzerland, in 1910—just three years after enthusiasts organized in 1907 to preserve the breed—local farmers exhibited 107 dogs.

Genetic studies show that the breed carries two separate SOD1 mutations linked to degenerative myelopathy: the widespread canine Exon 2 variant and a rare Exon 1 mutation (c.52A>T) found almost exclusively in Bernese Mountain Dogs.

faq.question: Where did the Bernese Mountain Dog originate and what was its original job?
faq.answer: The breed developed in the pre-Alpine valleys and farming midlands around Bern, Switzerland—particularly near Burgdorf and the hamlet of Dürrbach—where farmers used it to guard homesteads, drive dairy cattle, and pull carts loaded with milk and cheese.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Bernese Mountain Dog?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 64 to 70 cm at the withers (with an ideal height of 66 to 68 cm) and weigh 80 to 115 lb. Adult females stand 58 to 66 cm at the withers (with an ideal height of 60 to 63 cm) and weigh 70 to 95 lb.

faq.question: What coat colours and markings are accepted in the Bernese Mountain Dog?
faq.answer: Every purebred individual has a tricolour coat with a jet-black ground colour, rich rust-red markings above the eyes, on the cheeks, on both sides of the chest, on all four legs, and under the tail, plus symmetrical crisp white markings on the blaze, muzzle band, throat and chest, feet, and tail tip. Any ground colour other than black is a disqualification.

faq.question: What is the typical lifespan of a Bernese Mountain Dog?
faq.answer: The expected lifespan is 7 to 10 years, summarized in an popular Swiss and English breed adage: 'Three years a young dog, three years a good dog, and three years an old dog—anything more is a gift.' Hereditary cancers, particularly histiocytic sarcoma, are the primary reason for this shorter longevity.

faq.question: Does a Bernese Mountain Dog drool or shed heavily?
faq.answer: The breed sheds heavily throughout the year and blows its dense undercoat twice annually, requiring weekly brushing and daily grooming during seasonal moults. However, because it has a dry-mouthed lip structure with close-fitting flews, it drools far less than many loose-lipped giant breeds.

faq.question: Are Bernese Mountain Dogs good with children and other pets?
faq.answer: Yes, well-socialized adults are typically affectionate, patient, and gentle with children and friendly toward other household dogs. Because a mature dog weighs 70 to 115 lb, adults should always supervise interactions around toddlers so an exuberant dog does not accidentally bump them over.

faq.question: Which health screenings should prospective buyers look for when choosing a puppy?
faq.answer: Look for parents and litter relatives tested for hip and elbow dysplasia, veterinary ophthalmologist eye clearance, cardiac evaluation, and DNA testing for both SOD1 degenerative myelopathy mutations (Exon 2 c.118G>A and Exon 1 c.52A>T), along with optional testing for von Willebrand disease Type I, thyroid function, or polygenic histiocytic sarcoma risk.

faq.question: Can a Bernese Mountain Dog live comfortably in warm weather or an apartment?
faq.answer: Its heavy, black-dominated double coat retains heat, making hot or humid climates challenging unless the dog lives in an air-conditioned home and exercises only during cool morning or evening hours. Because of its large size and working heritage, it is much better suited to a house with a securely fenced yard than a compact apartment.

overview.summary: A rugged, versatile American homestead and treeing dog prized for endurance, scenting and baying ability, livestock handling, and steadfast loyalty to its family.
overview.description: Built for demanding field work rather than ring glitz, the Black Mouth Cur is a medium-to-large, squarely proportioned athlete with a deep chest, powerful hindquarters, and long enough legs to cover rough ground effortlessly. The head is broad and flat-skulled with muscular cheeks, high-set drop ears, and a strong muzzle whose lips and oral mucosa—apart from the tongue—commonly carry dark slate-to-black pigment. The tight, weather-resistant short coat ranges from yellow, fawn, buckskin, and red to brown, black, brindle, and paler dilute shades, with or without a dark facial mask. Because generations of rural families bred these dogs for regional hunting and stock tasks rather than uniform show appearance, size and build vary noticeably across established working strains.
overview.history: The Black Mouth Cur took shape across the American South from multi-purpose herding, scenting, and catch dogs brought by Irish, Scottish, English, and French settlers. Whether the earliest populations coalesced in the hills of Tennessee or the piney woods of southern Mississippi and Alabama remains debated, as frontier families maintained private working strains for well over a century before formal studbooks existed. Settlers moving westward carried these dogs through Kentucky, Missouri, North Carolina, and Florida into the Big Thicket of Southeast Texas, relying on them to drive unruly cattle and hogs, tree squirrels and raccoons, bay wild boar and bear, and guard isolated cabins. Distinct regional lineages—including Mississippi treeing stock recorded from the 1960s, Alabama red homestead curs documented in the 1940s, and heavier Texas cattle lines—preserved those traits into the modern era. A dedicated breeders' association organised in 1987 to standardise pedigree records, leading to formal national working-registry recognition on 1 November 1998.
overview.originalPurpose: All-around frontier homestead work, including baying and treeing big and small game, gathering range cattle and feral hogs, and protecting family members and property.
currentRoles: Treeing and baying hunting dog for squirrel, raccoon, feral hog, bear, and mountain lion
Ranch and farm stock dog for gathering and penning cattle and hogs
Homestead, livestock, and property guardian
Search-and-rescue, tracking, and scent-detection partner
Active outdoor companion for hiking, trail running, agility, and weight-pulling sports

exercise.level: high
activities: Brisk long-distance hikes, trail runs, and cross-country excursions over varied terrain
Scent-tracking trails, nosework puzzles, and treeing or baying field drills
Structured livestock-handling tasks, agility courses, or weight-pull conditioning
Vigorous fetch, tug, and impulse-control retrieval sessions in a securely fenced paddock
Long-line recall practice and problem-solving enrichment games

grooming.brushing: Go over the short coat once or twice a week with a rubber curry brush or hound glove to lift loose dead hairs, distribute skin oils, and spot ticks or briars after field outings.
grooming.bathing: Bathe every few months or whenever the dog gets muddy from outdoor work, using a gentle, dog-specific cleanser that preserves natural coat oils.
notes: Inspect the drop ears weekly for trapped moisture, wax buildup, or plant awns, wiping the outer flap with a vet-approved ear cleanser.
Examine the webbed toes, nail beds, dewclaws, and thick paw pads after rough-terrain runs for thorns, cuts, or split nails.
Keep nails trimmed short so the feet remain compact and well-arched.
Brush the teeth several times per week using enzymatic canine toothpaste.

training.difficulty: moderate
tips: Use calm, reward-based reinforcement and clear boundaries; harsh physical corrections can erode trust and trigger defensive pushback in a sensitive working cur.
Channel the dog's natural scenting and working drive into purposeful jobs such as tracking, nosework, or structured retrieval.
Establish a reliable emergency recall on a long line before allowing off-leash freedom, as strong prey and treeing instincts can override casual calls.
Teach clear doorstep manners so this naturally territorial guardian learns to look to its handler when guests arrive.
Keep training sessions brisk, varied, and task-oriented to prevent boredom.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and steadily to welcoming visitors, well-mannered dogs, livestock, varied noises, and unfamiliar settings so their natural protective instincts mature into calm discernment rather than reactivity.

climates: Well adapted to warm, humid southern climates thanks to its short, close-lying coat
Tolerates temperate four-season regions when given insulated indoor sleeping quarters during freezing or wet weather
Requires shade, abundant drinking water, and early-morning or evening work schedules during extreme summer heat
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Bonds closely with its people and tolerates only moderate solo stretches; dogs left isolated all day without vigorous prior exercise and mental work can become vocal or destructive.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete canine diet formulated for active medium-to-large working dogs, adjusted to seasonal workload, age, and body condition.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed three to four measured meals daily during rapid growth, transitioning to twice-daily feeding around six months of age.
feedingFrequency.adult: Provide two measured meals per day—morning and evening—rather than free-feeding.
feedingFrequency.senior: Feed two easily digestible meals daily tailored to reduced caloric expenditure and joint support needs.

nutrition.guidelines: Portion daily rations to maintain a lean, muscular build—where ribs are easily felt under a light layer of flesh and a clear waist tuck is visible—increasing caloric density during heavy hunting or ranching seasons.
considerations: Withhold heavy meals for at least an hour before and after intense running or baying work to reduce the risk of gastric distress or bloat in deep-chested dogs.
Ensure constant access to clean water, especially when working in warm, humid brush country.
Include training treats within the total daily calorie budget so the dog stays in hard working condition.
Consult a veterinarian before adding joint supplements or high-fat performance rations.
nutrition.note: Nutritional guidance reflects general veterinary management for athletic, deep-chested working dogs rather than a breed-specific clinical trial.

health.overview: Selected for generations on tough frontier homesteads for endurance and functional soundness, the Black Mouth Cur is generally a hardy, long-lived working breed with an expected lifespan of 12 to 16 years. No breed-specific inherited disorder registry mandate has been established, though active working dogs can experience orthopedic wear, ear inflammation, and occasional idiopathic conditions seen across medium-to-large hounds and curs.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia (developmental laxity of the hip joint that can lead to hind-limb stiffness and secondary osteoarthritis, particularly in heavier stock-working lines)
Otitis externa (outer ear canal inflammation or infection promoted by high-set drop ears trapping moisture, wax, or plant debris during field and water work)
Idiopathic epilepsy (recurrent neurological seizures without a structural brain lesion, occasionally observed in working cur populations)
Field-related orthopedic and skin trauma (cruciate ligament strain, pad abrasions, interdigital foreign bodies, and tick-borne exposures from dense brush)
preventiveCare: Maintain year-round flea, tick, heartworm, and intestinal parasite prophylaxis, particularly for dogs working in wooded or swampy terrain.
Inspect and dry the drop ears after water work or humid field outings to prevent moisture accumulation.
Keep the dog in lean, hard muscular condition to minimise mechanical stress on hips, stifles, and hocks.
Check skin, paw pads, interdigital webbing, and eyes after brush hunting for ticks, foxtails, and scratches.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip and elbow evaluation prior to breeding or heavy athletic conditioning
Routine otoscopic and ophthalmic examinations during annual veterinary wellness visits
Baseline complete blood count, serum chemistry, and thyroid panel as part of adult and senior health monitoring
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times weekly with canine toothpaste and schedule professional veterinary dental cleanings as needed to maintain healthy gums and dentition.
health.earCare: Check the drop ears weekly and after brush or water excursions; clean gently with a pH-balanced veterinary ear solution and seek prompt care if redness or odour develops.
health.skinCare: Part and inspect the short coat after outdoor work to remove ticks, burrs, or briars, and treat minor field abrasions promptly.

idealFor: Experienced, active households that spend substantial time outdoors hiking, running, hunting, or working stock
Rural and semi-rural homeowners with securely fenced acreage who value an alert, devoted family guardian
Handlers interested in scent work, tracking, search-and-rescue, agility, or weight pulling
notIdealFor: Apartment dwellers or sedentary households unable to provide at least 90 minutes of vigorous daily activity
Owners who are away from home for long workdays without outdoor relief or mental stimulation for their dog
Novice handlers unprepared to socialise and guide a strong-willed, territorial working breed

funFacts: The breed's name comes from the dark slate-to-black pigment lining the lips, gums, and roof of the mouth—as well as the dark facial mask many individuals wear—though dilute-coated dogs lack black hair and dark mouth pigment.

Rather than descending from a single kennel club studbook, the breed was preserved for over a century by southern farm families who passed down distinct regional lines named after their breeders or states, such as the Mississippi treeing line, the Alabama red line, and Texas cattle strains.

In Fred Gipson's classic 1956 frontier novel Old Yeller, the heroic yellow stray working dog that fends off wild hogs, a bear, and a rabid wolf in post-Civil War Texas was modelled on the traditional southern yellow Black Mouth Cur.

On the hunting trail, these curs are prized for running silent or only semi-open so they do not spook game prematurely, before switching to a resonant chop or slight yodel once quarry is bayed or treed.
Many individuals have partially webbed toes that help them power through muddy river bottoms, swamps, and marshy southern hunting grounds.

faq.question: Does every Black Mouth Cur have a black muzzle mask and dark gums?
faq.answer: Most individuals display dark pigmentation on the lips and inside the mouth (excluding the tongue) and often wear a melanistic facial mask, but dilute red or yellow dogs have pale nails, green or amber-brown eyes, and lighter mouth pigment without black hairs.

faq.question: Where did the Black Mouth Cur originate?
faq.answer: The breed developed in the American South, with competing historical accounts pointing to the mountains of Tennessee, southern Mississippi, or Alabama before settlers carried the dogs across the Southeast and into Texas.

faq.question: How much daily exercise does a Black Mouth Cur require?
faq.answer: Adult dogs generally need around 90 minutes or more of purposeful daily physical and mental activity, such as brisk hiking, running, scent games, or ranch chores, rather than a brief neighbourhood stroll.

faq.question: Are Black Mouth Curs good family dogs with children?
faq.answer: Yes, when raised with proper socialisation and clear household boundaries, they are famously affectionate, gentle, and fiercely protective toward the children in their own family, though interactions with visiting youngsters should always be supervised.

faq.question: Can a Black Mouth Cur live comfortably in an apartment?
faq.answer: Apartment living is rarely a good fit. Their high stamina, territorial watchdog instincts, and need for room to run make them much better suited to a house with a securely fenced yard or rural acreage.

faq.question: Why do size and appearance vary so much between individual Black Mouth Curs?
faq.answer: Because rural hunters and ranchers selected breeding stock for specific regional jobs—such as treeing squirrels in Mississippi versus catching feral hogs or working range cattle in Texas—different bloodlines range from compact 18 kg tree dogs to powerful 43 kg stock curs.

overview.summary: The Black Norwegian Elkhound is a compact, athletic Nordic hunting Spitz from Norway. Its glossy black coat, upright pointed ears and tightly curled tail give it a distinctive outline. Bred to work with a handler while tracking large game, it is energetic, alert and courageous, and benefits from regular outdoor activity, consistent training and a close relationship with its household.
overview.description: Squarely built and agile, the Black Norwegian Elkhound has a wedge-shaped head, erect pointed ears, a firm neck and a short, tightly curled tail carried over the back. Its dense coat lies close to the body and is predominantly glossy black, with a soft black undercoat; a little white on the chest and feet is permitted by the breed standard. The breed was developed for Nordic hunting, particularly work on elk and deer in which the dog stays connected to its handler. It is a purposeful working dog rather than a breed whose needs are met by companionship alone. Daily walks, opportunities to use its nose, thoughtful training and safe outdoor management help support its physical and mental well-being.
overview.history: The Black Norwegian Elkhound, known in Norway as Norsk Elghund Sort, developed from local Spitz-type dogs in the border regions between Norway and Sweden. It has been maintained as a distinct breed since the mid-nineteenth century. Historically used for hunting elk and bear, it became especially valued for working on a lead with the handler close by. During the early twentieth century, breeding attention shifted more strongly toward the Grey Norwegian Elkhound, and the black variety became scarce. Dedicated breeders later helped rebuild its population while preserving its characteristic appearance and hunting ability.

grooming.brushing: Brush regularly with a suitable dog brush to remove loose hair and debris. Increase brushing when the individual dog sheds more heavily.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-safe shampoo. Rinse thoroughly and dry the coat well; avoid unnecessary clipping of the natural coat.

Inspect the ears regularly for dirt, redness or odour.

tips: Use reward-based training and short, purposeful sessions.
Begin recall and leash training early, practising in gradually more distracting environments.
Use secure areas for off-leash exercise unless the individual dog is reliably safe in the setting.
Provide scent games and tracking tasks that engage the dog's working instincts.
Reward calm attention and voluntary check-ins with the handler.
Practise settling and impulse control as well as active skills.

Avoid strenuous activity during peak heat and adapt exercise to the individual dog.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: A reliable breed-specific duration was not established. Build alone time gradually and provide adequate exercise, companionship and enrichment rather than routinely leaving the dog alone for long periods.

nutrition.guidelines: Use the food manufacturer's feeding guidance as a starting point, then adjust portions according to body condition, activity and veterinary advice. Keep fresh water available and review feeding needs as the dog matures or its workload changes.
considerations: Adjust food intake to the dog's activity and body condition rather than assuming all dogs need the same portions.
Monitor body condition during periods of increased hunting or outdoor exercise.
Introduce diet changes gradually unless a veterinarian advises otherwise.
Discuss persistent digestive issues, unexplained weight changes or supplements with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Norwegian breeding programme includes screening for hip dysplasia, hereditary glaucoma and hereditary ataxia. It also sets breeding rules concerning epilepsy and recommends considering regular eye examinations. These are screening priorities and reported health topics, not evidence that an individual dog will develop a condition. Ask for documented test results and discuss them with a veterinarian familiar with the breed.

health.earCare: Inspect the ears routinely for dirt, redness, discharge or odour. Use a dog-safe cleaner only when needed and ask a veterinarian about persistent irritation.
health.skinCare: Check the skin and coat after outdoor activity, particularly after hunting or travelling through dense vegetation. Seek veterinary advice for wounds, persistent itching, redness or hair loss.

It has been maintained as a distinct breed since the mid-nineteenth century.
It is especially associated with hunting while working closely with its handler.
The breed's standard describes a glossy black coat and allows a small amount of white on the chest and feet.
The Black and Grey Norwegian Elkhounds are separate FCI-recognised breeds with different standards.

faq.question: Where does the Black Norwegian Elkhound come from?
faq.answer: The breed comes from Norway and developed from local Spitz-type dogs in the border regions between Norway and Sweden. It has been maintained as a distinct breed since the mid-nineteenth century.

faq.question: What was the Black Norwegian Elkhound bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed for hunting large game, especially elk and deer. Its traditional work places importance on tracking and cooperation with the handler.

faq.question: How tall is a Black Norwegian Elkhound?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 46–49 cm for males, with an ideal height of 47 cm. For females it gives 43–46 cm, with an ideal height of 44 cm.

faq.question: How much does a Black Norwegian Elkhound weigh?
faq.answer: The FCI standard does not specify a weight range. Norwegian breed information gives approximate figures of around 15 kg for males and 13 kg for females; these are reference figures rather than an official weight range.

faq.question: What colour is the Black Norwegian Elkhound?
faq.answer: Its coat is predominantly glossy black, with a soft black undercoat. The breed standard allows a small amount of white on the chest and feet.

faq.question: How much exercise does it need?
faq.answer: It needs regular outdoor exercise and activities that use its nose and working instincts. The exact daily amount depends on the dog's age, health, fitness and workload.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip status and results of DNA testing for hereditary glaucoma and hereditary ataxia. Discuss eye examinations and family history of epilepsy with the breeder and your veterinarian.

faq.question: Is the Black Norwegian Elkhound the same as the Grey Norwegian Elkhound?
faq.answer: No. They are separate recognised breeds. The black variety has a predominantly glossy black coat, while the grey variety has its own standard and coat description.

overview.summary: A massive, noble, and powerfully built scent hound originating from the Ardennes of Belgium, world-renowned for its unmatched cold-trail scenting ability, long velvety curling ears, abundant head and neck folds, and gentle, sensitive nature at home.
overview.description: The Bloodhound—officially known in continental Europe as the Chien de Saint-Hubert and historically celebrated as the 'Sleuth Hound'—is the most powerful and substantial of all scent hounds. Built on a harmonious rectangular outline (roughly a 10:9 ratio of body length to withers height, with chest depth equal to half the withers height), it combines heavy, round bone and strong muscle with a solemn, dignified bearing and a free, elastic, slightly rolling trot capable of covering ground effortlessly for hours. Its majestic head—measuring 30 cm (12 inches) or more in adult males and 28 cm (11 inches) or more in females—is narrow relative to its length, crowned by a pronounced occipital peak, and draped in thin, supple skin that falls into deep forehead and cheek ridges and a pronounced double dewlap when the nose is lowered to the ground. Extremely long, low-set, velvety ears curl inward and backward past the tip of the nose, working alongside the loose facial folds to funnel and trap scent particles. Off duty, the Bloodhound is a gentle, placid, and affectionate companion that gets along well with people and other dogs, yet on a trail it becomes single-minded and unstoppable. Prospective owners must be prepared for heavy drooling (including 15-foot 'slobber missiles' when the dog shakes its head), a resonant baying voice, a high physical fence, leashed exercise, and daily cleaning of the ears and facial folds.
overview.history: One of the oldest scent-hunting breeds, the modern Bloodhound traces its primary lineage to the Ardennes forest region of Belgium, where black and black-and-tan pack hounds were bred from the seventh century onward by the monk Hubert (later Bishop of Liège and canonised as Saint Hubert, the patron saint of hunters) and maintained for centuries by monks at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert to hunt wild boar and stag. In 1066, William the Conqueror brought Saint-Hubert hounds—alongside white hounds of similar type known as Talbots—to England, where the breed was recorded by around 1300 and acquired the English name 'Bloodhound', derived from 'blooded hound' (meaning a hound of pure, aristocratic breeding kept carefully recorded) or from its skill in tracking wounded, bleeding game. Along the Anglo-Scottish border through the sixteenth century, these hounds were known as 'sleuth hounds' and were used to track cattle raiders ('reivers'), with law dictating that anyone who barred a sleuth hound on a hot trail was deemed an accomplice. By the seventeenth century, scientist Robert Boyle documented a Bloodhound trailing a quarry seven miles along busy thoroughfares to an upstairs room, and in 1805 the Thrapston Association for the Prevention of Felons in England recorded the first organized law-enforcement use of a Bloodhound to catch poachers and thieves. Exported to North America by the nineteenth century (where the breed was formally registered in 1885 and where trailing evidence from a proven Bloodhound is accepted in courts of law, though historical records also note its misuse in the antebellum American South), North American and continental lines later helped replenish British stock after the breed nearly died out in Britain during the Second World War.
overview.originalPurpose: Trailing large game (such as wild boar and deer) and tracking wounded animals as a leash hound, as well as long-distance human scent-trailing (mantrailing) in law-enforcement and search-and-rescue operations.
currentRoles: Law-enforcement, search-and-rescue, and forensic human mantrailing dog
Leash hound for tracking wounded game and blood-scenting trials
Competitive mantrailing, tracking, and scent-work participant
Devoted family and household companion
Active leashed hiking and walking partner

physical.coatType: Short, dense, close-lying, and weatherproof single coat that is quite harsh on the body, very short, soft, and velvety on the head and ears, and slightly longer and coarser (about 5 cm / 2 inches) along the underside of the tapering tail.
physical.coatLength: Short
coatColors: Black and tan (bicolour with either a predominant black mantle or a more limited dorsal black saddle, sometimes interspersed with lighter or badger-coloured hairs)
Liver and tan (bicolour in mantle or saddle pattern with brown/liver nose and lip pigment, sometimes interspersed with lighter or badger-coloured hairs)

Red (unicolour ranging from light red/blond to deep red; across all three colours, a small amount of white on the forechest, toes/feet, and tip of the tail is permissible, whereas widespread white reaching the wrists/hocks or white patches on the muzzle or blaze are disqualifying faults)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate year-round, with heavier seasonal shedding twice a year in late spring and late autumn.
physical.droolingLevel: High
distinctiveFeatures: Most powerful and massive of all scent hounds, built on a rectangular 10:9 body-length-to-height ratio with a deep, oval chest forming a prominent keel between the forelegs (chest depth equal to half the withers height)

Majestic, narrow, flat-sided head (measuring 3/7 of body length, or at least 30 cm [12 in] in males and 28 cm [11 in] in females) with a very pronounced occipital peak ('cone head'), slight stop, and deep, square-profiled muzzle equal in length to the skull

Abundant, thin, supple skin over the forehead and cheeks that falls into deep pendulous ridges and wrinkles when the head is carried low, blending into long upper lips (hanging about 5 cm below the lower jaw) and a pronounced double dewlap (less marked in females)
Extremely long, thin, velvety ears ('leathers') set at or below eye level, falling in graceful inward- and backward-curling folds that reach well beyond the tip of the nose

Moderate-sized, oval dark brown or hazel eyes (amber to yellow in liver-and-tan or red hounds without a black saddle/mantle) conveying a solemn, wise, and dignified expression; conformation standards emphasize that loose skin and eyelid shape must never obscure vision or allow eyelashes to irritate the cornea
High-set, thick, tapering tail ('stern') furnished with ~5 cm harsher hair underneath and carried high in a graceful sabre/scimitar curve on the move without curling over the back
Elastic, swinging, ground-covering trot with a characteristic slight roll, strong rear drive, and straight, heavy-boned legs ending in compact, well-knuckled cat feet

Adult withers height of 68 cm ideal (64–72 cm with ±4 cm tolerance) for males and 62 cm ideal (58–66 cm with ±4 cm tolerance) for females in international standards—or 63–69 cm (25–27 in, average 66 cm / 26 in) for males and 58–63 cm (23–25 in, average 61 cm / 24 in) in British and American standards—with weights of 46–54 kg (101–119 lbs) for males and 40–48 kg (88–106 lbs) for females internationally (41–50 kg [90–110 lbs] for males and 36–45.5 kg [80–100 lbs] for females in British and American standards, and tall individuals occasionally exceeding 55–60 kg / 120–130+ lbs)

traits: Gentle, placid, and kind-hearted ('nature's gentleman') indoors
Deeply affectionate and strongly bonded to its owner and family
Sociable, courteous, and non-quarrelsome with people, kennelmates, and other dogs
Relentless, single-minded, and independent once locked onto a scent trail
Equally sensitive to praise and correction
Somewhat reserved or shy, yet never aggressive
Stubborn and inclined to test boundaries if not guided with patient consistency
Rarely barks like a guard dog, but communicates with a resonant, melodious bay or howl ('rooooo')
Curious mouth-explorer and counter-surfer capable of reaching standard kitchen tables without lifting its paws

exercise.level: Moderate to high. Despite a laid-back indoor demeanour, the Bloodhound was bred to follow a scent trail for hours and requires daily sustained leashed walks, safe enclosed play, and regular nose-work enrichment.
activities: Long daily walks and hikes on a strong leash and harness where the dog can safely sniff
Mantrailing (human scent trailing), tracking trials, and blood-scenting games
Structured nose work and hidden-scent search games in the yard or home
Supervised play and romping with other dogs in a securely fenced enclosure
Jogging, swimming, or rally/obedience exercises for skeletally mature adult hounds

grooming.brushing: Brush weekly with a rubber grooming mitt, hound glove, or medium-bristle brush to remove dead hair and distribute natural skin oils; increase brushing frequency during spring and autumn coat sheds.
grooming.bathing: Bathe as needed (every few weeks to months, or when smelly) using a mild dog-safe shampoo, rinse thoroughly, and dry all facial, neck, and dewlap folds completely so moisture is never trapped against the skin.
notes: Inspect and wipe the facial wrinkles, lip folds, and neck dewlap daily with a warm damp cloth or pet-safe wipe, then dry thoroughly to prevent moisture, food debris, and skin-fold dermatitis.

Check the long, heavy hanging ears ('leathers') daily—and clean them regularly with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser—because they dip into food and water bowls, sweep the ground, and trap warmth and moisture.
Keep 'slobber cloths' (towels) handy around the house and when travelling: a head shake can fling ropes of saliva 15 feet across furniture, walls, and clothing.
Check the eyes daily for dust, debris, redness, or irritation from eyelid folds.
Trim toenails regularly and inspect the compact cat feet after outdoor walks.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging. Affectionate and capable of remarkable focus in scent work, yet independent-minded, quick to become set in its ways, and deeply sensitive to harsh handling.
tips: Start puppy socialization and basic obedience classes early so polite leash manners and household rules are established before the dog reaches 40 to 54+ kg.

Be firm, patient, and kind, using positive reinforcement (high-value food rewards and warm praise); Bloodhounds are equally sensitive to kindness and correction and will shut down or resist under harsh methods.
Never trust a Bloodhound off-leash in an unenclosed area—even obedience-titled hounds will ignore recall when they strike a compelling scent and have no road or traffic sense.
Enclose yards with a sturdy 5- to 6-foot (1.5–1.8 m) above-ground fence and guard against digging under the fence line.

Do not rely on electronic ('invisible') underground fences: a Bloodhound's high pain threshold, thick loose neck skin, and intense scent drive allow it to charge right through the shock zone and never return.

Dog-proof counters, tables, and rubbish bins: an adult Bloodhound stands tall enough to rest its chin on a 29-inch dining table with all four feet on the floor and is notorious for swallowing non-food items.
Channel the dog's natural nose into mantrailing or tracking games, which build a strong cooperative bond between handler and hound.
training.socialization: Provide early, calm, positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, children, surfaces, and veterinary/grooming handling. Because Bloodhounds are gentle pack hounds that enjoy canine company but are often unaware of their own bulk, supervise interactions with young children (particularly toddlers under 5 years old who can be accidentally knocked over by a wagging tail or playful nudge).

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. As pack-oriented hounds that bond closely with their families, Bloodhounds left isolated alone for long periods often become bored, bay loudly enough to disturb neighbours, or chew furniture and household objects.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality large-breed dog food (commercial or veterinarian-formulated home-prepared diet) matched to life stage (large-breed puppy, adult, or senior), body condition, and workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Several smaller measured meals daily using a large-breed puppy formula to support steady, controlled skeletal growth, adjusted with veterinary guidance.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two to three smaller meals daily rather than a single large meal to help reduce the risk of life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
feedingFrequency.senior: Two to three smaller daily meals tailored to body condition, mobility, dental health, and veterinary advice.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions appropriate for a large, deep-chested hound (typically 4 to 8 cups of dry food daily for an 80- to 110-pound adult depending on calorie density, age, and activity level, confirmed with a veterinarian). Divide the daily ration into two or three smaller meals, avoid elevated food bowls unless specifically directed by a veterinarian, and restrict vigorous exercise for at least an hour before and after mealtimes to help minimize gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV) risk. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times (wiping the ears and flews after drinking).
considerations: Feed a dedicated large-breed puppy diet during growth so bone and joint development proceed at a steady pace without excess weight.
Divide daily food into two or three smaller meals and avoid strenuous exercise immediately before or after eating to reduce bloat (GDV) risk.

Discuss prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking' surgery, often performed during spaying or neutering) with your veterinarian, as epidemiological studies rank the Bloodhound among the breeds at highest risk of GDV.
Keep all non-food objects, socks, rocks, corn cobs, and rubbish strictly out of reach; Bloodhounds are notorious for indiscriminate ingestion leading to gastrointestinal foreign-body obstruction.
Monitor body condition score regularly and deduct training treats from the daily food ration so excess weight does not overload the hips and elbows.
Consult a veterinarian before adding joint supplements (such as omega-3 fatty acids, glucosamine, or chondroitin).
nutrition.note: Exact caloric needs vary widely across individuals ranging from 36 to over 54 kg (80 to 130+ lbs) and between working mantrailing hounds and family companions; establish portion sizes and bloat-prevention routines with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Bloodhound has an average life expectancy of 10 to 12 years, and health priorities centre on risks linked to its large, deep-chested build, heavy bone, abundant skin folds, and long pendulous ears. In both British breed-health surveys and a peer-reviewed UK epidemiological study of 15,881 deceased and 36,006 living pedigree dogs across 165–169 breeds (Evans & Adams, 2010), gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) and cancer were identified as the two leading causes of mortality, with the Bloodhound ranking among the breeds at greatest risk of both GDV mortality and GDV morbidity. Orthopaedic, cardiac, ocular, and neurological screening data are tracked in North American and British health registries: in cumulative North American orthopaedic registry evaluations through December 2014, 25.4% of 2,941 hip evaluations were graded abnormal (72.6% normal), 14.2% of 1,224 elbow evaluations were abnormal (85.3% normal), 0.7% of 732 cardiac evaluations were abnormal (98.1% normal), 2.7% of 150 patellar evaluations were abnormal (97.3% normal), 5.7% of 159 thyroid panels were abnormal with 19.5% equivocal, and among 311 dogs DNA-tested for degenerative myelopathy (SOD1), 49.5% tested clear/normal, 44.1% carriers, and 6.4% genetically at-risk/affected (figures reflecting tested cohorts rather than random population prevalence). Conformation-related concerns include eyelid abnormalities (entropion, ectropion, prolapsed third-eyelid gland ['cherry eye'], and keratoconjunctivitis sicca ['dry eye']), recurrent otitis externa, and skin-fold dermatitis or atopic dermatitis, though careful selective breeding has reduced severe skin and eyelid exaggerations (reflected in the breed's reclassification from Category 3 to Category 2 in the United Kingdom effective 1 January 2025, alongside a reported breed-average inbreeding coefficient of 10.0%).
commonConditions: Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / gastric torsion / bloat) — a sudden, life-threatening emergency in which the stomach distends with gas and twists on its axis; UK epidemiological research (Evans & Adams, 2010) and breed mortality surveys identify the Bloodhound as one of the breeds at highest risk of GDV morbidity and mortality.

Hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia — developmental joint malformations causing osteoarthritic pain and lameness; in North American registry statistics, 25.4% of 2,941 tested Bloodhounds showed hip dysplasia and 14.2% of 1,224 showed elbow dysplasia.

Eyelid and ocular surface disorders — entropion (inward-rolling eyelid causing eyelashes to rub the cornea), ectropion (outward-sagging lower lid exposing the conjunctiva), prolapsed gland of the third eyelid ('cherry eye'), and keratoconjunctivitis sicca ('dry eye') linked to loose facial skin and heavy flews.

Recurrent otitis externa (ear canal infections) — the long, heavy, low-set ears ('leathers') restrict airflow and trap moisture, wax, and debris, predisposing the ear canals to bacterial and yeast overgrowth.

Skin-fold dermatitis (intertrigo), atopic dermatitis, and eczema — trapped moisture, saliva, and friction within the deep forehead, cheek, lip, and neck folds can cause bacterial or yeast skin infections.

Gastrointestinal foreign-body ingestion and obstruction — Bloodhounds are notorious for swallowing non-food objects, rocks, clothing, or household items, frequently requiring emergency veterinary intervention.
Neoplasia (cancer) — identified alongside gastric torsion as one of the two leading causes of death in British breed health surveys, a risk shared across many large and giant breeds.

Degenerative myelopathy (DM) — a late-onset (typically 8+ years) progressive spinal cord neuropathy associated with the SOD1 gene; in North American DNA-testing statistics of 311 Bloodhounds, 44.1% were carriers and 6.4% tested genetically at risk.

Congenital cardiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis (hypothyroidism), and patellar luxation — monitored through pre-breeding cardiac auscultation/echocardiography, thyroid antibody panels, and knee examinations.
preventiveCare: Learn the emergency warning signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV)—distended or tight abdomen, unproductive retching, restlessness, stretching in pain, pale gums, or sudden collapse—and seek immediate emergency veterinary care if suspected.
Feed two to three smaller meals daily rather than one large meal, avoid vigorous exercise before and after eating, and discuss prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking') with your veterinarian.
Inspect and clean the hanging ears and wipe and thoroughly dry the facial, lip, and neck folds daily, especially after drinking, eating, bathing, or swimming.

Verify documented pre-breeding health clearances for both parents before acquiring a puppy, including hip and elbow radiographs, veterinary cardiac evaluation, eye examination, and degenerative myelopathy (SOD1) DNA status (as well as low pedigree inbreeding coefficient).
Keep counters, rubbish bins, laundry, and yard areas clear of swallowable objects to prevent foreign-body intestinal obstructions.
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition and avoid over-exercising or jogging growing puppies before skeletal maturity to protect the hips and elbows.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement; distraction-index hip evaluation is also used as an optional screening tool).
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement).
Cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian—preferably a board-certified veterinary cardiologist or specialist, with echocardiography when indicated (core pre-breeding requirement).

Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist or accredited eye-scheme examiner (recommended in British breeding guidance and optional in North American health certification).
Degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1) DNA test from an approved laboratory (optional pre-breeding test in North American and British health programs).

Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation and laboratory thyroid panel (optional pre-breeding evaluations, alongside permanent microchip or tattoo identification and pedigree inbreeding-coefficient review).
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and schedule periodic veterinary dental assessments. Conformation standards require strong jaws with complete dentition in a regular scissor bite (a pincer/level bite is also tolerated, whereas overshot, undershot, or wry jaws are disqualifying faults).
health.earCare: Inspect the long, velvety, low-set ears daily for redness, foul odour, excess wax, or discharge, and wipe them clean after meals and drinks. Clean the ear canals routinely—and after every bath or swim—using a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser, drying carefully without inserting cotton swabs deep into the canal.
health.skinCare: Check and wipe the facial wrinkles, hanging flews, and double dewlap daily with a damp cloth or pet-safe facial wipe, then dry every fold thoroughly so trapped saliva or water cannot cause skin-fold dermatitis. Monitor the rest of the short coat for parasites, hot spots, or allergic irritation.

idealFor: Active, patient owners and handlers who enjoy mantrailing, tracking, scent work, and long daily leashed hikes
Households with a securely fenced yard (5 to 6 feet high) and ample indoor space for a 40- to 54+ kg hound
People who are relaxed about housekeeping and comfortable with heavy drooling ('slobber cloths') and daily ear and wrinkle care
Families with children (ideally aged 5 and older, with adult supervision) or multi-dog homes seeking a gentle, pack-friendly companion
Owners financially prepared for the food, preventive gastropexy, and veterinary care costs of a large-to-giant breed
notIdealFor: Fastidious or house-proud owners bothered by ropes of drool on walls, ceilings, furniture, and clothing
Apartment dwellers or densely packed urban neighbourhoods sensitive to deep, resonant baying and howling
Owners seeking reliable off-leash recall in unfenced areas or expecting an Electronic/Invisible fence to contain a scent hound
People who want an aggressive property guard dog rather than a friendly, non-quarrelsome pack hound
Sedentary households or homes where the dog is left isolated alone for long workdays

funFacts: The word 'blood' in Bloodhound does not refer to bloodthirstiness: it derives from 'blooded hound', meaning a hound of pure, aristocratic breeding whose lineage was carefully preserved (along with its historic work tracking wounded game).
So legendary is the breed's nose—estimated to contain roughly 250 to 300 million olfactory receptors—that trailing evidence from a proven Bloodhound is admissible in courts of law.

The Bloodhound's long, velvety ears ('leathers') and loose facial wrinkles are functional scent-tracking tools: as the dog lowers its head, the ears sweep scent particles up from the ground while the skin folds trap them near the nostrils.
In 1805, the Thrapston Association for the Prevention of Felons in England recorded the first organized law-enforcement use of a Bloodhound, acquiring a hound to track down poachers and thieves.

Along the Scottish border up to the late sixteenth century, the Bloodhound was known as the 'sleuth hound' (the origin of the modern word 'sleuth' for a detective), and anyone who refused entry to a sleuth hound pursuing a cattle thief was legally considered an accomplice.

In the seventeenth century, pioneering chemist Robert Boyle documented a trial in which a Bloodhound followed a person's scent trail for seven miles along busy footpaths and located the quarry in an upstairs room.

Standing up to 68–72 cm (27+ inches) at the shoulder, an adult male Bloodhound can rest its chin directly on a standard 29-inch dining table and help itself to dinner without lifting a single paw off the floor.
In 2022, a Bloodhound named Trumpet made dog-show history by winning Best in Show at the 146th Westminster Dog Show—the first Bloodhound ever to take the top prize.

faq.question: Where does the Bloodhound originate, and why is it also called the Chien de Saint-Hubert?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the Ardennes region of Belgium, where black and black-and-tan scent hounds were bred from the seventh century onward by the monk Hubert (later Bishop of Liège and canonised as Saint Hubert, patron saint of hunters) and maintained for centuries at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert. In French-speaking Europe and international standards, the breed is still officially named the Chien de Saint-Hubert.

faq.question: Where do the names 'Bloodhound' and 'Sleuth Hound' come from?
faq.answer: After Saint-Hubert hounds were brought to Britain following the Norman Conquest of 1066, their descendants became known as 'blooded hounds'—meaning hounds of pure, aristocratic blood—as well as hounds used to track wounded, bleeding game. In medieval Scotland and northern England, they were called 'sleuth hounds' (from the Old Norse word slóð, meaning 'trail' or 'track'), which gave English the modern word 'sleuth' for a detective.

faq.question: How big does an adult Bloodhound get?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify an ideal withers height of 68 cm for males and 62 cm for females, with a tolerance of ±4 cm (64 to 72 cm for males; 58 to 66 cm for females), and typical weights of 46 to 54 kg (101–119 lbs) for males and 40 to 48 kg (88–106 lbs) for females. British and American standards specify a height range of 25 to 27 inches (63–69 cm, average 26 in / 66 cm) for males and 23 to 25 inches (58–63 cm, average 24 in / 61 cm) for females, and weights of 90 to 110 pounds (41–50 kg) for males and 80 to 100 pounds (36–45.5 kg) for females, though large individuals frequently reach 120 to 130+ pounds (54–59+ kg).

faq.question: What coat colours are accepted in the Bloodhound?
faq.answer: Three colours are recognized: black and tan, liver and tan, and solid red. In the bicolour varieties (black and tan or liver and tan), the darker colour may form either a full mantle (where black or liver predominates) or a smaller dorsal saddle with more extensive tan, and darker areas may be interspersed with lighter or badger-coloured hairs. Red dogs range from light golden-blond red to deep red. A small amount of white is permitted on the forechest, toes/feet, and tip of the tail.

faq.question: How long does a Bloodhound typically live?
faq.answer: The average lifespan is 10 to 12 years.

faq.question: Does a Bloodhound drool and make a lot of noise?
faq.answer: Yes to both. Because of its square muzzle, long hanging upper lips (flews), and loose neck folds, the Bloodhound drools heavily—especially after drinking, eating, or sniffing—and a single head shake can fling saliva 15 feet across a room. While Bloodhounds rarely bark like guard dogs, they have a deep, resonant, melodious bay ('rooooo') when excited or on a scent trail.

faq.question: Is a Bloodhound a good family dog or guard dog?
faq.answer: Bloodhounds are gentle, placid, and deeply affectionate with their families and get along well with other dogs and children. Because of their sheer size and wagging tails, interactions with toddlers and children under 5 years old should always be supervised. However, they are terrible guard dogs: they may bay when someone approaches, but their friendly, non-aggressive nature means they are more likely to welcome an intruder than guard property.

faq.question: Can a Bloodhound be let off-leash or kept behind an electronic ('invisible') fence?
faq.answer: No. Once a Bloodhound catches an interesting scent, its tracking instinct overrides recall commands and road awareness—even in obedience-titled dogs. Electronic underground fences are ineffective because the breed's high pain threshold, thick loose neck skin, and scent drive allow it to bolt right through the shock boundary. Always walk a Bloodhound on a leash and enclose yards with a sturdy 5- to 6-foot physical fence.

faq.question: How much daily grooming and ear care does a Bloodhound need?
faq.answer: The short coat needs only a weekly brushing with a hound glove or rubber mitt (more often during spring and autumn sheds), but the ears and facial wrinkles require daily attention. Because the long ears dip into food and water bowls and trap warm moisture, inspect them daily and clean them regularly with a veterinary ear cleanser. Wipe the facial, lip, and neck folds daily with a damp cloth and dry them thoroughly to prevent skin-fold dermatitis.

faq.question: Why is bloat (GDV) such an important concern in Bloodhounds, and how can risk be reduced?
faq.answer: Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV, or gastric torsion/bloat) occurs when the deep, narrow stomach fills with gas and twists, cutting off blood flow. Epidemiological studies in pedigree dogs rank the Bloodhound among the breeds at highest risk of GDV morbidity and mortality. Owners can help reduce risk by feeding two to three smaller meals daily instead of one large meal, avoiding vigorous exercise around mealtimes, avoiding elevated food bowls unless advised by a vet, discussing prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking' surgery) with their veterinarian, and seeking immediate emergency care if abdominal swelling, unproductive retching, or restlessness occurs.

faq.question: What pre-breeding health screenings should I ask a breeder for?
faq.answer: Ask for documented results of the three core pre-breeding evaluations—hip dysplasia radiographs, elbow dysplasia radiographs, and a veterinary cardiac examination (ideally by a veterinary cardiologist)—along with optional screenings such as a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye exam, patellar luxation check, thyroid panel, and DNA testing for degenerative myelopathy (SOD1).

overview.summary: An enchanting, small Italian toy companion belonging to the ancient bichon family, distinguished by its pure white flocky coat, dark expressive eyes, square silhouette, serene dignity, and deeply devoted domestic loyalty.
overview.description: The Bolognese is a small, compact, and square-built companion dog whose body length equals its height at the withers. Known for centuries as an aristocratic lapdog of Italian noble courts, the dog carries a distinctive cloud-like silhouette created by a long, airy, flocky coat that falls in open ringlet tufts rather than forming straight fringes. Its pure snow-white fur is set off by a jet-black nose, dark-rimmed lips, and large, luminous dark ochre eyes that radiate calm intelligence and steady affection. In domestic life, the dog is markedly quiet, composed, and non-hyperactive, forming an exceptionally tight emotional attachment to its human family while greeting new situations with quiet observation and gentle charm.
overview.history: The origins of the breed trace back to antiquity along the Mediterranean basin, where small white lapdogs were mentioned by Aristotle as early as the fourth century BCE under the Latin designation Canes Melitenses. During the Renaissance, the breed was refined in the northern Italian city of Bologna, becoming the prized status symbol and diplomatic gift of noble dynasties including the Medici, Gonzaga, and d'Este families. Renaissance masters, including Titian, Pieter Bruegel the Elder, and Francisco Goya, immortalized these dogs in royal portraits, and historical letters record Cosimo de' Medici transporting eight puppies to Brussels as gifts for Belgian noblemen. In the eighteenth century, Madame de Pompadour and Empress Catherine the Great of Russia were passionate patrons. Following the political upheavals of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the breed neared extinction, but dedicated Italian breeders successfully gathered foundation stock in the mid-twentieth century to safeguard its authentic historical type.
