grooming.brushing: Brush once a week with a soft-bristle brush or rubber hound glove to remove loose hair and dust and keep the short, vitreous coat sleek and gleaming.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally as needed using a mild, dog-safe shampoo, and dry thoroughly afterward so the thin-skinned, low-body-fat dog does not become chilled.
notes: The short, close-lying single coat has no feathering and requires minimal upkeep compared with long- or double-coated breeds.
During the seasonal molt, slightly lighter, undefined coat patches may temporarily appear on the shoulders, sides of the neck, or thighs.
Inspect the large, erect, open-fronted ears every week for dust, plant debris, excess wax, redness, or odour, and clean gently if needed with soft gauze and a veterinarian-recommended ear cleanser.
Trim nails frequently if they do not wear down naturally on hard ground, as overly long nails cause foot discomfort and splaying.
Check the paw pads and interdigital spaces after runs over rocky, thorny, or hot terrain.
Brush teeth frequently with dog-specific toothpaste and accustom puppies early to calm, reward-based handling.

training.difficulty: Moderate; quick to learn and often more biddable than many traditional sighthounds, yet independent-minded and powerfully motivated by hunting instincts
tips: Use patient, upbeat, reward-based positive reinforcement; harsh physical or verbal corrections are counterproductive with this sensitive, primitive-type hound.
Give the dog a purposeful outlet—such as lure coursing, nose work, tracking, agility, rally, or obedience—to satisfy its inquisitive, working mind.
Practise recall in securely fenced enclosures, and never trust off-leash reliability near roads, highways, or open wildlife areas where a fleeting scent or movement can trigger an instant chase.
Provide secure physical fencing around yards, as Cirnechi are agile jumpers built to bound from rock to rock.
Supervise carefully and introduce household cats and small furry pets gradually, recognizing that high prey drive toward squirrels, rabbits, and outdoor cats is innate.
Start puppy training classes and broad socialization early so the dog develops confident manners around unfamiliar people and environments.
training.socialization: Begin gentle, positive exposure early in puppyhood to diverse people, friendly dogs, novel sights, sounds, and surfaces. Because primitive hunting hounds raised in isolation can become wary or diffident toward strangers, consistent early socialization is essential to nurture an outgoing, confident companion.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Despite its independent working drive in the field, the Cirneco bonds closely with its family, loves to stay alongside its people indoors, and should never be left isolated alone in a backyard or kennel for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced dog food appropriate for the dog's life stage (puppy, adult, or senior), activity level, and individual health needs.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions of a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and workload. Monitor body condition so the dog maintains its lean, athletic silhouette with visible musculature and a gently rising underline without excess weight. Keep clean, fresh drinking water available at all times, and consult a veterinarian or breeder regarding individual portion sizes and diet questions.
considerations: Active coursing, hunting, or agility dogs require higher caloric intake than dogs in lighter companion routines.
Count training treats within the daily calorie allowance to prevent unwanted weight gain.
Avoid feeding unsafe human foods, cooked bones, or rich table scraps.
Transition between diets gradually over several days unless directed otherwise by a veterinarian.
Consult a veterinarian if unexplained weight loss, digestive upset, or changes in appetite occur.
nutrition.note: No universal numerical daily meal schedule is prescribed for puppies, adults, or seniors; determine meal frequency and portion sizes with a veterinarian based on the individual dog and food.

health.overview: The Cirneco dell'Etna is widely regarded as a hardy, long-lived breed with a typical life expectancy of 15 to 16 years and a historically low incidence of documented hereditary disease. In North America, no routine breed-wide health test requirements are currently mandated, while in Italy selected breeding registration (Riproduzione Selezionata) from 18 months of age requires radiographic hip dysplasia grading of HD A or B. However, because the global population derives from a relatively small gene pool—with genomic studies showing higher homozygosity in self-coloured fawn lines than in tan-and-white blazed lines—responsible breeders monitor genetic diversity and emerging research closely. In February 2024, a peer-reviewed genomic study identified an autosomal recessive frameshift deletion in exon 15 of the AMPD2 gene on chromosome 6 (c.2131delG / p.D711Mfs12Stop) as the likely cause of Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome (CONS) in two male littermates that developed episodic head tremors and forelimb dyskinesia/atypical seizures at 2 to 2.5 years of age followed by progressive retinal degeneration (PRA) and cerebral white-matter thinning by 4 years of age. Genotyping of 35 Cirnechi found the variant only in the two affected littermates and three related carriers (including their shared grandmother and a related European dog), indicating that the mutation likely originated within a specific bloodline rather than being widespread across the breed. A targeted AMPD2 DNA test is available to help breeders screen breeding stock, prevent carrier-to-carrier matings, and avoid creating a genetic bottleneck.
preventiveCare: Schedule regular veterinary wellness examinations and maintain appropriate vaccination and parasite-prevention protocols (including vector protection against Leishmania infantum in endemic Mediterranean regions).
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition and provide safe, enclosed exercise to prevent traffic trauma—one of the primary real-world hazards for high-prey-drive hounds.

Monitor adult dogs for any episodic head bobbing, tremors, forelimb cramping, cervical pain, or signs of dim-light vision loss, and discuss targeted AMPD2 genetic testing or specialist ophthalmic and neurological evaluation with a veterinarian if signs or family history warrant.

For breeders, utilize pedigree analysis, genomic diversity tools, hip evaluations (where required for selected breeding), and AMPD2 carrier testing thoughtfully so deleterious recessive variants are managed without narrowing the breed's small gene pool.
Inspect the upright ears weekly for dirt or wax buildup, brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste, and keep nails trimmed short.
Check paw pads, nails, and thin skin for cuts, thorns, or abrasions after running on rocky or brushy terrain, and provide a warm coat in cold or wet weather.
recommendedScreenings: No routine breed-wide mandatory health test panel is currently established in North American registration programs.
Hip dysplasia radiographic screening (graded HD A or B) is required from 18 months of age for dogs entering the Italian Selected Breeding Register (Riproduzione Selezionata).

Targeted DNA testing for the AMPD2 frameshift variant (c.2131delG on chromosome 6, associated with Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome / CONS) is recommended by veterinary geneticists and breed health foundations to monitor allele frequency and avoid carrier-to-carrier matings, particularly in related bloodlines.
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist and neurological assessment are advised for any dog displaying visual deficits, tremors, or paroxysmal movement episodes.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth frequently using dog-specific toothpaste and a soft canine toothbrush, and schedule periodic veterinary dental assessments. Conformation standards require a complete, regular scissor bite with incisors set square to the jaws (absence of PM1 and M3 premolars/molars is permissible under international rules).
health.earCare: Inspect the high-set, rigid upright ears every week for dust, plant awns, excess wax, redness, or unusual odour, especially after field runs. Clean gently when needed using soft gauze and a veterinarian-recommended ear-cleaning solution, and never insert cotton swabs deep into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: Examine the fine, taut skin and short, vitreous coat during weekly brushing for scratches, ticks, or irritation, noting that minor honourable working scars are never penalized in conformation. Protect the paw pads on rough lava rock or hot pavement, and provide warm bedding and cold-weather clothing when temperatures drop.

funFacts: Between the fifth and second centuries BC, Greek cities across Sicily minted hundreds of coin varieties bearing the image of a prick-eared hound remarkably similar to the modern Cirneco dell'Etna.

The breed takes its name from Mount Etna, Europe's largest active volcano on the east coast of Sicily, where it leaps sure-footedly across jagged volcanic lava fields in pursuit of wild rabbits; the suffix 'dell'Etna' was officially added when the first breed standard was approved in 1939.

In 1932, after Adrano veterinarian Dr. Maurizio Migneco warned that the ancient Sicilian hound was nearing extinction, Baroness Agata Paternò Castello dei Duchi di Carcaci ('Donna Aga') spent 26 years reviving the breed under her Aetnensis kennel affix.

Unlike pure sighthounds that rely mainly on vision, the Cirneco is a triple-sense hunter: it scans the landscape by sight, listens through its rigid upright ears for rabbits moving underground, and relies primarily on its keen nose to track and flush quarry.

In traditional Sicilian rabbit hunting, the Cirneco works in a classic partnership with a ferret: once the dog locates a rabbit deep inside a lava crevice or burrow and signals with excited barks, it steps aside and waits silently while the handler releases the ferret to bolt the quarry.

Every part of a Cirneco dell'Etna is meant to be monochromatic: its coat, skin, nose leather, eyelid rims, lips, paw pads, nails, and amber-to-ochre irises all harmonize in shades of fawn, tan, and flesh, and any trace of black pigment is a disqualification.

A 2021 Italian genomic study found that the Cirneco dell'Etna is genetically closest to Malta's Kelb tal-Fenek (Pharaoh Hound) and the Segugio Italiano, and identified the MITF gene as the primary locus distinguishing tan-and-white blazed Cirnechi from self-coloured fawn dogs.

faq.question: Where does the Cirneco dell'Etna originate, and what does its name mean?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the island of Sicily in southern Italy, particularly the volcanic slopes around Mount Etna. The word 'Cirneco' (pronounced 'cheer-NEK-oh', plural 'Cirnechi') is thought to derive either from ancient Cyrene in North Africa (Kyrenaikos / Cyrenaecus) or from the Latin verb cernere / cirniri ('to sift' or 'search'), while 'dell'Etna' was added in 1939 to honour its volcanic homeland.

faq.question: Is the Cirneco dell'Etna a sighthound or a scent hound?
faq.answer: Although often informally called the 'Sicilian Greyhound' and eligible for sighthound lure coursing, the Cirneco is classified internationally as a primitive-type hunting dog that hunts primarily by scent, while also using its acute hearing to detect rabbits underground and its keen sight to scan rocky terrain and course flushed game.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Cirneco dell'Etna?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify a withers height of 46 to 50 cm for males and 44 to 48 cm for females (with a ±2 cm tolerance resulting in an overall range of 44 to 52 cm for males and 42 to 50 cm for females) and an adult weight of 10 to 13 kg for males and 8 to 11 kg for females. North American standards specify 18 to 20 inches (45.7–50.8 cm) and 20 to 28 pounds (9.1–12.7 kg) for males, and 17 to 19 inches (43.2–48.3 cm) and 19 to 25 pounds (8.6–11.3 kg) for females.

faq.question: How long does a Cirneco dell'Etna typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 15 to 16 years, making the Cirneco dell'Etna a notably long-lived medium-sized breed.

faq.question: What coat colours and markings are allowed in the Cirneco dell'Etna?
faq.answer: Accepted colours are self-coloured fawn or tan ranging from light wheaten, sand, or isabella to dark tan (with wheaten and honey-golden shades traditionally prized and deep mahogany less desired), as well as fawn/tan with white markings on the head (blaze), chest, throat, feet, tail tip, or belly (a white collar is less appreciated). Nose, eye rims, lips, pads, and nails must be flesh-coloured to brown; any black pigment, solid brown/liver, or brindle coat is a disqualification.

faq.question: How does a Cirneco dell'Etna differ from a Pharaoh Hound?
faq.answer: The two breeds are close Mediterranean cousins from neighbouring islands—the Cirneco from Sicily and the Pharaoh Hound (Kelb tal-Fenek) from Malta—and share an upright-eared, amber-eyed, tan-coated appearance. However, the Cirneco dell'Etna is substantially smaller and lighter (standing 44–50 cm and weighing 8–13 kg, compared with 53–63.5 cm and 20–25 kg for the Pharaoh Hound) and is built on a square 1:1 outline rather than the Pharaoh Hound's slightly longer rectangular profile.

faq.question: Does the Cirneco dell'Etna require much grooming?
faq.answer: Very little. Its short, sleek, vitreous coat stays clean with a quick weekly brushing using a soft bristle brush or hound glove and an occasional bath as needed. Weekly ear checks, frequent nail trimming, and regular tooth brushing complete its routine care.

faq.question: Can a Cirneco dell'Etna be trusted off-leash in open areas?
faq.answer: No. Because the breed was selected for millennia to pursue rabbits independently across rugged terrain, a fleeing squirrel, rabbit, or cat can instantly override recall training. Off-leash running should be restricted to securely fenced enclosures far from road traffic.

faq.question: Is the Cirneco dell'Etna good with cats and small pets?
faq.answer: Caution is essential. While some Cirnechi raised from puppyhood with an indoor cat coexist peacefully under supervision, the breed's innate drive to chase small furry animals is very strong, and outdoor cats or small pets may be viewed as quarry.

faq.question: What is Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome (CONS), and what health tests exist for the breed?
faq.answer: Historically, the breed has had very few reported hereditary diseases and no mandatory North American screening panel (while Italian selected breeding requires HD A or B hip scores). In 2024, researchers identified an autosomal recessive frameshift deletion in the AMPD2 gene on chromosome 6 causing Cirneco oculo-neurological syndrome (CONS) in two male littermates that developed episodic head tremors and forelimb movement episodes at 2 to 2.5 years of age and progressive retinal degeneration by 4 years of age. Genotyping showed the mutation was confined to the affected family and three related carriers rather than widespread across the breed, and a targeted AMPD2 DNA test is now available to help breeders avoid carrier-to-carrier matings.

faq.question: Is the Cirneco dell'Etna suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Yes, provided its daily need for brisk leashed walks, enclosed running play, and mental enrichment is met. Indoors, a well-exercised Cirneco is calm, clean, affectionate, and fond of curling up under blankets next to its owners.

overview.summary: A massive, low-set British flushing spaniel renowned for its heavy bone structure, pensive expression, gleaming white coat with lemon or orange markings, and steady, dignified demeanor.
overview.description: The Clumber Spaniel is the heaviest of the sporting spaniels, distinguished by a rectangular, substantial frame, a deep chest, and strong, short limbs. Its noble, broad head features a marked stop, deep-set amber eyes, and large, vine-leaf-shaped hanging ears. Developed to push methodically through dense brambles and flush upland game within range of hunters on foot, it works at an unhurried, relentless pace with a characteristic rolling gait. In the home, the Clumber is affectionate, gentle, and quiet, yet its substantial body mass, regular coat brushing needs, and tendency to drool require thoughtful commitment.
overview.history: The breed developed during the late eighteenth century at Clumber Park, the Nottinghamshire estate of the Duke of Newcastle. Tradition recounts that foundational stock originated from French kennel dogs presented by the Duc de Noailles during the French Revolution. Refined through crossings with heavy hunting spaniels and scent hounds, the Clumber became the favoured hunting partner of British aristocrats and royalty. Valued for working quietly in dense undergrowth, it gained early prominence at nineteenth-century exhibitions and is recognized today as a vulnerable native heritage breed in Great Britain.

exercise.level: Moderate. Up to about an hour of daily activity generally meets its needs, tailored to age and joint health. As a heavy-bodied breed, avoid repetitive high-impact jumping, particularly during growth periods.

grooming.level: Moderate to high. The dense, feathered coat benefits from brushing more than once a week, and the ears, facial folds and coat beneath the body need regular attention.
grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly two to three times weekly, focusing on ear feathering, chest, belly, and thighs to prevent matting.
grooming.bathing: Bathe periodically as needed with gentle canine shampoo, ensuring complete drying of the thick undercarriage and ear leather.
notes: Clean and dry the heavy drop ears weekly to prevent moisture and wax accumulation.
Inspect the facial skin folds and flews daily, wiping dry after drinking to avoid lip fold dermatitis.
Examine eyes regularly for excessive discharge or irritation.
Trim feathering between foot pads and keep nails clipped short to support substantial body weight.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Highly intelligent and willing to please, though possessed of a deliberate, independent thinking style that disdains rush or harshness.
tips: Employ positive reinforcement with appetizing training rewards and praise.
Keep training lessons calm, purposeful, and structured rather than frantic.
Practice early recall and loose-leash walking around scent distractions.
Acclimate puppies early to cooperative grooming, ear cleaning, and mouth handling.
training.socialization: Expose puppies gradually to diverse people, friendly canines, novel environments, and domestic sounds to develop composed confidence.

climates: Well-adapted to temperate and cool climates through its dense insulating coat
Ensure air-conditioned indoor comfort, shade, and fresh water during hot weather spells
Provide warm, supportive bedding to protect large joints in damp or cold seasons
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: A reliable breed-specific maximum duration was not established. Build up alone time gradually and avoid routinely leaving a companion dog alone for long stretches without appropriate care, exercise and enrichment.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced diet formulated for large-breed sporting dogs.
nutrition.guidelines: Provide measured rations split into two daily meals. Carefully manage caloric density to prevent excessive weight gain that stresses joints and spine.
considerations: Avoid free-feeding, as the breed exhibits a hearty appetite and tendency toward obesity.
Prevent vigorous running or exercise immediately before or after meals.
Account for treats in the daily caloric allotment.
nutrition.note: No fixed calorie target or universal portion size is recorded because requirements vary with age, activity, body condition and medical status.

health.overview: The Clumber Spaniel is a substantial, long-bodied gundog with an average lifespan of 10 to 12 years. Recognized genetic and orthopedic screening priorities include exercise-induced collapse (EIC), pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase 1 (PDP1) deficiency, hip and elbow dysplasia, and ophthalmic assessments for entropion and ectropion.
commonConditions: Exercise-induced collapse (EIC), an inherited neuromuscular condition managed via DNA testing
Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase 1 (PDP1) deficiency, an inherited metabolic disorder
Hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia
Ectropion and entropion (eyelid conformation defects)
Intervertebral disc disease (IVDD) related to disproportionate body length
Otitis externa associated with heavy, pendulous ears
preventiveCare: Verify parental DNA clearances for EIC and PDP1 deficiency prior to breeding or purchase.
Request documented veterinary hip, elbow, and eye evaluation scores for both parents.
Maintain a lean, conditioned body weight to protect spinal discs and weight-bearing joints.
Keep hanging ears dry and clean to prevent fungal and bacterial infections.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation
Ophthalmologist eye examination
Exercise-induced collapse (EIC) DNA test
Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase 1 (PDP1) DNA test
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and have the mouth checked during routine veterinary visits. Professional dental cleaning should be based on clinical need and veterinary advice.
health.earCare: The heavy, hanging ears should be inspected regularly. Keep them dry, and ask a veterinarian about safe cleaning if there is redness, odour, discharge, head shaking or persistent scratching.
health.skinCare: Inspect the facial folds and dense coat during grooming. Keep folds clean and dry, remove trapped debris and consult a veterinarian if redness, odour, itching or recurrent skin problems appear.

notIdealFor: Apartment living where stairs or tight quarters restrict comfortable movement

funFacts: The breed derives its name from Clumber Park in Nottinghamshire, the historic estate of the Duke of Newcastle.
Its predominantly white coat was purposefully developed so gun handlers could easily spot the dog working through thick, tangled brambles.
Despite being the heaviest of the sporting spaniels, it works with a steady, tireless rolling gait that it can sustain all day.
Early historical accounts attribute foundational stock to French Alpine spaniels gifted by the Duc de Noailles during the eighteenth century.
It is designated as a vulnerable native British breed due to relatively small annual registration numbers.

faq.question: How large is a Clumber Spaniel?
faq.answer: Males typically stand 18 to 20 inches at the withers and weigh between 70 and 85 pounds, while females measure 17 to 19 inches and weigh between 55 and 70 pounds.

faq.question: What colour is a Clumber Spaniel?
faq.answer: The coat is primarily pure white with lemon markings, though orange markings are also recognized. Markings are typically concentrated on the ears and face, accompanied by light freckling on the muzzle and legs.

faq.question: Does a Clumber Spaniel need a lot of exercise?
faq.answer: It needs regular daily activity of up to one hour, focused on steady walking, scent exploration, and gentle retrieving, rather than high-impact jumping or strenuous running.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Clumber Spaniel need?
faq.answer: The dense, feathered coat requires brushing two to three times a week, alongside routine cleaning of the heavy drop ears and facial flews to prevent irritation.

faq.question: What health tests should a Clumber Spaniel breeder discuss?
faq.answer: Key pre-breeding clearances include hip and elbow evaluations, eye examinations, and DNA tests for exercise-induced collapse (EIC) and PDP1 deficiency.

faq.question: Is a Clumber Spaniel suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Generally no. While calm indoors, its massive body bone, weight, shedding, and drool make a home with easy outdoor yard access much more suitable.

faq.question: How long does a Clumber Spaniel live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 10 to 12 years when maintained at a lean body weight with proper preventive veterinary care.

overview.summary: An elegant, heavily coated Scottish herding dog prized for its keen intelligence, gentle sensitivity, family devotion, and agile, effortless stride.
overview.description: The Rough Collie is a medium-to-large herding breed immediately recognisable by its luxurious double coat, prominent neck ruff and frill, clean wedge-shaped head, obliquely set almond eyes, and semi-pricked ears whose top third tips forward when alert. Beneath the profuse jacket lies a lithe, well-balanced working frame built to cover ground smoothly and change direction rapidly without cloddiness or coarseness. Typically attentive, affectionate with household members, and highly responsive to calm guidance, the breed thrives on daily companionship, purposeful mental engagement, and steady outdoor activity. Because the dense undercoat and long outer hair trap loose coat easily, owners should plan on consistent brushing alongside thoughtful socialisation and veterinary health screening.
overview.history: The Rough Collie traces its roots to traditional sheep-herding dogs of the Scottish Highlands and Lowlands, where local shepherds relied on agile, weather-resistant working collies to gather and drive livestock across rugged hills and market roads. Early woodcuts published by Thomas Bewick around 1800 already depict recognisable regional collie types. During the 1860s, Queen Victoria admired the breed while staying at Balmoral Castle in Scotland and established a royal kennel that brought the sable-and-white and tricolour pastoral dogs into fashionable Victorian society. Late nineteenth-century British exhibitors—drawing heavily on foundational sires such as Old Cockie, born in the late 1860s—refined the head profile and abundant coat while preserving the breed's balanced movement. Organised breed representation followed in Britain and North America during the mid-1880s, and twentieth-century literature and cinema—from Albert Payson Terhune's Sunnybank stories to Eric Knight's Lassie Come-Home—cemented the long-coated variety's global reputation as both a devoted household companion and a versatile working and sporting dog.
overview.originalPurpose: Herding, gathering, and driving sheep and other livestock across Scottish pastures and upland terrain
currentRoles: Family and household companion
Herding trials and livestock management where opportunities exist
Obedience, rally, and agility competition
Conformation exhibition
Therapy, assistance, and scent or tracking activities

physical.coatType: Weather-resistant double coat combining a straight, harsh outer coat with a very dense, soft, furry undercoat
physical.coatLength: Long and profuse over the body, forming a heavy mane and frill around the neck and chest, rich feathering on the forelegs and upper thighs, and a bushy tail, while remaining short and smooth on the muzzle, skull, ear tips, and lower legs below the hocks.
coatColors: Sable and white (light gold to rich mahogany or shaded sable with white markings)
Tricolour (predominantly black with rich tan head and leg markings and white collar, chest, legs, feet, and tail tip)
Blue merle (silvery blue splashed and marbled with black, typically with white and tan markings)
White (predominantly white body coat with sable, tricolour, or blue merle head and body markings, accepted in North America)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate to high year-round, with heavy seasonal moults of the dense undercoat
physical.droolingLevel: Low
distinctiveFeatures: Abundant, straight outer coat over a close, furry undercoat that forms a pronounced neck mane, chest frill, and bushy tail
Clean, blunt wedge-shaped head with flat skull planes that run parallel to a smooth, well-rounded muzzle of equal length
Medium-sized, almond-shaped dark eyes set obliquely to produce a gentle, intelligent, questioning expression (with blue or china eyes permitted in blue merles)
Moderately small ears set on top of the skull that rest folded back when relaxed and rise to a two-thirds erect carriage with the top third tipping forward when alert
Slightly longer-than-tall body with a deep chest, well-sprung ribs, firm level back, and slight rise over the loins
Moderately long tail with bone reaching at least to the hock joint, carried low with an upward swirl at the tip when quiet and raised gaily without curving over the back when moving
Effortless, ground-covering stride that converges toward a single centre line as speed increases
Shares its foundational heritage with the Smooth Collie, differing primarily in coat length rather than underlying structure

traits: Intelligent, observant, and quick to learn household routines
Deeply loyal and closely bonded with family members
Gentle and responsive to patient, reward-based guidance
Sensitive to harsh voices, tension, or heavy-handed correction
Alert and watchful around the home without unprovoked sharpness
Generally amiable with children, familiar dogs, and other household pets when properly socialised
Capable of sustained outdoor activity paired with a settled indoor demeanour
Prone to vocalising when alerting, excited, or left without sufficient mental occupation

exercise.level: Moderate to high. Daily brisk walks, off-leash running in a secure area, and problem-solving games keep both body and mind satisfied, with duration tailored to age, weather, and individual fitness.
activities: Brisk daily walks with time for scent exploration
Fetch, frisbee, and interactive play in a securely fenced space
Reward-based obedience, rally, and trick training
Agility, hoopers, or tracking and nosework exercises
Supervised herding instinct tests or stockwork where available
Interactive food puzzles and indoor scent games on inclement days

grooming.level: Moderate to high. Regular line-brushing down to the skin is essential to keep the dense undercoat free of mats and compacted dead hair.
grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly at least once or twice a week using a pin brush, slicker brush, and metal comb, parting the coat in sections to reach the soft undercoat. Increase to daily sessions during spring and autumn coat blows, checking friction zones behind the ears, under the elbows, in the groin, and along the leg feathering and breeches.
grooming.bathing: Bathe every few weeks or as needed with a gentle canine shampoo, rinsing and drying right down to the skin with a warm—never hot—dryer so trapped moisture does not irritate the skin.
notes: Use a misting conditioning spray before brushing dry hair to prevent static and reduce coat breakage.
Part the coat line by line down to the skin; skimming only the outer guard hairs leaves compacted undercoat behind.
Inspect behind the ears, under the collar, inside the armpits, and along the hind trousers frequently for small knots.
Trim excess hair between the paw pads and tidy hock feathering as needed to reduce tracked mud and debris.
Check ears, nails, teeth, and skin during weekly grooming, and avoid shaving the insulating double coat unless medically directed by a veterinarian.

training.difficulty: Generally straightforward for attentive handlers. High intelligence and eagerness to cooperate make learning rapid, provided sessions stay upbeat, fair, and free of harsh pressure.
tips: Use food rewards, play, and calm praise in short, varied training sessions to maintain enthusiasm.
Avoid loud reprimands or forceful handling, which can cause a sensitive herding dog to shut down or hesitate.
Establish a polite 'quiet' cue early so natural watchfulness does not turn into nuisance barking.
Channel herding instincts constructively if the dog tries to circle, eye, or nip at running children, cyclists, or other pets.
Practice relaxed settling and gradual departures so a people-oriented dog stays comfortable during brief periods alone.
Introduce grooming tools, paw handling, and eye or ear checks positively from early puppyhood.
training.socialization: Begin gentle, structured exposure in puppyhood across varied sights, surfaces, sounds, calm dogs, and friendly visitors, allowing the youngster to observe and approach new situations at a confident, unhurried pace.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced canine diet formulated for the dog's life stage, activity level, and health profile
nutrition.guidelines: Feed a complete, life-stage-appropriate diet in measured portions, adjusting energy intake to maintain a lean waist and easily palpable ribs underneath the heavy coat. Dividing the daily ration into two or more smaller meals rather than a single large feeding is commonly advised to help reduce the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat). Keep clean water accessible at all times.
considerations: Hands-on rib and waist checks are essential because the thick double coat can easily conceal gradual weight gain or loss.
Serve two or more measured meals daily and avoid vigorous jumping or running immediately before and after eating to help lower bloat risk.
Adjust calorie intake across growth, seasonal activity changes, neutering, and senior years in consultation with a veterinarian.
Account for training treats within the daily caloric budget so reward-based sessions do not lead to excess weight.
Do not administer supplements, antiparasitics, or over-the-counter drugs (such as loperamide) without verifying safety for dogs that may carry the MDR1 mutation.
nutrition.note: Exact meal counts and daily kilocalorie targets depend on age, diet energy density, metabolic rate, and medical status; consult a veterinarian for an individualised feeding plan.

health.overview: Rough Collies are generally hardy companions, typically living 12 to 14 years, with large-scale veterinary records reporting a median longevity around 13.3 years. However, the breed carries well-characterised hereditary ocular, pharmacological, dermatological, and neurological risks that can be substantially managed through pre-breeding DNA panels and early puppy ophthalmic screening. Prospective owners should review documented parent test certificates and share the dog's genetic status—especially for MDR1 drug sensitivity—with their veterinarian.
commonConditions: Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA / NHEJ1-related choroidal hypoplasia and optic disc coloboma), a congenital ocular malformation present from birth

Multidrug Sensitivity (MDR1 / ABCB1 c.296_299del4 mutation), impairing P-glycoprotein drug transport across the blood-brain barrier and causing neurotoxicity from ivermectin, loperamide, and certain sedatives or chemotherapeutics
Progressive Retinal Atrophy, Rod-Cone Dysplasia Type 2 (PRA-rcd2), an early-onset autosomal recessive retinal degeneration

Canine Familial Dermatomyositis (DMS), an immune-mediated inflammatory disease of the skin and muscle influenced by three genetic risk loci (A, B, and C) and environmental triggers such as ultraviolet light or physiological stress
Cyclic Neutropenia (Grey Collie Syndrome), an autosomal recessive stem-cell disorder causing diluted silver-grey coat pigment and cyclical immune neutropenia
Degenerative Myelopathy (DM), a late-onset progressive spinal cord neuropathy
Hip Dysplasia and Gastric Dilatation-Volvulus (bloat)
preventiveCare: Verify and record the dog's MDR1 (ABCB1) genotype in its permanent veterinary file before administering antiparasitics, anti-diarrhoeals, sedatives, or anaesthetic agents.
Ensure puppies receive a specialist veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination at 5 to 8 weeks of age, before normal retinal pigmentation can mask mild choroidal hypoplasia.
Schedule routine veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and MDR1-safe heartworm, flea, and tick prevention.
Protect dogs with elevated dermatomyositis (DMS) genetic risk from intense sun exposure and seek prompt dermatological assessment for facial, ear-tip, or tail-tip crusting or alopecia.
Avoid merle-to-merle (double merle, MM) breedings, which carry a high risk of severe congenital deafness, microphthalmia, and vision loss.
recommendedScreenings: Specialist veterinary ophthalmologist examination of puppies at 5–8 weeks of age and breeding stock for Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA) and other ocular anomalies
Multidrug Sensitivity (MDR1 / ABCB1) DNA test
Progressive Retinal Atrophy, Rod-Cone Dysplasia Type 2 (PRA-rcd2) DNA test
Dermatomyositis (DMS) 3-locus (A, B, and C) genetic risk panel
Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA / NHEJ1) DNA test
Radiographic Hip Evaluation to assess for hip dysplasia
Optional DNA screening for Cyclic Neutropenia (Grey Collie Syndrome) and Degenerative Myelopathy (DM)
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week using a canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary oral assessments to prevent plaque accumulation and periodontal disease.
health.earCare: Inspect the semi-erect ears weekly for wax buildup, redness, debris, or odour, and clean the outer ear gently with a veterinarian-recommended solution without inserting swabs into the canal.
health.skinCare: Part the dense coat regularly to inspect the skin for redness, hot spots, external parasites, or crusting lesions around the eyes, muzzle, ear tips, and bony prominences.

idealFor: Households seeking an affectionate, people-oriented companion that participates in daily family life
Owners who enjoy gentle, reward-based training, obedience, agility, rally, or herding activities
People committed to thorough weekly line-brushing and seasonal undercoat maintenance
Active individuals or families who can provide steady daily walks, play, and mental enrichment
notIdealFor: Owners unwilling or unable to maintain a heavy, shedding double coat
Households where a dog would be left isolated for long hours with minimal companionship or stimulation
People seeking a completely silent dog without investing time in polite alert-barking training
Buyers unwilling to verify parent DNA health panels, puppy ophthalmic certificates, and MDR1 medication precautions

funFacts: The Rough Collie and Smooth Collie share the same historical ancestry and underlying body structure, differing chiefly in coat length—and because the long-coat gene is recessive, two Rough-factored Smooth Collies can produce Rough Collie puppies.

Queen Victoria fell in love with Scottish herding collies while staying at Balmoral Castle in the 1860s, and her royal patronage transformed a regional Highland working dog into an international favourite.

Author Eric Knight's 1940 novel Lassie Come-Home and the 1943 film starring a male Rough Collie named Pal made the sable-and-white Rough Collie one of the most recognisable dogs in cinema and television history.
In nineteenth-century terminology, blue merle Collies were frequently referred to by shepherds and fanciers as 'tortoise shell' Collies.

faq.question: How long does a Rough Collie usually live?
faq.answer: Typical life expectancy is 12 to 14 years (within a broader 10 to 14 year range), and large-scale UK veterinary records report a median lifespan of 13.3 years. Individual longevity depends on genetics, preventive care, body condition, and overall health.

faq.question: Does a Rough Collie shed heavily?
faq.answer: Yes. The dense, furry undercoat sheds moderately year-round and blows heavily during seasonal changes in spring and autumn. Weekly line-brushing down to the skin—and daily brushing during seasonal moults—prevents dead undercoat from matting inside the long outer guard hairs.

faq.question: How much daily exercise does a Rough Collie need?
faq.answer: Most adults thrive on brisk daily walks, secure off-leash play, and mental tasks such as obedience, trick training, scent games, or dog sports. Because needs vary with age, climate, and individual fitness, no single fixed daily-minute quota applies to every dog.

faq.question: What health tests should I request from a Rough Collie breeder?
faq.answer: Ask for documented parent DNA results for Multidrug Sensitivity (MDR1), Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA-rcd2), Dermatomyositis (DMS across loci A, B, and C), and Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA), along with hip evaluations and an official specialist veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination certificate for the puppy completed at 5 to 8 weeks of age.

faq.question: Why is MDR1 medication sensitivity important in Rough Collies?
faq.answer: A high proportion of Rough Collies carry one or two copies of the MDR1 (ABCB1) gene mutation, which impairs the P-glycoprotein pump that protects the brain from certain drugs. Affected dogs can suffer severe neurological reactions to normal doses of ivermectin, loperamide, and specific sedatives or cancer drugs, so every Collie's MDR1 status should be tested and recorded with a veterinarian.

faq.question: Can a Rough Collie live comfortably in an apartment?
faq.answer: Suitability depends more on daily exercise, companionship, and training than on floor space alone. Because Rough Collies are observant and can be vocal when alerting or bored, apartment owners must commit to consistent outdoor exercise, mental enrichment, and early training for quiet indoor manners.

overview.summary: A cheerful, intelligent, and deeply affectionate small companion dog from southwestern Madagascar, distinguished by its soft, cotton-textured coat, expressive dark eyes, and devoted bond with its household.
overview.description: The Coton de Tulear is a sturdy, small, long-coated companion breed built on a rectangular outline where height at the withers is roughly two-thirds of the body length. Beneath its profuse, supple white coat—which has the dry, airy feel of a natural cotton boll rather than silky or woolly hair—lies a well-muscled frame with a slightly convex topline that arches gently over a short loin to a low-set tail. Round, dark, wide-set eyes and black-pigmented lips and eyelids give the face a bright, inquisitive expression. Lively, stable, and highly sociable with people and other dogs, Cotons are renowned for their clownish antics, habit of walking on their hind legs to please their owners, and repertoire of purr-like, grunting, and trilling vocalizations. While their compact size adapts well to apartments and houses alike, their coat requires committed brushing and their people-oriented nature calls for daily companionship, positive training, and interactive play.
overview.history: Originating on the island of Madagascar off the southeastern coast of Africa, the breed takes its name from the French word coton ('cotton') and the southwestern port city of Toliara, historically known as Tuléar. Around the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, small white European Bichon-type dogs travelled aboard merchant and pirate vessels sailing around the Cape of Good Hope into the Indian Ocean, serving both as shipboard ratters and as companions to passengers. Traditional island lore recounts that survivors of a shipwreck near Tuléar swam ashore, adapted in packs, and interbred with local island dogs, though exact early ancestry narratives remain undocumented in primary historical records. By the seventeenth century, these small white dogs had been adopted by the native Malagasy and the ruling Merina tribal monarchy, which restricted ownership to nobility and royalty—earning the breed the enduring title 'Royal Dog of Madagascar'. French colonists later brought specimens to France, leading to formal international breed recognition in 1970 (with the first international standard published in 1971), organized studbook preservation in North America beginning in 1976, introduction to the United Kingdom in 1987, and subsequent national recognitions in 1996 and 2014.
overview.originalPurpose: Companion dog of Malagasy royalty and nobility (with ancestral shipboard ratter and pack-foraging roots).

physical.coatType: Very soft, supple, dense, and profuse coat with the dry, airy texture of cotton; straight or very slightly wavy, standing slightly away from the body without a woolly undercoat, and never hard, rough, tightly curled, or silky.
physical.coatLength: Long (reaching approximately 8–16.5 cm / 3–6.5 inches in maturity; presented untrimmed except for neatening hair on the bottom of the feet and between the pads)
coatColors: White with slight light-grey (intermingled white and black hairs) or red-roan / lemon / light-tan (intermingled white and fawn hairs) shading on the ears

White with limited light-tan, champagne, or grey body shading that does not alter the overall white appearance (puppies born with tan, brown, chestnut, or grey patches typically fade to white or faint champagne by 12 to 18 months of age, while some traditional Malagasy and North American lines also recognize black-and-white and tri-colour varieties)
physical.sheddingLevel: Low
physical.droolingLevel: Low
distinctiveFeatures: Soft, dense, dry cotton-textured coat from which the breed takes its name
Rectangular body outline with a 2:3 ratio of withers height to body length (head-to-body ratio of 2:5, skull-to-muzzle ratio of 9:5, and neck-to-body ratio of 1:5)
Short head that appears triangular from above, with a slightly rounded wide skull, slight stop, and well-developed zygomatic arches
Round, dark, wide-set eyes with black or brown pigmented eyelid rims and a lively, intelligent expression
High-set, pendulous triangular ears carried close to the cheeks and reaching the corners of the lips
Slightly convex topline arching gracefully over a short, muscular loin into an oblique croup
Low-set tail reaching below the hock with an upturned tip at rest, and carried curved cheerfully over the back on the move

Ideal withers height of 26–28 cm for males (25–30 cm with tolerance) and 23–25 cm for females (22–27 cm with tolerance) and weight of 4–6 kg for males and 3.5–5 kg for females (with North American standards listing 10–11 inches and 9–15 pounds for males, and 9–10 inches and 8–13 pounds for females)

exercise.level: Moderate
activities: Daily leashed walks at a comfortable, unhurried pace suited to the dog's age and fitness

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb gently all the way down to the skin 3 to 4 times per week—or daily when maintaining a full adult coat—using a quality pin brush (without balls on the pin tips, which can snag and tear the hair) and a metal comb. Mist the coat lightly with a leave-in spray conditioner before brushing to prevent hair breakage and mat formation next to the skin.
grooming.bathing: Bathe as needed using a gentle, dog-safe shampoo and conditioner formulated for long coats, rinse thoroughly, and dry the coat completely while brushing so damp hair does not felt or mat.
notes: Pay special attention to coat maintenance between 9 and 14 months of age, when the softer puppy coat transitions to the denser adult coat and matting risk is at its peak.
Inspect high-friction areas carefully during every brushing session, including behind the ears, under the collar or harness, around the elbows and armpits, in the groin, and down the legs.

Keep hair on the bottom of the feet and between the paw pads trimmed neat for traction and cleanliness; otherwise, the coat is traditionally kept in its natural, un-scissored state unless clipped into a shorter pet trim for easier upkeep.
Check the pendulous ears a couple of times each week for excess hair, wax, redness, odour, or debris to help prevent ear canal infections.
Trim nails regularly and accustom puppies early to gentle handling of their paws, face, ears, and tail.
Although low-shedding, no dog breed is completely non-allergenic; prospective owners with allergies should spend time around the breed before committing.

training.difficulty: Generally trainable and eager to please when taught with upbeat, reward-based methods
tips: Use positive reinforcement with small food rewards, play, and enthusiastic praise; Cotons are sensitive and shut down under harsh or negative corrections.
Keep training sessions short, lively, and varied so the dog stays mentally engaged and does not grow bored.
Channel their natural desire to entertain into trick training, rally, obedience, or agility.
Teach calm household manners and polite responses to doorway noises, as the breed is naturally alert and watchful of its home.
Condition puppies gradually to grooming brushes, combs, nail trims, tooth brushing, and baths as positive bonding routines.
Practice gradual alone-time conditioning early so the dog's close attachment to its people does not develop into separation distress.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and positively to a wide variety of people, gentle children, friendly dogs, household sounds, travel, and novel environments so their naturally sociable, adaptable temperament flourishes.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Bred solely for human companionship, the Coton thrives as an indoor family member that follows its people from room to room; leaving the dog isolated for long workdays without gradual conditioning and enrichment can lead to boredom, vocalizing, or destructive behaviour.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality dog food appropriate for the dog's life stage (puppy, adult, or senior), body size, and individual health needs.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions of a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and activity level. Because some individuals are prone to gaining excess weight, monitor body condition regularly, limit high-calorie table scraps, and account for training treats within the daily calorie allowance. Provide constant access to clean, fresh water.
considerations: Watch calorie intake and body condition closely to prevent overweight and unnecessary strain on the patellas, hips, and spine.
Keep training treats small and deduct them from the daily food ration.
Avoid feeding cooked bones or high-fat table scraps that can trigger digestive upset or pancreatitis.
Transition between foods gradually over several days unless directed otherwise by a veterinarian.
Consult a veterinarian promptly if sudden weight changes, picky eating, or excessive water consumption occur.
nutrition.note: A single universal meal schedule is not assigned because optimal feeding frequency depends on age, caloric density of the diet, activity level, and individual health; confirm portion sizes and daily meal counts with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Coton de Tulear is generally a hardy, long-lived breed with a typical life expectancy of 15 to 19 years, and documented hereditary diseases occur at a relatively low incidence (often estimated at 1% to 5% in screened populations). Health management distinguishes between clinical orthopedic, ophthalmic, and cardiac conditions monitored through pre-breeding veterinary examinations—namely patellar luxation, hip dysplasia, inherited eye anomalies, and congenital cardiac murmurs—and specific autosomal recessive mutations for which validated DNA tests allow breeders to avoid carrier-to-carrier matings. Molecularly characterized recessive disorders in the breed include Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (GRM1 mutation), canine multifocal retinopathy 2 (BEST1 mutation), and primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (AGXT mutation), alongside broader canine DNA tests for von Willebrand disease, degenerative myelopathy, hyperuricosuria, and FGF4 retrogene intervertebral disc disease predisposition.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation — a potential orthopedic issue in small breeds in which the kneecap slips out of its trochlear groove; veterinary patellar evaluation is a core pre-breeding requirement.
Hip dysplasia — reported occasionally in the breed and monitored through mandatory pre-breeding radiographic hip evaluation.

Ocular disorders and Canine Multifocal Retinopathy 2 (CMR2) — periodic veterinary ophthalmologist examinations screen for cataracts and retinal anomalies, while an autosomal recessive BEST1 gene mutation (c.482G>A) causes CMR2, producing discrete subretinal blisters around 15 weeks of age that typically stabilize by 1 year without causing blindness.

Cardiac abnormalities — congenital heart murmurs or valve defects are screened via pre-breeding veterinary cardiac evaluations; the screening requirement reflects preventive stewardship rather than high clinical prevalence.

Intervertebral disc disease (spinal disc disease) and FGF4 retrogene variants — back and disc problems are occasionally reported in the breed, and elective DNA testing is available for the chromosome 12 FGF4 retrogene (CDDY) associated with premature intervertebral disc degeneration as well as the chromosome 18 FGF4 retrogene (CDPA) associated with short-limbed chondrodysplasia.

Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (BNAt / NCA) — a severe autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia caused by a retrotransposon insertion in exon 8 of the GRM1 gene on chromosome 1; affected puppies exhibit intention tremors, head nodding, and inability to stand or walk from about 2 weeks of age, and a separate autosomal recessive juvenile cerebellar ataxia is also under genomic investigation.

Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH) — a rare, fatal neonatal autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a missense mutation (c.996G>A / p.Gly102Ser) in the AGXT gene, leading to calcium oxalate crystal accumulation and acute renal tubular necrosis at 3 to 4 weeks of age (identified with an 8.5% carrier rate in a Finnish study cohort).

Additional conditions included in elective pre-breeding genetic or clinical panels — type 1 von Willebrand disease (vWD), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), hyperuricosuria (HU / SLC2A9), autoimmune thyroiditis, elbow dysplasia, and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease.
preventiveCare: Request documented pre-breeding health clearances for both parents—covering veterinary ophthalmologist exams, patellar luxation, hip radiographs, cardiac evaluation, and relevant breed-appropriate DNA tests—before acquiring a puppy.
Maintain a lean body weight and healthy muscle tone through daily walks and portion control to minimize mechanical stress on the knees, hips, and spine.
Brush the coat thoroughly down to the skin several times a week to prevent painful mats that trap moisture and hide skin irritation.
Check and gently clean the drop ears a couple of times weekly to prevent wax accumulation and otitis externa.
Brush teeth regularly and schedule routine veterinary wellness and dental examinations throughout the dog's long lifespan.
Seek prompt veterinary evaluation for limping, skipping gaits, back pain, eye cloudiness or redness, coughing, or urinary changes.
recommendedScreenings: Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (core pre-breeding requirement, performed from 6 months of age and periodically thereafter).
Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement at 12 months of age or older).
Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement; preliminary radiographs before 24 months and final certification after 24 months of age).
Cardiac examination by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist (performed at 12 months of age or older prior to breeding).

Elective genetic and clinical evaluations based on lineage and breeding program requirements: DNA tests for Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (GRM1), canine multifocal retinopathy 2 (CMR2 / BEST1), primary hyperoxaluria (PH / AGXT), type 1 von Willebrand disease (vWD), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), hyperuricosuria (HU / SLC2A9), chondrodystrophy (CDDY / FGF4), and chondrodysplasia (CDPA / FGF4), as well as laboratory thyroid profiling, elbow radiographs, and Legg-Calvé-Perthes evaluation.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week—ideally daily—using dog-safe toothpaste and a small, soft canine toothbrush. Because small companion breeds are prone to plaque accumulation and periodontal disease over a 15- to 19-year lifespan, combine home brushing with regular veterinary dental assessments and professional cleanings when indicated.
health.earCare: Inspect the high-set, pendulous triangular ears two to three times a week and after baths. Gently remove excess hair, wax, or debris as advised by a veterinarian, keep the ear canals dry, and seek veterinary care for redness, foul odour, discharge, or head shaking.
health.skinCare: Part the dense cottony coat down to the skin during brushing to check for hidden tangles, redness, parasites, or dry skin. Use a gentle dog shampoo and leave-in conditioning spray to keep the skin and hair supple, and ensure the coat is dried completely after bathing or rain.

funFacts: The breed's name combines the French word coton ('cotton'), referring to its soft, airy cotton-boll coat texture, with Tuléar (now Toliara), the southwestern Malagasy port city associated with its early history.
In seventeenth-century Madagascar, the ruling Merina monarchy restricted ownership of these small white dogs to royalty and nobility, earning the breed the title 'Royal Dog of Madagascar'.
Madagascar has honoured the Coton de Tulear as its Official National Dog and featured the breed on national postage stamps, including a well-known 1974 stamp issue.

Cotons are famous for two endearing habits when interacting with their families: rising up to walk or hop on their hind legs and conversing through unique purr-like, grunting, or trilling vocalizations.
Unlike several other Bichon-family breeds with flat backs, the Coton de Tulear has a distinctive slightly convex topline that rises gently over a short, muscular loin to a low-set tail.

Many Coton puppies are born with noticeable yellow, tan, brown, chestnut, or grey patches on the head, ears, or body that gradually fade over their first 12 to 18 months, leaving an adult coat that is predominantly white or lightly shaded with champagne or grey on the ears.

faq.question: Where does the Coton de Tulear come from?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the island of Madagascar off the southeastern coast of Africa. Its name refers to its cotton-like coat texture and the southwestern port city of Toliara, formerly called Tuléar.

faq.question: How big is an adult Coton de Tulear?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify an ideal withers height of 26 to 28 cm for males (with a tolerance of 25 to 30 cm) and 23 to 25 cm for females (with a tolerance of 22 to 27 cm), and an adult weight of 4 to 6 kg for males and 3.5 to 5 kg for females. North American standards list an ideal height of 10 to 11 inches (9–15 pounds) for males and 9 to 10 inches (8–13 pounds) for females, while some traditional Malagasy-type lines reach heights up to 12.5 or 13 inches (25–33 cm) and weights up to 14 or 18 pounds.

faq.question: How long does a Coton de Tulear typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 15 to 19 years, making the Coton de Tulear one of the longest-lived companion dog breeds.

faq.question: Does the Coton de Tulear shed, and is it hypoallergenic?
faq.answer: The breed sheds very little—primarily losing small amounts of hair during brushing or in springtime—and has hair rather than a typical fur undercoat. While many people with mild sensitivities tolerate the breed well, no dog is completely hypoallergenic because allergens are also carried in dander and saliva.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Coton de Tulear need?
faq.answer: Maintaining a full, flowing adult coat requires gentle brushing and combing all the way to the skin 3 to 4 times a week (or daily), misting lightly with a leave-in conditioner to prevent breakage and mats. Particular care is needed between 9 and 14 months of age when the puppy coat transitions to the adult coat. Owners who do not show their dogs often opt for a shorter 'puppy clip' to simplify daily maintenance.

faq.question: Is the Coton de Tulear suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Yes. Its small stature, moderate exercise needs, and polite indoor demeanor make it well suited to apartments as well as houses with yards, provided it receives daily walks, interactive play, and plenty of human companionship.

faq.question: Is the Coton de Tulear good with children and other pets?
faq.answer: Yes. The breed is known for a stable, cheerful, and sociable temperament toward people, children, other dogs, and household cats. As with any small breed, interactions with young children should be supervised so the dog is handled gently.

faq.question: What health screenings and DNA tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Prospective buyers should ask for documented results of four core clinical evaluations—board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination, patellar luxation evaluation, hip radiographs, and cardiac examination—along with relevant DNA tests used to prevent carrier-to-carrier matings, such as Bandera's neonatal cerebellar ataxia (GRM1), canine multifocal retinopathy 2 (CMR2 / BEST1), primary hyperoxaluria (PH / AGXT), von Willebrand disease (vWD), degenerative myelopathy (DM), and hyperuricosuria (HU).

faq.question: What colour is a Coton de Tulear, and why do puppies change colour?
faq.answer: In most conformation standards, the adult ground colour is white, with slight light-grey or light-tan/red-roan shading permitted on the ears and only minimal shading (up to 5% to 10%) tolerated on the body. Puppies are frequently born with darker tan, brown, chestnut, or grey patches on the head and body controlled by colour-dilution genes; these markings progressively fade into white or pale champagne by 12 to 18 months of age. Some traditional Malagasy and North American lines also recognize black-and-white and tri-colour varieties.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Coton de Tulear need?
faq.answer: The breed is moderately active and thrives on daily leashed walks at a comfortable pace combined with indoor or backyard games such as fetching a ball, trick training, or agility. Rather than following a rigid daily minute quota, tailor the duration and pace of exercise to the individual dog's age, health, and conditioning.

overview.summary: A rustic, medium-sized Croatian pastoral sheepdog celebrated for its wavy-to-curly jet-black coat, fox-like short-haired head, erect triangular ears, boundless athletic agility, and intensely loyal, biddable devotion to its handler.
overview.description: The Croatian Sheepdog is a lithe, compact, and rectangular-built herding dog combining rustic physical stamina with lightning reflexes and keen intelligence. Originating on the fertile agricultural plains of Slavonia in eastern Croatia, the dog is instantly recognizable by the striking textural contrast between its body and head: its torso is draped in a dense, wavy-to-curly weather-resistant black double coat, while the fox-shaped head, muzzle, and front of the legs are covered in short, smooth hair. Upright triangular ears and dark, almond-shaped eyes give the dog an intensely alert, questioning expression. Naturally agile, swift, and tireless, it thrives as a nimble livestock drover, an enthusiastic dog sports champion, and a deeply bonded household companion that remains an alert, incorruptible protector of its family and territory.
overview.history: The breed represents one of the oldest documented pastoral dog populations in southeastern Europe, with written archival descriptions tracing back over six centuries. In 1374, Peter, Bishop of Đakovo, documented the native Slavonian sheepdog under the Latin name Canis pastoralis croaticus, recording that the black, curly-coated herders had accompanied the Croatian tribes during their seventh-century migrations to the Adriatic. Subsequent ecclesiastical chronicles by Bishop Petar Bakić in 1719 and canonical records by Franjo Gotfrid in 1737 confirmed that the dogs had maintained their distinctive appearance and working traits unchanged across generations. In 1935, veterinarian and university professor Dr. Stjepan Romić launched a systematic selective breeding and preservation program centered in Đakovo, establishing purebred lines that were first exhibited in Zagreb in 1949. International recognition was finalized in 1969, securing the breed's status as a living national cultural treasure of Croatia.
overview.originalPurpose: Driving, gathering, and penning cattle, sheep, and pigs across open Slavonian pasturelands, accompanied by nocturnal farmstead guarding.
currentRoles: Traditional livestock drover, herder, and farm boundary guardian
Canine athlete in agility, flyball, disc dog, and competitive obedience
Search, rescue, and scent detection partner
Vigilant home and rural property watchdog
Devoted companion for energetic outdoor handlers

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly once or twice weekly with a pin brush and metal comb to remove loose undercoat, prevent tangles in the wavy curls, and keep the coat glossy; increase to daily brushing during seasonal spring and autumn molts.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally when soiled or muddy, using a gentle canine shampoo; the weather-resistant coat naturally sheds dried mud and pasture dirt once dry.
notes: The wavy double coat does not require clipping, scissoring, or professional trimming; it should be maintained in its natural rustic state.
Inspect the upright prick ears weekly for dust, wax, or foreign matter, wiping gently with an approved veterinary cleanser.
Check paw pads, toes, and skin for thorns, burrs, or scrapes after running in heavy brush or working stock.
Trim hard, fast-growing nails every two to three weeks to maintain correct compact foot structure.
Brush teeth several times weekly with canine enzymatic toothpaste.
The breed possesses very little natural dog odor and dries quickly after getting wet.

training.difficulty: Easy to moderate; exceptionally intelligent, eager to please, and quick-witted, learning new commands and complex routines in very few repetitions
tips: Use positive reinforcement, high-value food treats, and enthusiastic toy-based play praise.
Begin impulse-control, loose-leash walking, and quiet commands from early puppyhood.
Keep instructional sessions fast-paced, challenging, and varied to prevent boredom.
Avoid repetitive drilling once a skill is mastered, as the dog will invent its own variations.
Never use harsh verbal reprimands or physical coercion, which cause this sensitive shepherd to shut down or lose trust.
Channel natural herding drive into dog sports rather than allowing heel-nipping of running family members or cyclists.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy early, gradually, and positively to varied friendly people, calm vaccinated dogs of all sizes, household noises, vehicles, and novel surfaces. Early structured social guidance ensures natural guardian reservedness matures into poised, self-assured discernment in public.

climates: Temperate climates
Cold and snowy continental winter climates, where the dense double coat provides excellent weather protection
Warm climates, provided indoor cooling, shade, and fresh water are available and exercise occurs during cooler morning or evening hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; deeply attached to its family and prone to separation distress, boredom barking, or pacing if left isolated for extended workdays without interaction.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for medium-sized active working or sporting breeds, adjusted for age, activity level, and metabolic rate.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age, transitioning to two meals daily on a growth formula supporting steady development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support steady metabolism and digestive comfort.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic output, joint support, and lean muscle retention.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily rations carefully using a digital kitchen scale or standard measuring cup, adjusting amounts to maintain a lean, athletic body silhouette where the ribs are easily felt through the wavy coat. Divide daily food into two distinct meals, restrict vigorous exercise immediately before and after eating, and provide cool, clean drinking water continuously.
considerations: Maintain a lean, muscular body condition; excess weight places unnecessary mechanical wear on joints and stifles.
Account for training treats within the total daily caloric allowance to avoid creeping weight gain.
Increase caloric and protein density during active herding seasons or intense agility trial periods.
Avoid feeding high-fat table scraps that can trigger digestive upset or acute pancreatitis.
Provide clean drinking water at all times.
Transition between diet formulas gradually over five to seven days.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs vary significantly based on working workload, training intensity, and outdoor temperature. Consult a veterinarian to establish tailored daily feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The Croatian Sheepdog is an exceptionally robust, healthy, and long-lived pastoral landrace with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years. Having evolved through centuries of practical field selection on rural farms without cosmetic exaggerations, it has maintained high constitutional vitality and possesses very few hereditary genetic disorders. Primary health considerations focus on orthopedic screening for hip dysplasia and patellar luxation, hereditary eye conditions, natural bobtail genetic considerations, and field-related athletic trauma.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the coxofemoral joints, monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening programs
Patellar luxation — displacement of the kneecap from the femoral groove causing intermittent hind-limb hopping, evaluated via clinical orthopedic grading

Natural bobtail (brachyury) genetics — inherited trait caused by a mutation in the T-box transcription factor gene; homozygous mutation is embryonic lethal in dogs, meaning responsible breeders avoid mating two bobtailed individuals together
Hereditary cataracts and progressive retinal atrophy (PRA) — rare ocular conditions monitored through annual certified ophthalmologist examinations
Traumatic athletic injuries — minor sprains, paw pad abrasions, or muscle pulls sustained during high-speed agility, jumping, or livestock herding
Sensitivity to isolation — anxiety and distress resulting from prolonged confinement without mental stimulation or human contact
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has certified radiographic hip clearances, clinical patellar grading, and current certified eye examinations.
Ensure breeders manage bobtail pairings responsibly by avoiding bobtail-to-bobtail matings.
Maintain a lean, muscular body condition throughout life to minimize mechanical wear on joints and ligaments.
Inspect the erect prick ears weekly for dust, wax, or foreign matter, wiping gently with an approved cleanser.
Inspect footpads, toes, and skin after outdoor field work or agility trials for cuts or embedded seeds.
Brush teeth regularly and schedule periodic professional veterinary dental cleanings.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accredited national screening program prior to breeding
Clinical patellar luxation orthopedic evaluation and grading
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong, well-developed jaws with a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the erect prick ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or dirt. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather thoroughly.
health.skinCare: Part the dense wavy coat weekly during brushing to inspect the skin for external parasites, redness, or scratches. The coat naturally sheds dirt and requires minimal bathing beyond regular grooming.

funFacts: The Croatian Sheepdog is documented in church archives in Đakovo dating back to 1374, where Bishop Peter described the breed under the Latin name Canis pastoralis croaticus, noting that its appearance had remained virtually unchanged since the Croats' arrival in the Balkans in the seventh century.

A remarkable proportion of puppies in the breed are born naturally bobtailed (brachyury), a traditional working trait that ranges from a complete lack of tail to a short stump, which is fully accepted in the breed standard.
The breed displays a unique textural contrast: while its body is covered in thick, wavy or curly black hair, its head, face, and the front of its legs are covered in short, smooth, fox-like fur.

In agility and flyball competitions across Europe, the Croatian Sheepdog is celebrated for its incredible turning speed, explosive acceleration, and high jump-to-weight ratio, frequently rivaling the world's elite border collies.

Dr. Stjepan Romić, known as the 'father of the Croatian Sheepdog', surveyed over 800 working dogs across the villages of Slavonia during the 1930s to establish the foundation pedigree that saved the breed.
The breed is known in its native country as the Hrvatski ovčar, and its image has been celebrated on official Croatian postal stamps as a symbol of national heritage.

faq.question: What is a Croatian Sheepdog?
faq.answer: The Croatian Sheepdog (Hrvatski ovčar) is a medium-sized, agile working sheepdog native to eastern Croatia, known for its dense wavy-to-curly black coat, fox-like short-haired head, erect ears, and exceptional herding agility.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Croatian Sheepdog?
faq.answer: Adult males and females stand 40 to 50 cm at the withers (with an ideal height of 45 cm) and typically weigh between 13 and 20 kg, presenting a lean, compact, and muscular athletic build.

faq.question: How long does a Croatian Sheepdog live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, regular exercise, and preventive veterinary care, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Do Croatian Sheepdogs shed a lot, and how are they groomed?
faq.answer: They shed moderately throughout the year and blow their undercoat during seasonal changes. Weekly brushing with a pin brush and comb is sufficient to keep their wavy coat healthy; their coat naturally repels dirt and should never be clipped.

faq.question: Can a Croatian Sheepdog live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Due to their very high energy, strong working drive, and instinct to sound vocal alerts, they are not suited to apartment living and thrive best in a home with a securely fenced yard or working acreage.

faq.question: Are Croatian Sheepdogs good with children and family?
faq.answer: Yes, with active families. They are deeply devoted, affectionate, and playful with familiar children; however, because of their sharp herding instincts, interactions with toddlers should be supervised to ensure they do not attempt to herd or heel-nip.

faq.question: Is the Croatian Sheepdog easy to train?
faq.answer: They are exceptionally intelligent, quick to learn, and eager to please, ranking among the easiest breeds to train using positive reinforcement, high-value treats, and structured dog sports.

faq.question: Why do some Croatian Sheepdogs have short tails?
faq.answer: A natural bobtail (brachyury) occurs naturally in the breed due to an inherited genetic mutation; dogs may be born with a full-length tail, a partial bobtail, or no tail at all, all of which are natural and acceptable in the breed standard.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Croatian Sheepdog need each day?
faq.answer: The breed requires 60 to 90 minutes of vigorous daily physical activity, including brisk runs, trail hiking, fetch sessions, and mental challenges like agility, herding, or tracking.

faq.question: What health tests are recommended for breeding Croatian Sheepdogs?
faq.answer: Recommended pre-breeding screenings include radiographic evaluations for hip dysplasia, clinical patellar luxation grading, and annual veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams.

overview.summary: One of the oldest British retriever breeds, celebrated for its unique water-repellent jacket of small, tight, crisp curls, smooth-coated face, athletic stamina, and sensible, discerning, and self-reliant temperament.
overview.description: The Curly-Coated Retriever is a strong, upstanding, and athletic gundog displaying grace, power, and enduring substance in a balanced, slightly rectangular frame. Unlike all other retrievers, its body from occiput to tail tip is enveloped in a dense mass of small, crisp, and tight curls that lie close to the skin without an undercoat, providing exceptional water repellency and protection against thorny briars and icy waters. In striking contrast to the curly body, the face, foreface, front of the forelegs, and hocks are covered in smooth, short hair. The head is a modified wedge with a shallow stop, paired with large almond-shaped eyes harmonizing with coat color and small, curl-covered drop ears. Intelligent, composed, and independent, the breed combines passion and endurance in marshlands with a gentle, loyal, and dignified presence in the home.
overview.history: Recognized as one of the earliest distinct retriever breeds developed in the British Isles, the Curly-Coated Retriever has historical documentation tracing back to the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Gamekeepers and wildfowlers crossed the now-extinct English Water Spaniel and the St. John's Water Dog of Newfoundland with early Poodle and setter lines to create an unyielding water retriever capable of swimming long distances in freezing coastal waters and navigating impenetrable marshland thickets. The breed was among the very first retrievers to be exhibited in English dog shows, appearing at Birmingham in 1860. The first specialty club was established in England in 1896, and the breed was formally codified at the turn of the twentieth century. While other retriever breeds grew into mass companion popularity, the Curly has remained an authentic, unexaggerated working gundog cherished by wildfowlers, field trialers, and dedicated enthusiasts worldwide.
overview.originalPurpose: Locating, flushing, and retrieving waterfowl, ducks, geese, and upland game from icy coastal estuaries, heavy marsh reeds, and dense briar thickets.
currentRoles: Waterfowl and upland game retrieving gundog
