overview.summary: The Finnish Hound, known natively as the Suomenajokoira, is a medium-sized tricoloured scent hound bred in Finland to track hare and fox across rugged Nordic woodlands and snow. Celebrated for exceptional scenting ability, stamina, and a melodious hunting voice, it pairs a passionate working drive in the field with a peaceful, calm demeanor at home.
overview.description: Noticeably longer in body than it is tall at the withers, the Finnish Hound combines athletic substance with clean, efficient movement. A dense, weatherproof double coat carries a bold black saddle over rich tan shading, accented by crisp white markings on the muzzle, chest, feet, and tail tip. Long, hanging ears, dark expressive eyes, and a purposeful ground-scenting style reflect its deep working background. In the field, it is renowned for hunting independently over long distances, using resonant baying to signal the quarry's path. At home, once given sufficient physical exercise and scent-tracking outlets, it is gentle, composed, and affectionate with its family, though its powerful hunting instinct requires secure fencing and reliable leash management around small wildlife.
overview.history: Systematic breeding of the Finnish Hound began following the establishment of a national kennel club in Finland in 1889, driven by hunters seeking a tracking hound uniquely adapted to deep snow and cold Nordic terrain. By interbreeding regional Finnish hounds with selected Russian, French, German, and Swedish scent hounds, breeders crafted a sturdy dog possessing both endurance and a clear, carrying bark. The breed's distinct tricolour pattern and physical conformation were consolidated in the early twentieth century, establishing the hound as one of the most popular and culturally cherished working breeds in Finland and Scandinavia.
overview.originalPurpose: Tracking and pursuing hare and fox by scent over snowy and forested Nordic terrain, working independently and baying to guide the hunter.
currentRoles: Traditional hare and fox hunting hound
Field tracking and blood tracking athlete
Scent-work and nosework competitor
Active outdoor hiking companion for dedicated sporting households

physical.coatType: Dense, close-fitting double coat consisting of a straight, dense, harsh outer jacket and a short, soft, protective undercoat built for cold Nordic weather.

Striking tricolour pattern featuring a solid black saddle, rich tan on the head and limbs, and white markings on the blaze, neck, chest, feet, and tail tip
Long, supple drop ears set at eye level and hanging close to the cheeks
Dark brown, almond-shaped eyes with a calm, keen, and intelligent expression
Strong, straight legs and oval cat-like paws providing steady traction over rock and snow
Strong tail reaching the hocks, carried level or in a gentle downward curve

traits: Calm and gentle indoors
Friendly and good-tempered
Energetic and tireless in the field
Strongly scent-driven
Independent problem-solver
Persistent tracker
Resonant and melodious barker during pursuit
Alert and attentive

activities: Long daily cross-country walks and hikes on long tracking lines
Structured scent-trailing, blood tracking, and nosework games
Free running in tall, securely enclosed paddocks or training fields
Canicross or steady jogging with conditioned adult dogs in cool weather
Interactive food puzzles and cognitive scent-enrichment games indoors

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice weekly with a rubber curry comb or firm bristle brush to clear loose undercoat, increase circulation, and remove field debris after outdoor excursions.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when dirty or after muddy tracking work, using a gentle canine shampoo that preserves the natural protective oils of the weatherproof coat.
notes: Check long drop ears weekly for moisture, wax, or seeds, cleaning with a veterinarian-recommended ear solution.
Inspect the paws, pads, and between the toes after runs through brambles, frozen crust, or rocky ground.
Trim nails regularly to prevent toe splay and maintain sound footing.
Brush teeth multiple times weekly using canine-formulated toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging; very friendly and cooperative, but selective hearing can emerge once an enticing scent trail is picked up.
tips: Use positive, high-value reward-based methods and avoid harsh reprimands that diminish enthusiasm.
Establish reliable recall foundation early, keeping the hound on lead or long line in unenclosed rural areas where game scent abounds.
Channel instinctual tracking drive into organized nosework and search activities rather than attempting to suppress it.
Teach polite leash manners early to counter strong pulling when following scent lines.
training.socialization: Provide early and varied exposure to diverse environments, livestock, friendly dogs, and household visitors to cultivate an unshakeable, friendly adult demeanor.

climates: Cool and cold climates with snowy winters
Temperate climates
Warm climates with air conditioning, shaded yards, and exercise scheduled during cool morning and evening hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Moderate when adequate daily physical exercise and mental tracking enrichment are provided; under-stimulated hounds may bay or dig out of boredom.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality commercial dry kibble, wet food, or veterinary-formulated working dog diet rich in protein and healthy fats for endurance.

feedingFrequency.puppy: 3 to 4 measured meals daily during growth, transitioning to 2 meals daily around six months of age
feedingFrequency.adult: 2 measured meals per day, adjusted upward during rigorous hunting seasons and downward during rest periods

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily portions based on workload and body condition score, regularly feeling for the ribs beneath the dense coat to ensure the hound stays lean and athletic.
considerations: Increase calorie and fat intake during active hunting autumn and winter months, reducing portions in the off-season to avoid excess weight.
Account for all training rewards within the daily calorie allowance.
Ensure continuous access to fresh, clean drinking water, especially after arduous outdoor tracking sessions.
Avoid feeding large meals immediately before or after strenuous field work.
nutrition.note: Calorie needs vary dramatically between working hunting hounds and companion pets; consult a veterinarian for individualized feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The Finnish Hound is generally a robust and healthy working breed with a typical lifespan of 11 to 14 years. Breed-health programs in Finland focus on radiographic hip evaluation via breeding indices, alongside DNA screening for hereditary cerebellar ataxia (a severe neurodegenerative condition caused by an autosomal recessive SEL1L mutation).
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: developmental laxity of the hip joints monitored closely through national hip-index breeding databases.

Cerebellar ataxia (Finnish Hound type): an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by a mutation in the SEL1L gene, causing early-onset progressive incoordination; detectable via DNA testing.
Ear canal irritation (otitis externa): inflammation related to moisture retention beneath long hanging ear leather.
Hunting-related field injuries: minor pad abrasions, bramble cuts, or sprains sustained while traversing rough terrain.
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has been DNA-tested for cerebellar ataxia (SEL1L gene) and evaluated for hip dysplasia.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, core vaccinations, and appropriate parasite control.
Inspect ears, eyes, and foot pads thoroughly after tracking through brush or snow crust.
Maintain a lean, muscular body condition to prevent unnecessary joint stress.
recommendedScreenings: Cerebellar ataxia (SEL1L gene) DNA test
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accepted screening scheme
Regular veterinary ear and ocular examinations
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic paste to prevent tartar and maintain healthy oral tissues.
health.earCare: Lift and inspect the hanging ears weekly, wiping clean and ensuring the canals dry completely after outdoor rain or wet snow.
health.skinCare: Examine the skin and coat after field work for ticks, grass burrs, or scratches; treat any minor cuts promptly.

idealFor: Hunters and outdoor sportsmen seeking an exceptional, cold-hardy scent tracking partner
Active rural or suburban households with a securely fenced yard and time for long daily hikes
Enthusiasts of blood tracking, search-and-rescue, and competitive nosework sports
Families looking for an affectionate, even-tempered, and calm indoor companion between adventures
notIdealFor: Sedentary owners seeking a low-energy lap dog or apartment pet
Households expecting 100% off-leash reliability in open country near wildlife
Homes unwilling to provide substantial daily physical exercise and mental scent stimulation
Dense urban environments sensitive to loud, carrying baying barks

funFacts: The Finnish Hound, or Suomenajokoira, consistently ranks among the most registered and beloved native dog breeds in Finland.
Bred specifically to navigate thick snow, the hound possesses tight, arched cat-like paws that minimize snow clumping between the toes.
While tracking hare and fox, Finnish Hounds produce a melodious, carrying bay that echoes across dense Nordic forests, allowing handlers to track their progress from miles away.
Despite their fierce determination on a scent trail, Finnish Hounds are famously gentle, friendly, and placid family companions indoors.
Breed development began formally in 1889 following the founding of the Finnish Kennel Club, creating a hound capable of withstanding sub-zero Scandinavian winters.

faq.question: What was the Finnish Hound originally bred to do?
faq.answer: The Finnish Hound was developed in Finland to hunt hare and fox by scent, following trails independently across forests and deep snow while baying melodiously to guide the hunter.

faq.question: How big do Finnish Hounds get?
faq.answer: According to official measurements, males stand 55 to 61 cm at the withers and weigh about 20 to 29 kg, while females measure 52 to 58 cm and weigh about 20 to 25 kg.

faq.question: Are Finnish Hounds good family pets?
faq.answer: Yes, they are known for their calm, affectionate, and friendly nature in the home. They get along well with children and other dogs, provided their high exercise and scent-tracking needs are met daily.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Finnish Hound need daily?
faq.answer: A healthy adult Finnish Hound needs 60 to 120 minutes of vigorous daily physical activity. Long walks on tracking lines, hiking, and nosework games are ideal for keeping their minds and bodies engaged.

faq.question: What health tests should I look for in a Finnish Hound?
faq.answer: Prospective owners should ensure that both parent dogs have documented DNA testing for cerebellar ataxia (SEL1L gene) and certified hip evaluations.

faq.question: Can a Finnish Hound live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Their high energy, intense scent drive, and loud carrying bay make apartment living challenging, and they thrive best in homes with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Do Finnish Hounds shed a lot?
faq.answer: They are moderate shedders. Their dense double coat sheds hair continuously and blows coat seasonally, requiring weekly brushing with a rubber curry mitt to remove loose undercoat.

faq.question: What colors do Finnish Hounds come in?
faq.answer: The classic coloration is tricolour, consisting of a rich black saddle over the back and neck, warm tan on the head and limbs, and white markings on the muzzle, chest, feet, and tail tip.

faq.question: How long do Finnish Hounds typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy for a healthy Finnish Hound is 11 to 14 years when supported by proper nutrition, regular exercise, and preventive veterinary care.

overview.summary: An ancient, fox-like Nordic spitz renowned as the national dog of Finland, celebrated for its square athletic build, glowing red-gold stand-off double coat, lively intelligence, and unique rhythmic barking style used to indicate treed game birds.
overview.description: The Finnish Spitz is a smaller than medium-sized, square-profiled Nordic hunting dog that presents a striking, fox-like appearance. Lean, firm, and proud in posture, the dog carries itself with effortless dignity and agile coordination. Its dense stand-off double coat glows with bright golden-red or reddish-brown coloration, complemented by a soft, lighter undercoat, a pronounced neck ruff in males, and a plumed tail that arches vigorously forward and downward to rest firmly against the thigh. The head is cleanly chiseled with a clean scissor bite, dark almond-shaped eyes that express eager intelligence, and sharply pointed, erect ears that swivel constantly to register woodland sounds. In the home, it is a clean, affectionate, and cheerful family companion, while in the forest it acts as an impassioned, fearless hunter with an explosive gallop and an extraordinary vocal capacity.
overview.history: The ancestors of the Finnish Spitz accompanied Finno-Ugric tribes as they migrated into Fennoscandia several thousand years ago, serving as versatile aboriginal hunting and camp dogs across the taiga. By the late nineteenth century, cross-breeding with imported foreign dogs threatened the purity of the native landrace. Foreseeing the extinction of this ancient hunting partner, Finnish sportsmen Hugo Roos and Hugo Sandberg embarked on expeditions into northern forests to locate pure-blooded native specimens, establishing a studbook and standard in 1892. Originally called the Finnish Barking Bird Dog, the name was refined to Suomenpystykorva in 1897. In 1979, the breed was officially declared the National Dog of Finland, cementing its status as a living cultural treasure. Over the twentieth century, it gained international admiration as both a specialized bird dog and an engaging family pet.
overview.originalPurpose: Trailing, baying, and bark-pointing forest game birds (especially capercaillie and black grouse) up in trees, as well as tracking small fur-bearing animals, elk, and bear across dense boreal woods.
currentRoles: Traditional bark-pointing hunting dog for forest game birds

Watchful household watchdog
Canine athlete in agility, tracking, obedience, and rally trials

Alert, vigilant, and naturally observant watchdog
Courageous and determined in pursuing tasks
Polite yet reserved toward strangers without timidity or aggression
Gentle and patient with familiar children
Naturally vocal and communicative, possessing a musical hunting bark
Sensitive to handler emotions and household tone
Strong hunting instinct with high curiosity toward birds and small wildlife

exercise.level: Moderate to high; requires daily physical exercise and regular mental stimulation through scent tracking, play, and exploration
activities: Daily brisk neighborhood walks and woodland trail hikes on a secure leash
Interactive fetch and fetch-retrieval games in a securely fenced yard
Structured scent tracking and search enrichment games

Problem-solving cognitive toys and food puzzle challenges

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice weekly using a slicker brush and metal pin comb to lift loose hair and keep the stand-off coat clean; increase to daily brushing during seasonal undercoat shedding in spring and autumn.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally when muddy or soiled, as the harsh double coat is naturally clean, odorless, and dirt-repellent.
notes: Never shave or clip the double coat; the outer guard hairs and soft undercoat provide critical thermal insulation against winter freezing and summer heat.
Use an undercoat rake during spring shedding to remove compacted dead underfur without damaging the outer guard hairs.
Inspect the small erect ears weekly for dust, wax, or foreign matter, wiping the outer leather gently.
Trim strong, fast-growing nails every two to three weeks to maintain compact, cat-like foot posture.
Brush teeth multiple times weekly using dog-safe enzymatic toothpaste.
The coat has no strong doggy odor and sheds dried dirt naturally once brushed.

training.difficulty: Moderate; highly intelligent, alert, and eager to learn, but possesses an independent streak and will shut down if subjected to harsh handling or repetitive drills
tips: Use positive reinforcement, praise, and small high-value treats.
Keep sessions brief, cheerful, and fast-paced (5 to 10 minutes) to prevent boredom.
Teach a reliable quiet cue from early puppyhood to manage natural watchdog barking instincts.
Acknowledge its independent decision-making nature and build voluntary cooperation through mutual respect.
Avoid harsh verbal corrections or forceful methods, which cause this sensitive spitz to lose trust.
Always exercise within a securely fenced yard or on a leash, as its hunting drive can trigger sudden pursuit of birds or squirrels.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy calmly and positively to diverse people, friendly vaccinated dogs, household appliances, traffic sounds, and varied environments. Early socialization prevents natural reservedness around strangers from turning into aloof suspicion, ensuring a balanced, confident companion.

climates: Cold and snowy Nordic climates, where the dense double coat provides exceptional insulation
Temperate climates
Warm climates provided air-conditioned indoor shelter, shade, and fresh water are available and exercise is restricted to early morning or late evening hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; deeply attached to family and can develop nuisance barking, distress, or boredom behaviors if left alone for extended periods without companionship or mental tasks.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for medium-sized, active breeds, adjusted for life stage and physical workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age, transitioning to two meals daily on a growth formula supporting steady development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support steady metabolism and digestive comfort.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic output, joint support, and lean muscle retention.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure food portions carefully using a digital kitchen scale or standard measuring cup, as the breed possesses an efficient northern metabolism and can gain excess weight rapidly if overfed. Divide daily rations into two distinct meals, restrict vigorous exercise immediately before and after eating, and provide cool, clean drinking water at all times.
considerations: Maintain a lean, muscular body condition where the waistline is clearly visible and ribs are easily felt beneath the dense coat.
Account for training treats within the daily caloric budget to prevent stealth weight gain.
Avoid feeding high-fat table scraps that can trigger digestive upset or pancreatitis.
Provide clean drinking water, especially during active exercise in warm weather.
Adjust daily caloric intake upward for dogs active in autumn field hunting and downward during sedentary seasons.
Transition between diet formulas gradually over five to seven days.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs vary significantly based on age, sterilization status, and daily exercise. Consult a veterinarian to establish tailored daily feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The Finnish Spitz is a hardy, robust northern hunting dog with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 15 years. Developed through centuries of natural selection in the Finnish wilderness, it enjoys strong overall constitutional vitality. Primary hereditary health priorities include idiopathic epilepsy (which has been the focus of extensive Finnish veterinary genetic research identifying risk associations in the ADAM23 gene), patellar luxation, hip dysplasia, hereditary eye conditions (such as cataracts and progressive retinal atrophy), and diabetes mellitus.
commonConditions: Idiopathic epilepsy — recurrent unprovoked seizures, frequently presenting with focal-onset semiology; genetic research has identified a common risk haplotype in the ADAM23 gene on chromosome 37, and responsible breeding programs actively track pedigree incidence to minimize risk
Patellar luxation — kneecap displacement from the femoral groove causing intermittent hopping or hind-limb lameness, monitored through national orthopedic screening programs
Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the hip joints that can lead to osteoarthritis and stiffness, evaluated radiographically prior to breeding
Hereditary eye conditions — including juvenile cataracts and progressive retinal atrophy (PRA), screened through regular ophthalmologist examinations
Diabetes mellitus — an endocrine metabolic disorder documented at slightly elevated rates in Finnish veterinary health registries
Tooth absence and bite deviations — missing premolars or irregular alignment monitored during conformation assessments
preventiveCare: Acquire puppies from breeding stock with certified pre-breeding clearances for patellas, hips, and eyes, and verify that the pedigree has been carefully evaluated for epilepsy history.
Maintain a lean, athletic body condition to avoid placing unnecessary mechanical strain on stifle and hip joints.
Inspect the small erect ears weekly for wax or dust buildup and clean gently with an approved ear cleanser.
Brush teeth multiple times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste to prevent premature dental decay.
Avoid overfeeding and monitor body weight regularly to prevent obesity and associated metabolic risks.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: Clinical patellar luxation examination and grading prior to breeding
Comprehensive ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist prior to breeding
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accredited national screening scheme prior to breeding
Comprehensive pedigree risk assessment regarding idiopathic epilepsy prior to mating
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using dog-specific enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong jaws with a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the small erect ears weekly for wax accumulation, moisture, or redness. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather thoroughly.
health.skinCare: Part the dense double coat weekly to inspect the skin for external parasites, dryness, or irritation. The coat naturally sheds dirt and requires minimal skin intervention beyond regular brushing.

funFacts: In 1979, the Finnish Spitz was officially declared the National Dog of Finland, where it is regarded as an indispensable living cultural treasure.

In Finland, the breed is celebrated for its unique hunting style known as bark-pointing: when it trees a forest bird, it wags its tail, shifts its weight to distract the bird, and unleashes a rapid, musical bark that can reach up to 160 barks per minute.
An annual national hunting competition in Finland crowns the finest working hound with the prestigious title of 'King of the Barkers' (Haukkukuningas).

English breed enthusiasts, led by Lady Kitty Ritson in the 1920s, coined the affectionate nickname 'Finkie' because its native Finnish name, Suomenpystykorva, proved difficult for English speakers to pronounce.
Finnish Spitz puppies are often born dark grey or blackish, gradually molting into their radiant red-gold adult coloration as their coat matures.

The Finnish Spitz was preserved from near-extinction in the late 1800s when two dedicated sportsmen, Hugo Roos and Hugo Sandberg, recognized the native dog's plight and established the foundational studbook.
Finnish folklore considers the breed's glowing red coat a reflection of the northern forest autumn colors, blending naturally into the golden birch and pine woodlands.

faq.question: What is a Finnish Spitz?
faq.answer: The Finnish Spitz is a medium-sized Nordic hunting dog originating in Finland, known for its fox-like face, erect ears, plumed tail curled over the back, glowing red-gold double coat, and unique bark-pointing hunting style.

faq.question: Why does the Finnish Spitz bark so much?
faq.answer: Barking is an essential working trait bred into the dog for thousands of years. In the forest, the dog tracks game birds into trees and barks continuously to hold the bird's attention and guide the hunter; while this instinct can be managed with early training, it is a natural characteristic of the breed.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Finnish Spitz?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 44 to 50 cm (ideal 47 cm) at the withers and weigh 14 to 17 kg, while adult females stand 39 to 45 cm (ideal 42 cm) and weigh 10 to 13 kg, presenting an agile, almost square build.

faq.question: How long does a Finnish Spitz live?
faq.answer: The breed is known for robust health and good longevity, typically enjoying a lifespan of 12 to 15 years with proper care and nutrition.

faq.question: What does the Finnish Spitz coat look like, and how often does it shed?
faq.answer: The coat is a dense stand-off double coat with a soft, pale undercoat and bright red-gold or reddish-brown guard hairs. It sheds moderately year-round and blows its undercoat heavily twice a year in spring and autumn, requiring regular brushing.

faq.question: Is a Finnish Spitz good with children and other pets?
faq.answer: Yes. Within its own household, it is remarkably gentle, playful, and affectionate with children; it generally coexists peacefully with other family dogs, but its high prey drive requires supervision around pet birds and small rodents.

faq.question: Can a Finnish Spitz live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. While it is clean and compact indoors, its natural inclination to sound an alarm bark at unfamiliar noises and its need for active exercise make it poorly suited to noise-sensitive apartments; it thrives best in a house with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Is the Finnish Spitz easy to train?
faq.answer: The breed is highly intelligent and quick to learn, but it has an independent nature and easily becomes bored by repetitive drills. It responds best to patient, positive reinforcement training and short, varied sessions.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Finnish Spitz need each day?
faq.answer: The breed requires 45 to 60 minutes of daily physical activity, including brisk leashed walks, active play sessions, and scent enrichment games to keep its active mind engaged.

faq.question: Can a Finnish Spitz tolerate hot and cold weather?
faq.answer: Its double coat provides superb protection against freezing Nordic winters; it can tolerate warm weather if given air-conditioned indoor shelter, shade, and fresh water, with exercise scheduled during cooler morning or evening hours.

faq.question: What health conditions are known in the Finnish Spitz?
faq.answer: The breed is generally very healthy, but important health priorities include idiopathic epilepsy (which has been mapped to genetic markers in research studies), patellar luxation, hip dysplasia, eye conditions (cataracts and progressive retinal atrophy), and diabetes mellitus.

faq.question: What is the 'King of the Barkers'?
faq.answer: The 'King of the Barkers' is an annual championship hunting contest in Finland where top working Finnish Spitz dogs compete in the forest, evaluated on their tracking skill, endurance, and rapid bark-pointing rate.

overview.summary: An athletic, lively, and fearless British earthdog known for its sleek, predominantly white smooth coat, classic hunter-like stance on the tiptoe of expectation, V-shaped drop ears, and boundless game courage.
overview.description: The Fox Terrier (Smooth) is a compact, balanced, and energetic working terrier that embodies bone and strength in a small compass, standing like a well-made, short-backed hunter horse. Built with straight forelegs, a deep narrow chest, and strong muscular hindquarters, the dog was developed to accompany mounted foxhound packs and bolt red foxes from subterranean rocky earths. Its coat is straight, flat, hard, dense, and abundant, dominated by a crisp white ground highlighted by black, tan, or black-and-tan markings. The head is flat and moderately narrow, tapering smoothly towards the eyes and powerful jaws, framed by small, dark, circular eyes radiating keen expression and neat V-shaped drop ears. In family life, it is an affectionate, spirited, and playful companion that remains an alert watchdog and a determined, tireless athlete.
overview.history: The breed developed in eighteenth-century England alongside the rise of organized mounted foxhunting. Huntsmen required an agile, courageous terrier that could run alongside hounds and enter underground burrows to bolt foxes that had gone to ground. Breeding programs crossed ancient black-and-tan working terriers with smooth-coated Greyhounds, Bull Terriers, and Beagles to enhance speed, tenacity, scenting ability, and white coloration that prevented huntsmen from mistaking the dog for a fox. The breed was among the very first to enter modern conformation shows in England during the 1860s, and its first independent breed club was established in 1876. While originally registered under the collective Fox Terrier designation alongside its wire-coated relative, the two varieties were officially separated into distinct purebred breeds in the late twentieth century. Today, it is recognized globally as an adaptable family pet, competitive show champion, and enthusiastic canine sports competitor.

health.overview: The Fox Terrier (Smooth) is a hardy, robust, and long-lived earthdog with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 15 years. Developed over centuries for demanding physical work, it enjoys strong overall constitutional vitality. Primary hereditary health priorities include patellar luxation, primary lens luxation (PLL, screenable via DNA testing for the ADAMTS17 mutation), spinocerebellar ataxia with myokymia and seizures (SAMS / SCA, linked to the KCNJ10 gene), congenital sensorineural deafness in predominantly white individuals, and cardiac conditions.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation — displacement of the kneecap from the femoral groove causing intermittent hopping or hind-limb lameness, monitored through clinical orthopedic grading

Primary lens luxation (PLL) — an inherited ocular disorder caused by an autosomal recessive mutation in the ADAMTS17 gene, causing lens displacement and acute secondary glaucoma, fully preventable through DNA testing

Spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA / SAMS) — an inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by a mutation in the KCNJ10 gene, leading to progressive ataxia, muscle twitching (myokymia), and seizures, screenable via DNA testing
Congenital sensorineural deafness — unilateral or bilateral hearing loss associated with extreme piebald white pigmentation, evaluable via Brainstem Auditory Evoked Response (BAER) testing
Cardiac conditions — congenital heart anomalies including pulmonic stenosis and murmurs, monitored via veterinary auscultation and echocardiography
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease — aseptic necrosis of the femoral head in young dogs, leading to hip pain and lameness
Cataracts and distichiasis — ocular conditions monitored through annual certified ophthalmologist examinations
Traumatic injuries — minor cuts, punctures, or pad scrapes sustained while digging or vigorously pursuing quarry
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has certified clearances for patellar luxation, annual eye examinations, cardiac evaluations, and DNA clearances for PLL and spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA).
Perform BAER hearing testing on puppies from lines with extensive white head markings.
Maintain a lean, athletic body condition throughout life to minimize mechanical wear on joints and ligaments.
Inspect folding ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or dirt, wiping gently with a veterinary ear wash.
Brush teeth regularly and schedule periodic professional veterinary dental cleanings.
Administer consistent year-round parasite prevention against fleas, ticks, and heartworms.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: Clinical patellar luxation orthopedic evaluation and grading
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Congenital cardiac examination including auscultation by a veterinary specialist
DNA marker test for Primary Lens Luxation (ADAMTS17 gene mutation) prior to breeding
DNA marker test for Spinocerebellar Ataxia (KCNJ10 gene mutation) prior to breeding
Brainstem Auditory Evoked Response (BAER) hearing test
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has powerful jaws with a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the small V-shaped drop ears weekly for wax accumulation, moisture, or redness. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather thoroughly.
health.skinCare: Part the smooth coat weekly during brushing to inspect the skin for external parasites, redness, or dry patches. The coat naturally sheds dirt and requires minimal bathing beyond regular grooming.

funFacts: The Smooth Fox Terrier was the very first breed in the Fox Terrier family to be formally recognized and given an official breed standard in England in 1876.

A Smooth Fox Terrier named Ch. Warren Remedy achieved historic canine fame by winning Best in Show at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show three consecutive years (1907, 1908, and 1909), a record that has never been matched.
U.S. President Herbert Hoover owned two beloved Smooth Fox Terriers named Big Ben and Sonnie during his years in the White House.
The famous painting 'His Master's Voice' by Francis Barraud, which became the global corporate logo for RCA Victor and HMV, depicted a terrier named Nipper, widely believed to be a Fox Terrier cross.
The breed was historically described as 'standing like a well-made, short-backed hunter horse', reflecting its clean, athletic proportions designed to cover ground without cloddiness.

Because of their exceptional agility, quick wit, and trainability, Smooth Fox Terriers were among the most popular performing circus dogs in Europe and America during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

faq.question: What is a Smooth Fox Terrier?
faq.answer: The Smooth Fox Terrier is a small, athletic British working terrier known for its sleek, hard white-and-patched coat, V-shaped drop ears, lively energy, and historic role in fox hunting.

faq.question: What is the difference between a Smooth Fox Terrier and a Wire Fox Terrier?
faq.answer: While both share similar body proportions, size, and hunting temperament, the Smooth Fox Terrier has a short, flat, smooth coat that requires minimal grooming, whereas the Wire Fox Terrier has a harsh, wiry double coat with facial furnishings that requires hand-stripping.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Smooth Fox Terrier?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 36 to 39 cm at the withers and weigh 7.5 to 8 kg, while adult females stand 33 to 36 cm and weigh 7 to 7.5 kg, presenting an agile, compact outline.

faq.question: How long does a Smooth Fox Terrier live?
faq.answer: The breed enjoys good health and longevity, typically living a lifespan of 12 to 15 years with proper nutrition, exercise, and preventive veterinary care.

faq.question: Do Smooth Fox Terriers shed a lot, and how are they groomed?
faq.answer: They shed low to moderate amounts year-round. Their smooth coat is low-maintenance, requiring only a weekly brushing with a rubber hound mitt or soft brush, occasional nail trims, and ear checks; they do not need professional clipping.

faq.question: Can a Smooth Fox Terrier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes, provided they receive adequate daily exercise and play. While energetic outdoors, their compact size makes them adaptable to apartment living, though early training of a quiet cue is helpful to manage alert watchdog barking.

faq.question: Are Smooth Fox Terriers good with children and other pets?
faq.answer: They are affectionate, sturdy, and playful with familiar children; however, because of their high prey drive, they are generally unsafe around pet rodents, rabbits, or birds, and they may be assertive with other dogs if not socialized early.

faq.question: Is the Smooth Fox Terrier easy to train?
faq.answer: They are very smart, eager to learn, and food-motivated, but have an independent terrier mindset. Training requires patient, reward-based methods and variety rather than repetitive drills.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Smooth Fox Terrier need each day?
faq.answer: The breed requires 45 to 60 minutes of daily physical activity, including brisk walks, fetch sessions, and mental challenges like agility, puzzle toys, or barn hunt games.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for breeding Smooth Fox Terriers?
faq.answer: Recommended pre-breeding screenings include patellar luxation evaluations, annual veterinary eye exams, cardiac examinations, and DNA testing for primary lens luxation (PLL) and spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA).

overview.summary: The Gascon Saintongeois is an athletic French scenthound prized for its acute nose, resonant voice, steady endurance, and natural pack-working drive. Recognised in two size varieties—the larger Grand and the medium-sized Petit—it wears a short, dense white coat marked with black patches and pale tan points. While composed, gentle, and responsive with its handlers, its deep-rooted trailing instincts require dedicated daily exercise, scent-based enrichment, and secure outdoor containment.
overview.description: Combining muscular substance with refined French hound lines, the Gascon Saintongeois has a slightly rectangular build with a height-to-body-length ratio of 10 to 10.5. The head features divergent skull and muzzle planes of equal length, a domed and narrow skull with a pronounced occipital peak, a slight stop, a strong slightly arched nasal bridge, and oval brown eyes with a gentle, trusting expression. Thin, inward-curling ears are set well below eye level and reach at least to the tip of the black nose. A deep, broad chest extending to the elbows, firm back, well-muscled hindquarters, and sabre-carried tapering tail support effortless, regular movement across rough terrain. The short, tight coat is white with black patches—sometimes moderately ticked—accompanied by pale tan cheek and eyebrow markings and an occasional dead-leaf 'roebuck mark' on the lower thigh. The Grand variety is a large pack and tracking hound, whereas the Petit variety is a compact, versatile medium hound.
overview.history: In the mid-19th century, Count Joseph de Carayon-Latour of Château de Virelade in Gironde sought to save the nearly extinct Chien de Saintonge, one of France's oldest royal pack hounds. Obtaining the last surviving Saintongeois dogs—recorded as two males and one female—he crossed them with Baron de Ruble's Grand Bleu de Gascogne hounds. This alliance established the Grand Gascon Saintongeois, though the pure Chien de Saintonge gradually vanished in the process. During the mid-20th century, hunters in southwestern France selected the smallest puppies from Grand Gascon Saintongeois litters—initially to pursue hare—and fixed a distinct, smaller variety known as the Petit Gascon Saintongeois.
overview.originalPurpose: Pursuing large game (such as roe deer, red deer, and wild boar) and hare by scent, with the Grand variety working in packs or individually as a tracking hound (limier) and the Petit variety developed as a hare specialist and versatile gun-hunting hound.
currentRoles: Pack and small-group hunting scenthound for large game and hare
Individual cold-trail tracking hound (limier)
Nosework, mantrailing, and scent-sport participant
Active rural companion for households experienced with working hounds

grooming.level: Low to moderate. The short, close-lying coat is easy to keep tidy, though routine ear, foot, and skin checks are essential after outdoor excursions.
grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice weekly with a soft bristle brush or hound glove to lift loose hair and surface dust, and inspect the skin after woodland or brush walks.
grooming.bathing: Bathe occasionally with a gentle dog-specific shampoo when muddy or odorous, avoiding frequent washing that strips natural skin oils.
notes: Inspect the long, low-set curled ears several times a week for trapped moisture, debris, redness, or unpleasant odour.
Dry the ear leather and canal entrance gently after wet weather or swimming.
Check between the toes and around the black pads after field exercise for burrs, thorns, foxtails, or cuts.
Trim nails regularly so the feet remain compact and well supported.
Brush the teeth several times a week using canine toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate. While naturally calm, cooperative, and accustomed to following pack order, the breed possesses a powerful trailing instinct and a resonant voice that require patient, reward-based guidance.
tips: Build recall gradually using high-value rewards inside enclosed spaces before practicing on a long line outdoors.
Channel the hound's natural desire to puzzle out cold trails into structured tracking or scent-detection games.
Teach polite loose-leash walking early so the dog does not pull when catching ground or air scents.
Establish calm indoor routines and reward quiet behaviour to manage vocalization in residential settings.
Never rely on off-leash voice control near unfenced roads, livestock, or wildlife corridors.
Practice cooperative handling for ear cleaning, nail care, and veterinary examinations from puppyhood.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and positively to diverse people, calm dogs, household noises, vehicles, and varied footing. Because these hounds are naturally sociable with other dogs, structured group interactions work well when paired with handler focus and safe boundaries around smaller pets and wildlife.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced canine diet suited to the dog's life stage, variety size, body condition, and workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a balanced growth formula in three to four measured meals per day for young puppies, tapering to two daily meals as the dog matures while monitoring steady skeletal growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed two measured meals daily, adjusting calorie intake to match body condition and seasonal hunting or endurance activity.
feedingFrequency.senior: Feed measured meals tailored to weight maintenance, mobility, dental health, and any age-related veterinary needs.

nutrition.guidelines: Select a complete diet appropriate for medium-to-large active hounds and adjust rations using regular body-condition scoring rather than fixed package averages alone. Working hounds covering long distances in the field require higher energy density than companion dogs, and meals should be scheduled with rest periods before and after vigorous exercise.
considerations: Adjust daily portions to reflect seasonal changes in exercise and field work.
Allow rest before and after strenuous running rather than feeding large meals immediately around heavy exercise.
Count training treats within the total daily caloric intake.
Ensure constant access to fresh, clean drinking water.
Transition between foods gradually over seven to ten days to prevent digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Adult weights of 30 to 35 kg for males and 26 to 30 kg for females reflect the larger Grand variety, whereas Petit Gascon Saintongeois dogs are proportionally lighter; portion sizes should always be individualized to variety, stature, and body condition.

health.overview: The Gascon Saintongeois is generally a hardy, athletic working scenthound, and major cynological registries do not publish a mandatory breed-specific genetic disease panel. Conformation guidelines emphasize sound bone, a firm back, well-angulated hocks, and dark, close-fitting eyelids, while the long, low-set pendant ears and field lifestyle warrant attentive ear and paw care. In peer-reviewed veterinary literature, an isolated clinical case report documented a high-grade malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor of the vagus nerve causing cranial nerve dysfunction in a 5-year-old male Gascon Saintongeois, representing a rare individual case rather than an established breed-wide predisposition.
preventiveCare: Schedule routine veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and year-round internal and external parasite control.
Inspect and clean the long, curled ears regularly to prevent moisture buildup and otitis.
Examine feet, pads, ears, and skin after woodland or field outings for ticks, grass awns, and brush abrasions.
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition to protect joints during endurance activity.
Provide daily home tooth brushing and periodic veterinary oral evaluations.
Use secure fencing and leashes or long lines to prevent traffic injuries while trailing scents.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times weekly with dog-safe enzymatic toothpaste and schedule professional veterinary dental assessments as needed to control tartar and periodontal disease.
health.earCare: Because the thin, curled ears hang low and cover the ear canal, inspect them several times a week for redness, waxy buildup, or odour, and dry them thoroughly after wet outings using a veterinarian-approved cleanser when needed.
health.skinCare: Check the short, close white-and-black coat after outdoor runs for ticks, bramble scratches, and burrs, and consult a veterinarian promptly if localized irritation or hair loss develops.

funFacts: Count Joseph de Carayon-Latour created the breed in the mid-19th century at Château de Virelade by crossing the last three surviving Chien de Saintonge hounds with Baron de Ruble's Grand Bleu de Gascogne pack.

One breed encompasses two distinct size varieties developed a century apart: the 19th-century Grand for large game and the mid-20th-century Petit, originally selected by southwestern French hunters for pursuing hare.
Its white coat with black patches and pale tan points often displays a distinctive dead-leaf brown spot on the lower thigh traditionally called the 'roebuck mark' (marque de chevreuil).
In field work, it is prized as an 'excellent rapprocheur'—a methodical cold-nosed tracker capable of working out overnight scent trails on the ground or on brushed vegetation.
The breed's deep, resonant howling voice increases in volume as the hound closes in on the quarry's starting point and remains steady throughout the chase.

faq.question: What is a Gascon Saintongeois?
faq.answer: The Gascon Saintongeois is a historic French scenthound bred in southwestern France for tracking and pack hunting. It exists in two recognized size varieties—the large Grand and the medium-sized Petit—sharing the same conformation, white-and-black coat with pale tan points, and calm, pack-oriented temperament.

faq.question: What is the difference between the Grand and Petit Gascon Saintongeois?
faq.answer: Size and historical specialization are the primary differences. Grand males measure 65 to 72 cm at the withers and females 62 to 68 cm, whereas Petit males measure 56 to 62 cm and females 54 to 59 cm (each with a ±1 cm tolerance). The Grand was developed in the mid-19th century for large game and hare, while the Petit was selected in the mid-20th century from smaller Grand littermates primarily for hare and versatile gun hunting.

faq.question: How much does a Gascon Saintongeois weigh?
faq.answer: Reference data for the larger Grand variety lists adult males at 30 to 35 kg and females at 26 to 30 kg, whereas the medium-sized Petit variety is proportionally lighter. Because formal conformation rules do not fix an official weight range, body condition and muscular balance are prioritized over scale numbers.

faq.question: What coat colours and markings are typical of the Gascon Saintongeois?
faq.answer: The short, tight coat has a white background marked with black patches and occasional moderate ticking. Black patches typically cover the ears and surround the eyes, paired with pale tan cheeks, tan points above the eyes, tan traces inside the ears, and sometimes a dead-leaf fawn 'roebuck mark' on the lower thigh.

faq.question: Is the Gascon Saintongeois good with other dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. Having been bred for generations to hunt in packs, the breed has an instinctive affinity for working and living alongside other dogs. Early socialization and supervision are still important for smooth household introductions.

faq.question: Can a Gascon Saintongeois be walked off leash?
faq.answer: Off-leash exercise should be restricted to securely fenced areas. Like most dedicated scenthounds, a Gascon Saintongeois can lock onto a fresh or overnight trail and tune out handler recall near roads or wildlife.

faq.question: Does the Gascon Saintongeois have known breed-specific health problems?
faq.answer: No prevalent breed-wide hereditary disease list is established in major kennel registries, and only isolated clinical cases—such as a single published report of a vagus nerve sheath tumor—appear in veterinary literature. Routine preventive care focuses on checking the long pendant ears, protecting the feet during field work, and maintaining lean body condition.

faq.question: How long does a Gascon Saintongeois typically live?
faq.answer: Typical life expectancy is 12 to 14 years (with some reference datasets listing 11 to 13 years), depending on genetics, workload, nutrition, and preventive veterinary care.

overview.summary: The German Longhaired Pointer is a powerful, athletic German gundog developed to search, point and retrieve game across fields, woodland and water. It combines a calm, generally biddable temperament with substantial exercise needs and a dense, feathered coat.
overview.description: This medium-to-large working dog has a strong, muscular outline, brown eyes, hanging ears and a close-fitting coat that is smooth or slightly wavy. Longer feathering appears on the ears, backs of the legs and tail, while the hair below the hocks is shorter. The breed was developed for versatile hunting work rather than a single task, so it typically benefits from regular outdoor activity, scent-based games and structured training. Individual temperament, sociability and exercise needs still vary, and a working-bred dog may be a poor match for a household unable to provide sustained activity and engagement.
overview.history: The breed developed in Germany from several types of hunting dog, including bird, hawk and water dogs and scent hounds. Pure breeding was established from 1879, and Baron von Schorlemer prepared an early breed standard in 1897. The breed remains classified as a versatile pointing gundog, with work expected in fields, woodland and water.
overview.originalPurpose: Versatile hunting work, including searching for, pointing and retrieving game on land and in water.
currentRoles: Versatile hunting and field work
Pointing and retrieving
Scent work and other structured dog activities
Active companion in a home able to meet its working-dog needs

physical.coatType: Dense double coat with a close-fitting, firm outer coat that is smooth or slightly wavy; the undercoat is well developed.
physical.coatLength: On the back and sides, the coat is typically 3–5 cm long. Hair may be longer under the neck, on the chest and belly, with feathering on the ears, backs of the legs and tail.
coatColors: Brown with white or speckled markings, especially on the chest and feet
Mottled or flecked roan with small brown spots on a white background
Brown and white, including large patches or saddle/blanket markings
physical.sheddingLevel: Sheds; the dense coat and feathering require regular brushing, especially after outdoor work.
distinctiveFeatures: Strong, muscular, balanced build suited to sustained field work
Brown eyes and hanging ears with wavy feathering
Dense, close-fitting coat with a good undercoat
Feathering on the backs of the legs and a plumed tail
Coat colours based on brown, white and roan patterns
Ground-covering movement with drive from the hindquarters

traits: Generally calm and even-tempered
Good-natured and usually responsive to consistent training
Alert and closely engaged with its handler
Energetic, with a strong instinct for hunting and searching
Often people-oriented, though individual sociability varies
Can become restless or develop unwanted behaviours without sufficient activity

exercise.level: Very high; this is a working gundog that needs substantial daily physical activity and mental work. The UK Kennel Club describes its exercise requirement as more than two hours per day.
activities: Long, purposeful walks and hikes appropriate to age and fitness
Supervised retrieving and field-style games
Scent work, tracking and search games
Swimming where safe and suitable
Reward-based obedience and other structured dog sports
Securely managed exercise while recall and hunting-drive control are being trained

grooming.level: Moderate; brush more often after field work or when the coat tangles.
grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly at least several times each week, checking the feathering, tail and the hair around and behind the ears for knots, burrs and debris. Increase grooming after walks through dense vegetation.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when needed with a dog-appropriate shampoo, rinse thoroughly and dry the dense coat well.
notes: Inspect the ears regularly for wax, moisture, debris or irritation.
Check the feathering and tail for burrs, tangles and abrasions after outdoor activity.
Trim nails as needed and maintain routine dental care.
Do not shave the coat routinely; ask a professional groomer or veterinarian about any coat or skin concern.

training.difficulty: Moderate; the breed is described as trainable and biddable, but its stamina and hunting motivation require consistent handling and meaningful daily work.
tips: Use reward-based training with clear, consistent cues.
Teach recall progressively in controlled settings before considering greater freedom outdoors.
Channel searching and retrieving instincts into structured games.
Introduce calm, positive exposure to people, dogs, surfaces and environments from an early age.
Keep sessions engaging and appropriate to the dog's age, health and arousal level.
training.socialization: Provide early, ongoing positive socialisation and practise calm behaviour in varied environments. Do not assume that a generally good-natured breed description guarantees how an individual dog will respond.

climates: Provide shade, ventilation and fresh water in warm weather.
Avoid strenuous exercise during hot or humid periods and adjust activity to the individual dog.
A secure outdoor area is useful, but a yard does not replace structured exercise and training.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: A reliable breed-wide duration is not established. Build alone time gradually and provide adequate exercise and enrichment; avoid routinely leaving the dog alone for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced dog food suitable for the dog's life stage, body condition, activity and health.
nutrition.guidelines: Set portions according to the food's feeding guidance, body condition and the dog's workload. Keep clean water available and review diet and body condition with a veterinarian as activity or life stage changes.
considerations: Working dogs may need different energy intake on active days, but portions should be adjusted to body condition rather than assumed from breed alone.
Avoid vigorous exercise immediately around meals when advised by the veterinarian, particularly for a large, deep-chested dog.
Introduce dietary changes gradually and seek veterinary advice for persistent gastrointestinal signs, itching or suspected food reactions.
Discuss supplements and special diets with a veterinarian.
nutrition.note: No universal calorie target or breed-specific meal schedule is recorded; needs depend on age, workload, body condition and health.

health.overview: The breed club recommends pre-breeding hip scoring, eye examination including gonioscopy for goniodysgenesis, and a heart check. It also recommends DNA testing for the E locus associated with undesirable yellow/red coat colour and genetic markers associated with familial thyroid follicular cell carcinoma (FTFC). These are screening recommendations, not evidence that every dog will develop a condition. The club states that no FTFC cases had been identified in the UK breed population at the time of its page review, while cases have been reported in Europe.
preventiveCare: Ask breeders for documented results of the health tests recommended by the breed club.
Maintain routine veterinary examinations, vaccinations and parasite prevention.
Keep the dog lean and physically conditioned, increasing exercise gradually.
Seek veterinary advice for changes in vision, persistent lameness, exercise intolerance or other new symptoms.
Review any health-screening or genetic-testing advice with a veterinarian and the breeder, as recommendations can change.
recommendedScreenings: Hip scoring for breeding stock
Eye examination including gonioscopy to screen for goniodysgenesis
A veterinary heart check before breeding
E-locus DNA testing, as recommended by the breed club

health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks.
health.earCare: Check the hanging, feathered ears regularly for wax, moisture, odour, discharge or irritation; seek veterinary advice if symptoms occur.
health.skinCare: Inspect skin and coat while brushing, especially after field work. Persistent itching, redness, hair loss or sores warrant veterinary assessment.

notIdealFor: Households seeking a low-energy dog with minimal exercise needs

funFacts: The breed is listed by the FCI as Deutsch Langhaar, with standard number 117.
The breed standard records pure breeding from 1879 and an early written standard from 1897.
Its traditional work spans fields, woodland and water rather than a single hunting environment.
The coat is meant to be close-fitting and functional, with feathering but not excessive hair.

faq.question: What was the German Longhaired Pointer bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed as a versatile hunting dog for work in fields, woodland and water, including searching for, pointing and retrieving game.

faq.question: How tall is a German Longhaired Pointer?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives a height of 60–70 cm for males and 58–66 cm for females. Its preferred height ranges are narrower than those full limits.

faq.question: How much does a German Longhaired Pointer weigh?
faq.answer: The FCI standard gives an average weight of 30 kg, not a sex-specific weight range. This catalogue's weight-range field is therefore left unrecorded rather than turning the average into a minimum or maximum.

faq.question: How much exercise does the breed need?
faq.answer: It needs substantial daily activity. The UK Kennel Club lists more than two hours per day; the right amount and intensity still depend on age, health, fitness and workload.

faq.question: What grooming does the coat need?
faq.answer: Brush regularly and check the feathering, ears and tail for tangles and burrs, especially after walks or work in dense vegetation. Routine ear, nail and dental care is also important.

faq.question: Which health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask about hip scoring, an eye examination that includes gonioscopy, a heart check and the breed club's recommended DNA tests. Discuss the meaning of each result with a veterinarian; screening recommendations do not mean a dog will necessarily develop a condition.

faq.question: Is a German Longhaired Pointer suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: There is no universal yes-or-no answer supported by the sources reviewed. Its substantial exercise and enrichment needs may be difficult to meet in some apartments, so suitability depends on the individual dog and the household's daily routine.

overview.summary: The German Rough-haired Pointer—known natively as the Deutsch Stichelhaar—is the oldest German rough-coated pointing dog, distinguished by its harsh 4 cm bristly coat, oblique bushy eyebrows, moderate beard, and steady, versatile work across field, forest, and water.
overview.description: Built as a powerful, medium-to-large multipurpose hunting partner rather than a show-ring ornament, the German Rough-haired Pointer has a square to slightly rectangular frame supported by straight, strongly boned limbs and a deep, well-sprung chest. Its weatherproof coat consists of stiff, harsh, bristly hairs roughly 4 cm long that lie loosely along the body in the direction of growth, frequently backed by a sparse, barely visible undercoat. On the head, a moderate beard and strong, outward-arching eyebrows create a serious, workmanlike expression over clear brown eyes and a light-to-dark brown nose. Calm, poised, and self-controlled in everyday life, this handler-oriented gundog combines staunch pointing, water retrieving, and blood-tracking endurance with a sociable, composed nature inside an active household.
overview.history: Rough-coated continental bird dogs appear in Central European woodcuts and engravings as early as the sixteenth century across Brandenburg, Hesse, Bohemia, Moravia, and Austria. In 1888, cynologist Hans von Kadisch demonstrated that the harsh-coated Stichelhaar was the surviving rough-haired form of the historic German partridge dog (Hühnerhund) rather than a recent sport of the short-haired pointer, enabling breeders to rebuild the population from the few authentic remnants still working in Germany. A dedicated breed club was established in 1892—adopting its modern name in 1976—and from the outset strictly prohibited crossbreeding with English pointers or setters in order to preserve native continental working traits. After the Second World War and the division of Germany cut off traditional eastern breeding centres, enthusiasts rebuilt the studbook from 1945 onward in East Frisia (Ostfriesland). Definitive international recognition followed on 24 August 1961, and the breed remains an independent, pure-bred rough-coated pointer distinct from the later-developed German Wirehaired Pointer.
overview.originalPurpose: Versatile continental gundog used for work before and after the shot across field, forest, and water, including pointing upland game, flushing cover, retrieving waterfowl, and blood-tracking wounded game.
currentRoles: Versatile hunting gundog in field, woodland, and water (Vorstehen, Apportieren, Stöbern, and Nachsuche)
Blood-tracking and wounded-game recovery dog (Schweißarbeit)
Active family and outdoor companion for hunting or scent-sport households

physical.coatType: Stiff, harsh, bristly outer coat lying loosely against the body with all hairs growing in the same direction, frequently accompanied by a sparse, barely visible undercoat; the head must remain free of soft, woolly, or silky hair.
physical.coatLength: Approximately 4 cm over the trunk, slightly longer on the shoulders and along the midline of the throat, chest, and belly, with a moderate muzzle beard, bushy oblique eyebrows, light feathering down the backs of the legs, and close-lying hair on the tail without an off-standing brush or plume.
coatColors: Brown, with or without a white chest patch
Brown roan (Braunschimmel), with or without brown patches
Light roan (Hellschimmel), with or without brown patches
distinctiveFeatures: Square or nearly square body outline where body length equals or only slightly exceeds height at the withers (60 to 70 cm in males, 58 to 68 cm in females)
Stiff, harsh, bristly body coat roughly 4 cm long that lies loosely without parting down the spine
Strong, bushy eyebrows standing off in an oblique arch paired with a moderate beard on a long, blunt muzzle
Light-to-dark brown nose leather (never black or flesh-coloured) and medium-sized oval brown eyes (never yellow) with tight rims
High-set, medium-length hanging ears with blunt rounded tips lying smoothly against the cheeks without folding or twisting
Forelegs where the distance from elbow to ground slightly exceeds the distance from withers to elbow, ending in round, well-knit feet with tough pads
Medium-length tail strong at the root, carried straight or with a slight upward curve, covered in dense flat-lying hair without a plume

traits: Balanced, calm, and even-tempered indoors
Courageous, tenacious, and self-controlled in the field
Strongly bonded to its handler and eager to cooperate
Resilient and steady under demanding weather and cover conditions
Neither shy nor aggressive toward people or conspecifics during group hunts
Alert and watchful around the home with controllable protective instincts

exercise.level: high
activities: Versatile field, forest, and water hunting work before and after the shot
Blood-tracking trails (Schweißarbeit), scent discrimination, and nosework searches
Dummy retrieving on land and in deep water
Long, brisk countryside hikes and cross-country outings
Structured obedience and steadiness-to-game drills

grooming.brushing: Brush the harsh 4 cm coat once or twice weekly with a firm bristle brush or curry comb to clear out dead hair, forest litter, and burrs, paying extra attention to the beard, eyebrows, and leg feathering.
grooming.bathing: Rinse with plain water after muddy field or marsh work and bathe with a mild, dog-formulated shampoo only when necessary so the natural weather-resistant coat oils remain intact.
notes: Rinse and dry the muzzle beard after meals and water retrieves to prevent trapped debris or skin irritation.
Part the bristly coat and check the skin, armpits, groin, and interdigital spaces after woodland work for ticks, foxtails, thorns, and bramble scratches.
Inspect the high-set hanging ears weekly and dry them thoroughly after swimming.
Check the tough paw pads and well-arched nails regularly, trimming nails if they do not wear down naturally.

training.difficulty: moderate; highly handler-oriented and willing to learn, but requires purposeful hunting or scent-work outlets and steady leadership
tips: Channel the dog's natural nose and retrieving drive from an early age through structured tracking, pointing, and dummy-work progressions.
Use calm, consistent, reward-based guidance; this self-controlled working dog responds best to clear communication rather than harsh pressure.
Build rock-solid steadiness and recall around wildlife before working off lead in open cover.
Integrate mental scent challenges into daily routines so the dog's working intelligence is fully engaged.
Practise cooperative veterinary and grooming handling—including mouth, ear, and paw inspections—from puppyhood.
training.socialization: Provide early, well-structured exposure to diverse people, household routines, other hunting dogs, livestock, and varied outdoor environments so the puppy matures into a steady, socially composed adult.

climates: Well suited to cool, wet, and temperate four-season climates thanks to its harsh, weather-resistant coat
During warm summer weather, schedule strenuous field training for cool morning or evening hours and provide shade and fresh water

nutrition.dietType: Complete, balanced canine diet formulated for medium-to-large working gundogs, matched to the individual dog's age, body condition, and seasonal workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed several smaller measured meals daily during growth, tapering gradually to an adult twice-daily schedule under veterinary guidance.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed two measured meals per day, adjusting caloric density upward during intensive autumn and winter hunting seasons.
feedingFrequency.senior: Serve measured, easily digestible meals tailored to senior activity levels, body condition, and veterinary recommendations.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily portions to keep the dog firm and well muscled without excess weight, provide constant access to clean water, and introduce any ration changes gradually over several days.
considerations: Allow at least an hour of rest before and after vigorous field or water work before offering a full meal to reduce the risk of gastric distress in deep-chested gundogs.
Increase energy and fat intake appropriately during prolonged cold-weather hunting or tracking days.
Include training rewards within the total daily food allowance.
Consult a veterinarian regarding hydration and recovery nutrition during heavy working periods.
nutrition.note: These recommendations represent general veterinary nutrition guidance for athletic pointing dogs rather than a breed-specific clinical formula.

health.overview: Bred selectively for over a century for field endurance and functional soundness, the German Rough-haired Pointer is regarded as a robust, weather-hardy hunting dog. Only functionally and clinically healthy dogs with complete scissor dentition, tight-fitting eyelids free of entropion or ectropion, and sound temperament are permitted to breed, and the official parent club mandates pre-breeding radiographic evaluations for hip dysplasia (HD), elbow dysplasia (ED), and shoulder osteochondrosis (OC/OCD).
preventiveCare: Maintain year-round protection against ticks, fleas, and internal parasites, especially for dogs working through tall grass, woodland, and marshes.
Inspect and dry the hanging ear flaps after swimming or wet-weather retrieves to prevent ear canal inflammation.
Examine the eyes, interdigital webbing, paw pads, and coat after dense cover work for plant awns, thorns, and abrasions.
Keep the dog in lean, well-muscled working condition to minimise mechanical strain on hips, elbows, and shoulders.
Schedule routine annual veterinary wellness, dental, and vaccination check-ups.
recommendedScreenings: Official pre-breeding radiographic evaluation for hip dysplasia (HD)
Official pre-breeding radiographic evaluation for elbow dysplasia (ED)
Official pre-breeding radiographic evaluation for shoulder osteochondrosis / osteochondritis dissecans (OC/OCD)

Breeding soundness and conformation inspection verifying complete scissor dentition (at most two PM1 premolars absent), normal eyelid conformation free of entropion or ectropion, and normal descended testicles in males
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with canine toothpaste and check the powerful scissor bite for tartar accumulation or chipped teeth after retrieving work.
health.earCare: Check the medium-length hanging ears weekly and after water work; clean gently only as advised by a veterinarian and seek care if redness, odour, or head-shaking occurs.
health.skinCare: Part the stiff, bristly coat after field outings to check the tight, fold-free skin for ticks, burrs, or minor cuts.

idealFor: Active hunters and falconers seeking a versatile, handler-focused gundog for field, forest, and water
Experienced outdoors-oriented households that can provide daily scent work, retrieving, and vigorous exercise
Novice or experienced hunting-dog handlers who value a calm, biddable, and steady continental pointer
notIdealFor: Sedentary households unable to provide daily outdoor work and mental scent engagement
Owners seeking a purely casual indoor pet without structured training or purposeful activity

funFacts: In 1888, cynologist Hans von Kadisch proved that the Deutsch Stichelhaar was the surviving rough-coated form of the old German partridge dog (Hühnerhund) rather than a newly created offshoot of the short-haired pointer.

Since the foundation of its dedicated breed club in 1892, breeders have strictly rejected any crossbreeding with English pointers or setters, making it the oldest pure-bred German rough-coated pointing breed.
After the Second World War cut off historic breeding regions in eastern Europe, dedicated hunters rebuilt the breed from 1945 onward in East Frisia (Ostfriesland) in northwestern Germany.

Its characteristic oblique, bushy eyebrows and moderate muzzle beard protect the face in thorny cover while giving the dog a famously stern, serious expression that belies its calm, friendly household nature.

faq.question: How does the German Rough-haired Pointer differ from the German Wirehaired Pointer?
faq.answer: Although both are rough-coated German versatile gundogs, they have separate origins and coat structures. The German Rough-haired Pointer (Deutsch Stichelhaar) is the older breed, revived in the late nineteenth century from historic German partridge dogs without any English pointer blood, and carries a stiffer, harsher, more bristly coat of about 4 cm that lies loosely along the body. The German Wirehaired Pointer (Deutsch Drahthaar) was developed slightly later from crosses of several wire- and short-coated breeds.

faq.question: Why is this breed sometimes confused with the Slovakian Rough-haired Pointer in online databases?
faq.answer: Some third-party dog databases mistakenly attach the English name 'German Rough-haired Pointer' to data for the Slovakian Rough-haired Pointer (Slovenský hrubosrstý stavač), a post-World War II grey-coated Slovak breed developed from Weimaraners, Český Fousek, and German Wirehaired Pointers. The true German Rough-haired Pointer is the Deutsch Stichelhaar from Germany, which comes only in brown, brown roan, or light roan.

faq.question: How tall is an adult German Rough-haired Pointer?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 60 to 70 cm at the withers, while adult females stand 58 to 68 cm.

faq.question: What coat colours are permitted, and which are disqualified?
faq.answer: Permitted colours are solid brown (with or without a white chest patch), brown roan (with or without brown patches), and light roan (with or without brown patches). A black coat, or yellow or red (tan) markings on the head or legs, is a disqualification.

faq.question: Why are weight and lifespan left blank in the numeric fields of this profile?
faq.answer: Official conformation standards and national kennel-club profiles specify withers height (60 to 70 cm for males and 58 to 68 cm for females) but do not establish a fixed numerical weight range or official lifespan range.

faq.question: What pre-breeding health screenings are required for the breed?
faq.answer: Parent-club breeding regulations require official radiographic evaluations for hip dysplasia (HD), elbow dysplasia (ED), and shoulder osteochondrosis (OC/OCD), alongside a conformation and soundness inspection confirming a complete scissor bite, tight eyelids free of entropion or ectropion, and balanced working temperament.
