overview.summary: A compact, athletic, and intelligent Canadian retriever bred in southwestern Nova Scotia, celebrated for its red-to-orange water-repellent double coat, tireless love of swimming and retrieving, and fox-like shoreline play that lures curious waterfowl within gunshot range.
overview.description: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever—universally nicknamed the Toller—is the smallest of the retriever breeds, built with a muscular, compact, and well-boned frame that is slightly longer than tall (roughly a 10:9 ratio) without ever appearing heavy or clunky. Protected against icy maritime waters by a medium-length, water-repellent double coat in shades of golden red to dark coppery red (often accented by white markings on the tail tip, feet, chest, or blaze), it features a clean, wedge-shaped head, alert almond-shaped amber-to-brown eyes, high-set triangular drop ears, a heavily feathered tail that waves incessantly above the back when working, and strongly webbed feet. In the field, the Toller performs a dual job: darting, leaping, and retrieving sticks or balls silently along the shoreline so its flashing red coat and feathered tail arouse the curiosity of offshore ducks and geese, then plunging into frigid water to retrieve downed birds on command. At home, Tollers are deeply affectionate, playful, and attuned to their families, though they can be reserved with strangers, strong-willed if training becomes repetitive, and prone to an unmistakable high-pitched vocalisation ('the Toller scream') when brimming with excitement.
overview.history: Developed at the beginning of the nineteenth century in the coastal community of Little River Harbour in Yarmouth County, southwestern Nova Scotia, the breed was originally called the Little River Duck Dog or the Yarmouth Toller. Local hunters—drawing on Indigenous Mi'kmaq traditions and European observations of red foxes playing near the water's edge to entice rafting waterfowl toward shore—bred a small, fox-coloured dog that could both lure ('toll', from the Middle English tolian, meaning 'to entice or decoy') and retrieve waterfowl from icy tidal waters. Although exact early breeding records were not preserved, foundation stock is thought to have combined small European decoy spaniels (similar to the Nederlandse Kooikerhondje) with retrievers (including early Golden, Chesapeake Bay, or Flat-Coated Retriever stock and the extinct St. John's Water Dog), setters, spaniels, and local farm collies. After more than a century of regional breeding in Nova Scotia, the first 15 dogs were admitted to national studbook registration in Canada in 1945. When breed numbers dropped dangerously low in the 1970s, dedicated North American and European fanciers—including American pioneer Sue Van Sloun, who imported her first pair in 1978 and helped establish organized preservation in the United States in 1984—expanded preservation efforts. International recognition followed in 1987, the province of Nova Scotia proclaimed the Toller its official Provincial Dog in 1995, and full sporting-group recognition in the United States was granted in 2003.
overview.originalPurpose: Enticing ('tolling') offshore ducks and geese within gunshot range through silent, playful shoreline movement and retrieving downed waterfowl from icy water and land.
currentRoles: Active family and outdoor companion
Waterfowl tolling and retrieving gundog
Field trial and retriever hunt-test competitor
Agility, flyball, and dock-diving competitor
Obedience, rally, and trick-training participant
Tracking, nose work, and scent-detection participant
Search-and-rescue or therapy dog where individually trained and temperament-suited

physical.coatType: Water-repellent double coat consisting of a medium-length, moderately soft straight outer coat (a slight wave along the back and a loose curl at the throat in winter coat are permissible) over a denser, even softer insulating undercoat, with soft feathering at the throat, behind the ears, on the backs of the thighs, and moderately on the forelegs and underside of the tail.
physical.coatLength: Medium
coatColors: Red (ranging from golden red to dark coppery red, with lighter shadings on the feathering and underside of the tail)
Orange (various shades of orange, with pigment on the nose, lips, and eye rims matching the coat in flesh/liver or black)

Red or orange with at least one white marking on the tip of the tail, feet (not extending above the pasterns), chest, or facial blaze (solid red/orange without any white is also acceptable, whereas buff/silver dilution, brown, black, pinto, tricolor, or white on the shoulders, around the ears, on the back of the neck, or across the back/flanks are disqualifying faults)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate year-round, with heavier seasonal shedding twice a year during spring and autumn coat changes.
physical.droolingLevel: Low
distinctiveFeatures: Smallest of the retriever breeds, built on a compact, muscular, slightly rectangular outline (approximately 10:9 body length to withers height) with a deep chest reaching the elbows and a level topline

Clean-cut, slightly wedge-shaped head (measuring roughly 14 cm [5.5 in] between the ears tapering to 3.8 cm [1.5 in] at the nose bridge, and about 23 cm [9 in] from nose to occiput in a typical adult male, scaling with body size) with a flat-to-slightly-rounded skull and moderate stop
Almond-shaped, medium-sized eyes set well apart in amber to brown shades that harmonize with the coat, paired with flesh-coloured or black nose leather, tight-fitting lips, and eye rims
Triangular, medium-sized drop ears with rounded tips set high and well back on the skull, carried slightly raised at the base when alert and well feathered at the back of the fold

Broad-based, heavily feathered tail reaching at least to the hocks, carried below the level of the back only when standing at rest and curving high in continuous motion above the topline when alert or working (never touching the body)
Strong, round-to-oval, tightly webbed feet with thick pads and trimmed interdigital hair, functioning like paddles in cold water
Springy, effortless, ground-covering gait with strong rear drive and a level backline
Distinctive high-pitched, trembling vocalisation ('the Toller scream') expressed by many individuals when eager to retrieve or work

Ideal adult withers height of 48–51 cm (19–20 in) for males and 45–48 cm (18–19 in) for females over 18 months of age (with a ±2.5 to 3 cm [±1 in] allowance, or 18–21 in and 17–20 in in American standards), and substance-proportionate adult weight guidelines of 20–23 kg (45–51 lbs) for males and 17–20 kg (37–43 lbs; 35–50 lbs across both sexes in American profiles)

traits: Highly intelligent, observant, and quick to learn
Affectionate, loving, and playful with family members and familiar children
Outgoing, exuberant, and tireless when working or playing
Intensely driven to retrieve on land and in water
Alert, attentive, and determined
Patient with children when properly socialized and supervised
Often reserved or aloof (never aggressive or shy) toward unfamiliar people
Sensitive to handler tone yet persistent and capable of independent or strong-willed behaviour if bored
Expressive and vocal when excited (including the high-pitched 'Toller scream')

exercise.level: High
activities: Daily brisk walks, jogging, or trail hikes suited to the dog's age and conditioning
Structured retrieving games and field bumper work on land and in water
Swimming and dock diving in safe, supervised bodies of water
Canine sports such as agility, flyball, rally, and obedience
Tracking, nose work, and scent-detection games
Problem-solving puzzle toys and short, varied mental-enrichment drills

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly at least once a week with a pin brush, slicker brush, and metal comb to remove loose hair and prevent matting in the soft feathering behind the ears, around the throat, and on the hindquarters. Increase to daily brushing during seasonal spring and autumn coat sheds.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only as needed when dirty or after muddy or saltwater swims, using a mild dog-safe shampoo that preserves the natural oils of the water-repellent double coat, and rinse and dry thoroughly.
notes: The weatherproof double coat insulates against both icy water and summer heat; it should never be shaved, and show trimming is restricted to neatening the ears, feet, pasterns, and hocks.
Pay close attention to the fine, silky hair behind and under the ears, which tangles more easily than the body coat.
Trim excess hair between the paw pads and on the feet to maintain traction and prevent mud or ice buildup.
Rinse and dry the coat and inspect the drop ears after swimming in lakes, marshes, or the ocean.
Check toenails weekly and trim them regularly so they remain short and compact.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and accustom puppies early to calm grooming and handling.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Highly intelligent, eager to work, and quick to grasp new concepts, yet sensitive to heavy-handed methods and quick to invent its own rules if drills become monotonous.
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based positive reinforcement—combining food rewards with brief retrieving or tug play—and avoid harsh corrections.
Keep training sessions short, varied, and mentally challenging so this quick-thinking retriever does not become bored or self-employed.
Channel the breed's intense retrieving instinct as a high-value life reward for recall, impulse control, and obedience.
Teach calm steadiness and an 'off switch' indoors so the dog learns to settle quietly after high-arousal work or play.
Manage and redirect high-pitched excitement vocalisations ('the Toller scream') early by rewarding quiet focus before throwing a toy or releasing the dog to water.
Practise reliable recall in securely enclosed spaces and keep the dog on a leash or long line around wild waterfowl, small animals, and open water currents.
training.socialization: Begin positive, unhurried socialization early in puppyhood across diverse people, friendly dogs, children, surfaces, sounds, and environments. Because many Tollers are naturally reserved or discerning with strangers, allow the dog to observe and greet unfamiliar people without pressure so it matures into a confident, well-mannered adult. Supervise introductions to cats and small pets carefully due to the breed's innate bird- and small-game drive.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Tollers bond closely with their families and thrive on daily interaction, training, and outdoor activity. Leaving a Toller isolated for long workdays without adequate physical and mental outlets can lead to boredom, vocalising, or destructive chewing.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced dog food (commercial or veterinarian-formulated home-prepared diet) appropriate for the dog's life stage, workload, and health status.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions of a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age (puppy, adult, or senior) and daily activity level. Because Tollers are medium-sized athletic dogs whose caloric needs vary widely between active field/agility competitors and family companions, monitor body condition score regularly so the waist remains defined and the ribs are easily felt beneath a light layer of muscle. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Adjust daily calorie intake to match seasonal training, hunting, or sport workloads.
Count training treats within the total daily caloric allowance to prevent excess weight and unnecessary joint strain.
Transition between diets gradually over several days unless a veterinarian directs otherwise.

Consult a veterinarian promptly if unexplained weight loss, lethargy, intermittent vomiting, diarrhoea, or increased thirst/urination occur (which can also be early signs of endocrine or immune-mediated conditions).
Home-prepared diets should be formulated with a veterinarian or board-certified veterinary nutritionist to ensure complete micronutrient balance.
nutrition.note: No single daily meal count is prescribed across all puppies, adults, or seniors because optimal feeding schedules depend on age, caloric density, and individual metabolism; confirm meal frequency and portion sizes with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever is an energetic, hardy sporting dog with a typical lifespan of 12 to 14 years, but its historical population bottlenecks have led to several well-characterized autosomal recessive genetic variants as well as an elevated predisposition to immune-mediated and endocrine disorders. Epidemiological research in insured Swedish Tollers (2015) documented significantly higher relative risks than in the general dog population for steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA; incidence 20 per 10,000 dog-years at risk, relative risk 12) and immune-mediated rheumatic disease (IMRD; 6.8 per 10,000 dog-years at risk, relative risk 18), alongside a higher risk of lymphoma but lower overall rates of ear and heart disease. A follow-up 2024 Swedish owner-questionnaire survey (935 living and 177 deceased Tollers) estimated lifetime prevalence in living dogs at 3.0% for IMRD and 3.5% for SRMA, and reported neoplasia of any kind (benign or malignant, most commonly mammary and mast cell tumours) in 14% of living dogs and as the cause of death in 38.4% of deceased dogs—figures specific to that surveyed cohort rather than universal cancer rates. In 2026, a peer-reviewed genomic study identified an autosomal recessive missense variant in the RESF1 gene (c.3170C>T / p.Pro1057Leu on chromosome 27) associated with juvenile-onset Addison's disease (JADD) with incomplete (~75%–76%) penetrance by 1 year of age (average diagnosis 5 months) and multiple autoimmune syndrome (41.7%–70.8% of juvenile cases developing concurrent immune-mediated eye, blood, joint, gut, or thyroid disorders); this DNA test does not account for adult-onset Addison's disease. Earlier in 2023, researchers also identified an autosomal recessive frameshift variant in the LMNA gene (p.Asp576ThrfsTer124) causing fatal juvenile/young-adult cardiac laminopathy (CLAM, dilated and fibrosing cardiomyopathy). Validated DNA tests are likewise available for PRCD-progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-prcd), Collie eye anomaly (CEA/CH), cleft palate 1 (CP1 / DLX6), cleft lip/palate/syndactyly (CLPS / ADAMTS20), cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC / SNX14), degenerative encephalopathy (DE), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), and FGF4 retrogene chondrodystrophy (CDDY/IVDD).
commonConditions: Hypoadrenocorticism (Addison's disease) and multiple autoimmune syndrome — occurs in both an adult-onset form (average onset ~2.6–4 years) and a juvenile-onset form (JADD, average onset 5 months, range 8 weeks to 12 months) associated with an autosomal recessive RESF1 missense variant (c.3170C>T / p.Pro1057Leu) showing ~75%–76% penetrance and frequent concurrent autoimmune manifestations (such as corneal edema, conjunctivitis, uveitis, immune-mediated hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, polyarthritis, or inflammatory bowel disease).

Steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA, sometimes historically called 'Toller disease') — a non-infectious immune-mediated inflammation of the meninges and meningeal arteries affecting primarily young dogs (roughly 70% presenting before 18 months of age; 3.5% living prevalence in a 2024 Swedish survey), causing acute neck pain, stiffness, high fever, and depression that require prompt veterinary diagnosis and immunosuppressive therapy.

Immune-mediated rheumatic disease (IMRD) — a systemic lupus erythematosus-related non-erosive polyarthritis (3.0% living prevalence and median onset 5 years in a 2024 Swedish survey, often ANA-positive) causing cyclic joint stiffness, shifting leg lameness, pain after rest, and sometimes skin lesions or fever.

Cardiac laminopathy (CLAM) — a fatal autosomal recessive dilated and fibrosing cardiomyopathy caused by a frameshift deletion in the LMNA gene (p.Asp576ThrfsTer124), typically resulting in myocarditis, arrhythmias, heart failure, or sudden cardiac death before 1.5 to 2 years of age (with myocardial fibrosis also reported in a 5-year-old heterozygous carrier); preventable via pre-breeding DNA screening.

Progressive retinal atrophy, photoreceptor rod-cone degeneration (PRA-prcd) and Collie eye anomaly / choroidal hypoplasia (CEA/CH) — autosomal recessive inherited retinal and choroidal eye disorders for which validated DNA tests and annual veterinary ophthalmologist examinations are core screening tools.

Cleft palate 1 (CP1, DLX6 insertion) and cleft lip/palate/syndactyly (CLPS, ADAMTS20 deletion) — two distinct autosomal recessive congenital craniofacial malformation syndromes in the breed, both preventable through pre-breeding DNA carrier testing.

Cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC) and degenerative encephalopathy (DE) — rare autosomal recessive neurological disorders in the breed; CDMC (caused by an SNX14 frameshift variant) produces cerebellar ataxia, tremors, and masticatory/generalized muscle inflammation between 10 weeks and 6 months of age, while DE causes progressive neurological dysfunction.
Hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, and patellar luxation — developmental orthopaedic conditions monitored through pre-breeding radiographic and clinical evaluations.

Chondrodystrophy (CDDY) and intervertebral disc disease (IVDD) risk — associated with the semi-dominant chromosome 12 FGF4 retrogene insertion that predisposes discs to premature calcification and herniation.
Autoimmune thyroiditis (hypothyroidism) — an immune-mediated endocrine disorder monitored via periodic veterinary thyroid antibody panels.

Neoplasia (tumours) — population studies in Swedish Tollers have documented increased relative risk of lymphoma in insured dogs and reported benign or malignant tumours (most frequently mammary and mast cell tumours) in 14% of surveyed living dogs; tumour rates vary by age, sex, and spay/neuter status and do not represent a uniform breed-wide cancer probability.
preventiveCare: Verify documented pre-breeding health clearances for both parents before acquiring a puppy, including hip radiographs, current annual board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams, and breed-specific DNA test results.

Understand the scope of genetic testing: a Clear result on the RESF1 juvenile Addison's disease (JADD) DNA test rules out that specific juvenile-onset variant (which itself has ~75%–76% penetrance in homozygotes), but does not rule out adult-onset Addison's disease or other immune-mediated disorders.

Seek prompt veterinary evaluation if a young or adult dog develops acute neck pain, spinal stiffness, fever, shifting leg lameness after rest, waxing-and-waning lethargy, vomiting, diarrhoea, or increased drinking and urination, as early treatment is critical for SRMA, IMRD, and Addisonian crises.
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition and avoid excessive high-impact jumping in growing puppies to protect the hips, elbows, knees, and intervertebral discs.
Inspect, rinse, and dry the coat and drop ears after swimming to prevent moisture-related skin or ear irritation.

Keep routine veterinary wellness examinations, dental care, nail trimming, and regionally appropriate parasite prevention and vaccination schedules up to date (working with your veterinarian to tailor vaccination protocols for dogs with personal or family histories of immune-mediated disease).
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement).
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (core pre-breeding requirement).
Progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-prcd) DNA test (core pre-breeding requirement).
Juvenile Addison's disease (JADD / RESF1 c.3170C>T) DNA test — recommended to identify carriers and prevent homozygous matings while preserving genetic diversity.
Cardiac laminopathy (CLAM / LMNA p.Asp576ThrfsTer124) DNA test and clinical veterinary cardiac evaluation.
Cleft palate 1 (CP1 / DLX6) and cleft lip/palate/syndactyly (CLPS / ADAMTS20) DNA tests.

Cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC / SNX14), Collie eye anomaly (CEA/CH / NHEJ1), degenerative encephalopathy (DE), degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1), and chondrodystrophy (CDDY / FGF4) DNA tests.
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation, patellar luxation veterinary examination, and laboratory thyroid panel (including thyroglobulin autoantibodies).

Optional coat-colour dilution (Buff / D-locus MLPH) DNA test for breeding planning (identifies recessive buff coat dilution, which is a conformation disqualification rather than a medical disorder; note also that Tollers tested to date have not carried the MDR1 drug-sensitivity mutation).
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week—ideally daily—using dog-specific toothpaste, and schedule regular veterinary dental assessments. Conformation standards require strong jaws with a complete, tight scissor bite.
health.earCare: Check the high-set triangular drop ears weekly and after every swim or muddy outing. Gently clean and dry the outer ear and keep the feathering behind the ears free of mats, seeking veterinary advice if redness, foul odour, discharge, or head shaking occurs.
health.skinCare: Part the dense, water-repellent double coat during weekly brushing to check the skin for ticks, burrs, hot spots (acute moist dermatitis), or uncharacteristic hair loss. Rinse off salt or marsh water after swimming and dry the thick undercoat thoroughly.

idealFor: Active individuals and families who enjoy daily outdoor exercise, hiking, running, swimming, or canine sports

funFacts: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever is the smallest of all recognized retriever breeds, yet it has the strength and endurance to retrieve heavy geese from icy tidal waters.

The word 'toll' comes from the Middle English tolian ('to entice' or 'lure'): hunters patterned the breed's shoreline work after wild red foxes, which dart and play along the water's edge to lure curious ducks within range.

Developed in early nineteenth-century Little River Harbour in Yarmouth County, Nova Scotia, the breed was historically known as the Little River Duck Dog and the Yarmouth Toller before adopting its current name when registered in 1945.
In 1995, Nova Scotia declared the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever its official Provincial Dog—making it the first Canadian dog breed honoured as a provincial symbol.
At the thirty-three-letter mark (excluding spaces), 'Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever' is the longest official breed name in North American studbooks.
When eager to retrieve or work, many Tollers let out a famous high-pitched, trembling howl of pure anticipation known as the 'Toller scream' or 'Toller singing'.

Unlike most dogs whose tails hang or wag level with the spine, an alert or working Toller carries its heavily feathered tail curving high over its back like a waving flag so offshore ducks can spot it through shoreline reeds.
Tollers have strongly webbed, paddle-like feet and a water-repellent double coat so dense that icy water rarely reaches the skin.

faq.question: Where does the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever come from, and what were its early names?
faq.answer: The breed originated at the beginning of the nineteenth century in southwestern Nova Scotia, Canada—specifically around Little River Harbour in Yarmouth County. Before receiving its modern name upon national registration in 1945, it was known locally as the Little River Duck Dog and the Yarmouth Toller.

faq.question: What does 'tolling' mean, and how does a Toller hunt?
faq.answer: Tolling comes from a Middle English word meaning 'to entice' or 'lure'. Modeled on the behaviour of wild red foxes, the dog runs, leaps, and fetches sticks or balls thrown from a hunter's blind along the shoreline while remaining completely silent. Its flashing red coat and waving feathered tail arouse the curiosity of ducks and geese swimming offshore, drawing them within gunshot range; once the birds are downed, the dog swims out to retrieve them.

faq.question: How big is an adult Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever?
faq.answer: It is the smallest of the retrievers. International and Canadian standards specify an ideal withers height for dogs over 18 months of 48 to 51 cm (19–20 inches) for males and 45 to 48 cm (18–19 inches) for females, with a tolerance of ±2.5 to 3 cm (±1 inch), and weight guidelines of 20 to 23 kg (45–51 pounds) for males and 17 to 20 kg (37–43 pounds) for females. American standards specify 18 to 21 inches (ideal 19 inches) for males, 17 to 20 inches (ideal 18 inches) for females, and typical weights of 35 to 50 pounds (16–23 kg) in proportion to bone and substance.

faq.question: What coat colours and white markings are allowed?
faq.answer: The coat comes in shades of red and orange ranging from golden red to dark coppery red, with lighter shading on the feathering and the underside of the tail. Dogs commonly have at least one white marking on the tip of the tail, the feet (not extending above the pasterns), the chest, or as a facial blaze, though an otherwise sound dog without white markings is also accepted. Nose, lips, and eye rims must be flesh-coloured (blending with the coat) or black. Buff/silver dilution, solid brown/liver coat, black coat, pinto/tricolor patterning, or white on the shoulders, back, flanks, or around the ears are disqualifying faults.

faq.question: What is the 'Toller scream'?
faq.answer: The 'Toller scream' (sometimes called 'Toller singing') is a piercing, high-pitched, trembling vocalisation that many Tollers make when they are intensely excited—most often when they see water, birds, or a retrieving dummy. Not every Toller screams to the same degree, and handlers avoid reinforcing it in hunting blinds or quiet neighbourhoods by rewarding calm, quiet focus before releasing the dog.

faq.question: Is the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever a good family dog?
faq.answer: Yes, for active households. Tollers are deeply affectionate, playful, and patient with their own families and children when properly socialized and supervised. However, they are high-drive working dogs—not scaled-down Golden Retrievers—and can be reserved with unfamiliar people and restless if their daily physical and mental exercise needs are neglected.

faq.question: How much exercise and grooming does a Toller need?
faq.answer: Tollers have high energy and need daily brisk walks or runs paired with purposeful mental work such as retrieving drills, swimming, agility, flyball, or scent work. Their medium-length, water-repellent double coat is relatively easy to maintain with a thorough weekly brushing (paying extra attention to the fine hair behind the ears and feathering) and daily brushing during spring and autumn coat sheds. The double coat should never be shaved.

faq.question: Can a Toller live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Apartment living can succeed if the owner provides substantial daily outdoor exercise, retrieving and mental enrichment, and training to manage the breed's excitement vocalisations. Without committed daily activity and companionship, however, an apartment lifestyle is a poor fit.

faq.question: What health conditions are researched or reported in the breed?
faq.answer: Key health concerns include hypoadrenocorticism (Addison's disease, both adult-onset and juvenile-onset), steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis (SRMA), immune-mediated rheumatic disease (IMRD), juvenile cardiac laminopathy (CLAM), inherited eye conditions (PRA-prcd and Collie eye anomaly), congenital cleft palate syndromes (CP1 and CLPS), cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC), hip dysplasia, intervertebral disc disease predisposition (CDDY), and autoimmune thyroiditis. Swedish population studies estimated living lifetime prevalence at 3.0% for IMRD and 3.5% for SRMA, and reported tumours of any type (benign or malignant) in 14% of surveyed living dogs.

faq.question: What does the juvenile Addison's disease (JADD / RESF1) DNA test tell breeders and owners?
faq.answer: In 2026, researchers identified an autosomal recessive missense variant in the RESF1 gene (c.3170C>T / p.Pro1057Leu) associated with juvenile-onset Addison's disease (average onset 5 months, range 8 weeks to 12 months) and concurrent multiple autoimmune disorders. The variant has incomplete penetrance—approximately 75% to 76% of dogs with two copies (N/N -> JADD/JADD) develop Addison's disease by 1 year of age—and a carrier frequency of roughly 20% to 23% in tested cohorts. The DNA test allows breeders to avoid mating two carriers, but a Clear result does not prevent adult-onset Addison's disease.

faq.question: What is cardiac laminopathy (CLAM) in Tollers?
faq.answer: Cardiac laminopathy (CLAM) is a fatal autosomal recessive dilated and fibrosing cardiomyopathy caused by a frameshift variant in the LMNA gene (identified in 2023). Affected puppies and young dogs typically suffer heart failure or sudden cardiac death before 1.5 to 2 years of age. A validated DNA test allows breeders to screen breeding stock and prevent affected litters.

faq.question: Which health screenings should I ask a breeder for?
faq.answer: Ask for documented results of core pre-breeding evaluations—hip radiographs, a current annual examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist, and DNA testing for PRA-prcd—along with DNA panel results for juvenile Addison's disease (JADD / RESF1), cardiac laminopathy (CLAM / LMNA), cleft palate 1 (CP1), cleft lip/palate/syndactyly (CLPS), cerebellar degeneration-myositis complex (CDMC), Collie eye anomaly (CEA/CH), degenerative encephalopathy (DE), degenerative myelopathy (DM), and chondrodystrophy (CDDY), as well as elbow, patellar, cardiac, and thyroid evaluations where appropriate.

overview.summary: Scandinavia's only native pointing breed—a sturdy, rectangular Danish gundog with a short white-and-brown coat, pronounced sexual dimorphism, an unhurried close-working hunting style, and a calm, devoted nature at home.
overview.description: The Old Danish Pointer (Gammel Dansk Hønsehund, officially the Old Danish Pointing Dog) is a medium-sized, powerfully built continental pointing dog and the only native pointing breed of the Nordic countries. Built on a rectangular 8:9 ratio of withers height to body length, one of its most characteristic hallmarks is the marked difference between the sexes: the male (54–60 cm, above 56 cm preferred; 30–35 kg) is powerful and substantial, whereas the female (50–56 cm, above 52 cm preferred; 26–31 kg) is lighter, livelier, and more spirited without ever appearing finely boned. Its short, wide head features a rounded skull with a prominent occiput and no pronounced stop, a fleshy liver-coloured nose, deep overhanging flews, low-set broad ears with rounded tips, and a muscular neck with a characteristic throat dewlap. Covered in a short, dense, somewhat hard white coat marked with large brown patches or small brown speckles (with darker brown preferred), it works at a deliberate, unhurried pace that keeps constant contact with the hunter without disturbing the ground, making it equally suited to small and large hunting estates as well as wounded-game tracking. Indoors, it is peaceful, patient with children, sociable with strangers and other dogs, and deeply attached to its family.
overview.history: The breed traces its documented origins to around 1710 in Glenstrup, a village between Randers and Hobro in Jutland, Denmark. Over eight generations, a man named Morten Bak crossed dogs kept by travelling Romani people ('gypsy dogs') with local farm dogs to establish a pure breeding stock of piebald white-and-brown pointing dogs known as Bakhounds (Bakhunde) or Old Danish Pointing Dogs. Although local farmers called their farm dogs 'bloodhounds', historical and cynological records indicate they were likely descendants of estate scent hounds carrying strong Saint-Hubert Hound (Bloodhound) ancestry, while the Romani dogs—used for hunting as well as draught and pack work—likely carried Spanish Pointer and scent-hound blood. Thanks to its exceptional nose and close-working bond with the hunter, the breed became Denmark's most popular hunting dog during the nineteenth century. After nearly vanishing around the mid-twentieth century, the breed was revived by dedicated Danish enthusiasts, received definitive international recognition on 2 April 1969 (with the current valid standard dated 8 January 1998 and published 12 October 1998), and gained North American gun-dog recognition on 1 January 2006. Today its population is concentrated primarily in Denmark, with smaller numbers in Sweden and Germany.

Wide nasal bridge, fleshy liver-coloured nose with wide-open nostrils, and deep overhanging flews from the nose to the corners of the mouth that give the head its characteristic depth
Muscular, well-furnished neck with a characteristic throat dewlap ('throatiness' is a hallmark of the breed, though never exaggerated) and lip-corner fold

Medium-sized dark brown (or amber-brown) eyes that are neither sunken nor prominent, and low-set, broad, slightly rounded hanging ears whose front edges lie close to the cheeks and leave just over the outer third of the muzzle free when drawn forward

Powerful jaws with a complete scissor bite of 42 teeth (20 upper and 22 lower; pincer bite is a severe fault, and overshot, undershot, wry bite, or missing more than two PM1 plus one other tooth is a disqualification)

Deep, wide chest reaching the elbows with a well-developed forechest, firm muscular back sloping slightly from well-defined withers to a broad croup, and a medium-length tapering tail carried naturally drooping almost to the hocks (tail docking is forbidden)

Adult height of 54 to 60 cm (above 56 cm preferred; 21–23.5 in) and weight of 30 to 35 kg (66–77 lbs) for males, and 50 to 56 cm (above 52 cm preferred; 19.5–22 in) and 26 to 31 kg (57–68 lbs) for females, with size deviations of more than 2 cm (or 1 inch) outside the standard limits disqualified

traits: Quiet, calm, and emotionally stable indoors
Determined, solid, and courageous in the field
Methodical, unhurried searcher that stays in constant contact with the hunter and rarely strays
Exceptionally keen nose suited to both bird finding and tracking wounded game
Attentive, eager to learn, and happy to cooperate with its handler
Deeply loyal and closely bonded to the entire family
Patient and tolerant toward children and sociable with strangers and other dogs
Spirited and lively (especially in females), yet never aggressive or overly shy

exercise.level: High. A working gundog that needs substantial daily physical activity, opportunities to run freely in safe areas, retrieving tasks, and scent-tracking outlets alongside close human contact.
activities: Bird hunting, pointing, and field-trial work across small or large terrains
Blood-tracking (schweiss), scent games, and wounded-game trailing exercises
Dummy and game retrieving on land and in varied cover
Long, brisk daily country walks, hikes, and supervised free running in secure areas
Varied, reward-based obedience and handler-cooperation drills in changing environments

grooming.brushing: Wipe or brush daily with a rubber grooming brush or a damp chamois cloth to remove dust and loose hairs; daily upkeep prevents shed white hairs from accumulating visibly on furniture and carpets.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only as needed using a mild dog-safe shampoo, drying the coat, hanging ears, and throat folds thoroughly afterward.
notes: Although the short, dense, hard-feeling coat offers limited weather insulation on its own, the dog is sturdy and not overly sensitive to cold when active.
Inspect the low-set hanging ears regularly—especially after wet or brushy field work—and keep them clean and dry.
Check the deep flews, lip folds, throat dewlap, and tough paw pads after hunting outings for seeds, burrs, or ticks.
Keep nails trimmed and brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Attentive, eager to please, and naturally inclined to stay in contact with its handler, learning fastest and most durably through thoughtful, kind, and motivating consistency.
tips: Use thoughtful, friendly, reward-based consistency, delivering rewards promptly and varying the types of rewards used.
Change training locations and environments frequently so the dog stays engaged and generalizes cues reliably.
Capitalize on the breed's natural handler proximity and eagerness to cooperate rather than using harsh or repetitive pressure.
Incorporate nose work, laid scent trails, and retrieving exercises into daily routines to satisfy its strong hunting instincts.
Condition puppies early to calm show and veterinary handling, including mouth and tooth inspection.
training.socialization: Naturally peaceful, patient with children, and sociable toward strangers and other dogs, the Old Danish Pointer benefits from early, positive exposure to varied people, dogs, sights, and sounds, and thrives when included closely in family life.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Nordic breed guidance emphasizes that close human contact is essential to the Old Danish Pointer's wellbeing, making it poorly suited to long periods of isolation or kennel-only living.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality diet appropriate to the dog's life stage, body condition, and hunting or exercise workload.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete diet suited to age and activity level, adjusting portions according to body condition score, weight trends (30–35 kg in mature males and 26–31 kg in mature females), and seasonal hunting demands. Increase energy intake during active field-work periods and moderate portions during quieter periods to prevent excess weight. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Adjust caloric intake between active autumn/winter hunting seasons and lighter off-season routines.
Maintain a muscular, well-conditioned frame without excess weight that could burden the hips.
Factor training rewards—used frequently for prompt reinforcement—into the total daily energy allowance.
Allow rest before and after meals rather than feeding immediately before or after strenuous field work.
nutrition.note: No universal breed-specific meal schedule is mandated across life stages; individualize daily meal counts and portion sizes with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Old Danish Pointer is a sturdy, functional gundog whose small population—descended from a mid-twentieth-century genetic bottleneck and concentrated mainly in Denmark, Sweden, and Germany—is actively managed through mandatory Danish pre-breeding health regulations. Danish breeding rules and peer-reviewed veterinary genetics research document three primary hereditary focuses: hip dysplasia (HD), late-onset autosomal recessive progressive retinal atrophy (rcd4/PRA, caused by a C17H2orf71 frameshift insertion), and autosomal recessive congenital myasthenic syndrome ('muskeltræthed' / hereditary muscle fatigue, caused by a CHAT exon 6 missense mutation). In Denmark, puppies can only be registered in the national studbook if both parents have an official pre-mating hip status of HD A or B (or HD C only when paired with an HD A partner) and an official rcd4/PRA DNA test status, while Danish breeding approval also verifies DNA clearance for congenital myasthenic syndrome, a minimum 'Good' conformation rating at 15 months or older, and a hunting evaluation. In addition, conformation rules disqualify cleft palate/hare lip, entropion, ectropion, distichiasis, ribcage/sternum malformation, cryptorchidism, and jaw/dental malocclusions.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia (HD) — a developmental malformation of the coxofemoral joint; Danish studbook rules require both parents to hold official pre-mating hip scores of HD A or B (or HD C mated exclusively to HD A).

Progressive retinal atrophy (rcd4-PRA) — a late-onset autosomal recessive retinal degeneration diagnosed in the breed since the late 1990s; a 2018 Danish whole-genome sequencing study (Karlskov-Mortensen et al., 2018) identified a single-base insertion (c.3149_3150insC) in exon 1 of the C17H2orf71 (C2orf71 / PCARE) gene, and pre-mating rcd4/PRA DNA testing is now mandatory for studbook registration in Denmark.

Congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS / 'muskeltræthed') — an autosomal recessive presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder characterized clinically by severe exercise-induced muscle weakness in young dogs that does not respond to anticholinesterase drugs and lacks acetylcholine-receptor antibodies (Flagstad et al., 1989); a 2007 Danish study (Proschowsky et al., 2007) identified a G-to-A missense mutation (valine-to-methionine substitution) in exon 6 of the choline acetyltransferase (CHAT) gene, enabling targeted DNA testing that has largely eliminated affected litters in registered Danish stock.

Conformation-monitored ocular, oral, and skeletal defects — entropion, ectropion, distichiasis (double row of eyelashes), cleft palate or hare lip, overshot/undershot/wry bite, and sternum/ribcage malformations are explicitly listed as disqualifying faults to protect breed health.
preventiveCare: Verify before acquiring a puppy that both parents meet mandatory Danish pre-breeding requirements: official hip scores of HD A or B (or HD C paired with HD A), documented rcd4/PRA (C17H2orf71) DNA status, and clearance for congenital myasthenic syndrome (CHAT).
Inspect and dry the low-set hanging ears, deep flews, and throat dewlap after wet or brushy field work to prevent moisture buildup and skin or ear irritation.
Check the coat, interdigital spaces, and tough paw pads after hunting outings for thorns, grass awns, cuts, or ticks.
Maintain a lean, muscular body weight (30–35 kg for males; 26–31 kg for females) and keep routine vaccinations, parasite control, and dental care up to date.
Monitor adult dogs for any dim-light visual impairment (a sign of late-onset PRA) and young puppies for abnormal exercise-induced limb weakness.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia (HD) official radiographic evaluation prior to breeding (mandatory for Danish studbook registration: parents must be graded HD A or B, or HD C only if mated to an HD A partner; minimum age 15 months for Danish breeding approval).

Progressive Retinal Atrophy (rcd4/PRA — C17H2orf71 c.3149_3150insC mutation) DNA test prior to breeding (mandatory for Danish studbook registration unless documented hereditary clear via DNA-tested parents).

Congenital Myasthenic Syndrome (CMS / 'muskeltræthed' — CHAT exon 6 G>A missense mutation) DNA test or verified hereditary-clear pedigree status prior to breeding (required under Danish breeding approval rules).

Pre-breeding conformation, dentition (full 42-tooth scissor bite), eyelid (absence of entropion, ectropion, or distichiasis), and testicular examination (minimum 'Good' show rating at ≥15 months of age plus field/hunting evaluation for Danish breeding approval).
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and schedule routine veterinary oral checks. Conformation rules emphasize powerful jaws with a complete, regular scissor bite of 42 teeth (20 in the upper jaw and 22 in the lower jaw); a pincer (level) bite is a severe fault, and an overshot, undershot, or wry bite—or missing more than two PM1 premolars plus one other tooth—is a disqualifying fault.
health.earCare: Inspect the broad, low-set hanging ears regularly and dry them thoroughly after swimming or wet field work. Seek veterinary advice before applying ear cleaners or medications if redness, discharge, or odour develops.
health.skinCare: Brush or wipe the short, dense coat daily with a rubber brush or damp chamois, and inspect the looser skin of the deep flews, lip-corner folds, and throat dewlap after field activity to keep them clean, dry, and free of debris.

funFacts: The Old Danish Pointer (Gammel Dansk Hønsehund) is the only native pointing dog breed originating in Scandinavia.

Around 1710 in Glenstrup—between Randers and Hobro in Jutland—Morten Bak created the breed by crossing the sturdy hunting and pack dogs of travelling Romani people with local Saint-Hubert-type farm hounds over eight generations, earning the dogs the original name 'Bakhounds' (Bakhunde).

One of the breed's most celebrated features is its dramatic sexual dimorphism: the male is heavy, powerful, and substantial (30–35 kg), whereas the female is distinctly lighter (26–31 kg), livelier, and described as more spirited and 'capricious'.

Unlike high-speed pointers that range far ahead, the Old Danish Pointer works at a deliberate, measured pace and naturally maintains close contact with the hunter without disturbing the ground, making it equally effective on small holdings and large estates.

In 2007 and 2018, Danish geneticists solved two major inherited diseases in the breed—identifying a CHAT gene mutation for congenital myasthenic syndrome ('muskeltræthed') and a C17H2orf71 mutation for late-onset progressive retinal atrophy (rcd4/PRA)—allowing DNA testing to protect the breed's small gene pool.

faq.question: Where does the Old Danish Pointer come from, and why was it called the Bakhound?
faq.answer: The breed originated around 1710 in Glenstrup, between the towns of Randers and Hobro in Jutland, Denmark. There, Morten Bak crossed dogs kept by travelling Romani people (believed to carry Spanish Pointer and scent-hound blood) with local farm hounds (descended from Saint-Hubert Hounds / Bloodhounds) over eight generations, producing a white-and-brown pointing dog originally known as the Bakhound (Bakhund).

faq.question: How big is an adult Old Danish Pointer, and how do males and females differ?
faq.answer: The breed shows pronounced sexual dimorphism. Males stand 54 to 60 cm at the withers (above 56 cm preferred; 21–23.5 inches) and weigh 30 to 35 kg (66–77 pounds), presenting a powerful, substantial build. Females stand 50 to 56 cm (above 52 cm preferred; 19.5–22 inches) and weigh 26 to 31 kg (57–68 pounds), with a lighter, livelier, and more spirited expression while still remaining strongly boned.

faq.question: What does the Old Danish Pointer's hunting style look like?
faq.answer: Unlike wide-ranging, high-speed pointers, the Old Danish Pointer searches methodically at an average, measured pace while keeping constant contact with the hunter and avoiding unnecessary disturbance of the ground. Combined with its exceptional nose, this makes it suited to both small and large hunting grounds, as well as to tracking wounded game.

faq.question: How should the short white-and-brown coat be cared for?
faq.answer: Grooming is very simple: wipe or brush the short, dense, hard-feeling coat daily with a rubber grooming brush or a damp chamois cloth to lift dust and loose hairs. Daily wiping is recommended because shed white hairs are otherwise very noticeable on carpets and furniture.

faq.question: Is the Old Danish Pointer a good family dog?
faq.answer: Yes, for an active, outdoor-oriented household. Indoors, the breed is calm, quiet, and deeply devoted to its family, patient with children, and friendly toward strangers and other dogs. However, it requires abundant daily outdoor exercise, scent and retrieving outlets, and close human companionship.

faq.question: What hereditary health conditions and pre-breeding tests are established for the breed?
faq.answer: Three specific hereditary conditions are actively managed in Denmark through mandatory pre-breeding screening: hip dysplasia (HD), late-onset progressive retinal atrophy (rcd4/PRA, caused by a C17H2orf71 gene insertion identified in 2018), and congenital myasthenic syndrome ('muskeltræthed', an autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder caused by a CHAT gene mutation identified in 2007). For puppies to be registered in the Danish studbook, both parents must have official pre-mating hip scores of HD A or B (or HD C paired with an HD A partner) and official rcd4/PRA DNA test status, alongside verification of CHAT clearance.

overview.summary: The Old English Sheepdog is a large, sturdy herding breed recognised for its abundant shaggy coat, distinctive rolling gait and adaptable, intelligent nature. Originally used for moving livestock, it needs regular activity, companionship and consistent coat care. Its loud, ringing bark and substantial grooming needs are important considerations for prospective owners.
overview.description: The Old English Sheepdog has a compact, muscular build beneath a profuse double coat. Its coat is shaggy rather than curly, with a dense undercoat that provides insulation and weather protection when maintained properly. Accepted colours include shades of grey, grizzle, blue and blue merle, with or without white markings. The head is heavily coated, and the hair can obscure the eyes if left unmanaged. Despite its substantial appearance, the breed is agile and capable of purposeful movement. It was developed for demanding livestock work and generally benefits from regular exercise, training and activities that engage its mind. Many are sociable and adaptable companions, but individuals vary, and a dog's behaviour depends on its temperament, upbringing, health and environment. Owners should be prepared for thorough grooming and should not assume that a shaggy coat can be maintained with only occasional brushing.
overview.history: The Old English Sheepdog developed in Great Britain as a working dog associated with herding and driving livestock. Its sturdy body, shaggy protective coat and capable movement suited it to outdoor work. Over time, the breed became established in dog shows and as a companion as well as retaining its historical connection to farm work. The name is traditional; it does not mean that the breed is simply an ancient type of sheepdog unchanged over time.

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb the coat thoroughly at least weekly, working in sections down to the skin rather than only smoothing the surface. Dense undercoat can mat close to the skin, especially behind the ears, around the neck, beneath the legs and on the hindquarters. Many pet owners need more frequent sessions or professional grooming to keep the coat comfortable and manageable. A shorter pet trim can reduce the amount of coat to maintain, but still requires regular care.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when the coat is dirty or needs a refresh, using a dog-appropriate shampoo and rinsing thoroughly. The coat can take time to dry, so allow sufficient drying time and make sure the undercoat is not left damp. Ask a professional groomer or veterinarian for advice if the coat is heavily matted; do not pull painfully at mats.

health.overview: Old English Sheepdogs can be affected by inherited and acquired health conditions. Canine health guidance recommends comprehensive health screening for breeding dogs, including hip evaluation, eye examination, thyroid assessment and certain DNA tests. Other tests may be recommended for cardiac health, hearing and additional inherited conditions. These recommendations identify areas worth discussing with a breeder and veterinarian; they do not mean that every dog will develop these conditions. Review the actual test results rather than relying only on a certificate identifier.

faq.question: How big does an Old English Sheepdog get?
faq.answer: Official guidelines specify a minimum height of 22 inches for males and 21 inches for females. Typical adult weight generally ranges from 60 to 100 pounds across the breed.

faq.question: How long does an Old English Sheepdog usually live?
faq.answer: The published breed profile lists a life expectancy of 10–12 years. Individual lifespan varies with genetics, health, body condition and care.

faq.question: Does an Old English Sheepdog need a lot of grooming?
faq.answer: Yes. Its profuse double coat needs thorough brushing and combing down to the skin, usually at least weekly and often more frequently depending on coat condition. Some owners use professional grooming or a shorter pet trim.

faq.question: What coat colours are typical for an Old English Sheepdog?
faq.answer: Traditional descriptions include shades of grey, grizzle, blue and blue merle, with or without white markings. Brown and fawn shades are considered non-typical.

faq.question: Is the Old English Sheepdog good with children?
faq.answer: Some individuals are patient and sociable, but suitability depends on the dog's temperament, training and the children's behaviour. Supervise interactions, teach children respectful handling and provide the dog with a safe place to rest.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for verifiable hip and eye screening results, thyroid evaluation and relevant DNA tests such as exercise-induced collapse and MDR1. Cardiac, hearing and other genetic tests may also be recommended. A veterinarian can help interpret actual results.

faq.question: Is an Old English Sheepdog suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: There is no universal answer. Suitability depends on available space, daily activity, barking management, grooming routines, training and the individual dog. This record does not assign a blanket apartment-suitability rating.

overview.summary: A lively, fine-boned European toy spaniel prized for its silky flowing coat and distinctive ear varieties—the erect, butterfly-winged Papillon and the drop-eared Phalène.
overview.description: The Papillon and Phalène represent the two ear varieties of the Continental Toy Spaniel, sharing identical body structure, intelligence, and spirited temperament. These small, fine-boned dogs display a slightly elongated silhouette, a light and quick gait, dark expressive eyes, and an abundant, silky single coat devoid of an undercoat. Despite their delicate appearance, they are hardy, alert, and remarkably quick to learn, excelling in obedience, agility, and companion life. They thrive on close human interaction, daily walks, and mental challenges, while their small stature calls for gentle handling and supervision around young children and larger dogs.
overview.history: Originating among European dwarf spaniels popular at royal courts from the Renaissance onward, the Continental Toy Spaniel frequently appears in sixteenth-century paintings. Initially bred with drooping ears, the erect-eared type emerged later and earned the French name Papillon ('butterfly') for its wing-like ear silhouette, while the original drop-eared variety became known as the Phalène ('moth'). Both varieties frequently appear in the same litter and remain unified as two distinct ear forms within a single Continental Toy Spaniel heritage.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced small-breed or toy-breed diet matched to life stage, activity, and body condition.
nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily portions carefully to match energy expenditure and maintain a lean frame. Account for all training treats within the daily calorie budget, and provide continuous access to fresh water.

health.overview: Papillons and Phalènes are famously long-lived toy companions, frequently reaching their mid-to-late teens. Responsible breeders screen for patellar luxation, hereditary eye conditions, cardiac issues, and specific genetic disorders such as neuroaxonal dystrophy (NAD) and PRA-1. Their small stature also makes dental hygiene and safe handling essential.

funFacts: The name Papillon comes from the French word for butterfly, describing its erect, wing-like ears.
Phalène means moth in French and refers to the original drop-eared variety.
Both erect- and drop-eared varieties are recognized within the single Continental Toy Spaniel breed and can appear in the same litter.
Despite their delicate toy size, they are among the most agile and successful competitors in small-dog obedience and agility.

faq.question: Are Papillon and Phalène separate breeds?
faq.answer: No; they are recognized as two ear varieties of the single Continental Toy Spaniel breed—the Papillon has erect butterfly-like ears, while the Phalène has drop ears.

faq.question: Where do Papillon and Phalène dogs originate?
faq.answer: The breed originated in Belgium and France from European dwarf spaniels.

faq.question: How tall is a Papillon or Phalène?
faq.answer: Adults typically measure 8 to 11 inches at the withers.

faq.question: How much should a Papillon or Phalène weigh?
faq.answer: Published weight categories place adults between 1.5 and 4.5 kg for males and 1.5 and 5 kg for females, with a minimum threshold of 1.5 kg.

faq.question: What is the temperament like?
faq.answer: They are lively, alert, affectionate, and exceptionally quick to learn, thriving on human companionship and mental enrichment.

faq.question: Do Papillon and Phalène dogs need extensive grooming?
faq.answer: Because they have a single silky coat without an undercoat, they rarely mat heavily; brushing a few times a week keeps fringes smooth, alongside regular nail and dental care.

faq.question: What health checks should a breeder discuss?
faq.answer: Prospective owners should ask for documented eye, patella, and cardiac evaluations for breeding parents, plus DNA screening for PRA-1 and neuroaxonal dystrophy (NAD).

faq.question: Are they suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Yes, their compact size and adaptability make them well-suited to apartments when provided daily walks, play, and guidance on alert barking.

overview.summary: The Parson Russell Terrier is an agile, long-legged working earth terrier bred in southwestern England to trail mounted foxhounds and flush red foxes from underground dens. Bold, clever, and brimming with stamina, this predominantly white terrier thrives with active households that provide daily physical exercise, structured mental challenges, and secure outdoor containment.
overview.description: Built for endurance over open countryside as well as agility inside tight underground burrows, the Parson Russell Terrier combines a nearly square, laterally flexible torso with straight, ground-covering legs and a narrow, compressible ribcage that two average-sized hands can span right behind the elbows. Its harsh, weather-resistant double coat occurs in smooth, broken, or rough textures and is kept natural rather than sculpted. The coat is solid white or predominantly white with black, tan, lemon, grizzle, or tricolour markings chiefly around the head and tail base. Keen, dark almond-shaped eyes and forward-dropping V-shaped ears frame a wedge-shaped head with a strong scissor bite.
overview.history: This working terrier traces its lineage to Devon in southwestern England during the mid-nineteenth century, where Reverend John Russell—known as 'The Sporting Parson'—developed a uniform strain of predominantly white fox-working terriers starting from his foundation female, Trump, acquired near Oxford in 1819. Russell selected dogs with enough leg length to keep pace with mounted foxhounds across the countryside and enough chest flexibility and steady nerve to enter underground earths and bay to bolt the fox without killing it. After Russell's death in 1883, Arthur Heinemann drafted the first written description for the type in 1904 and in 1914 established the first dedicated society for these working terriers. Because the label 'Jack Russell' came to be applied loosely to diverse short-legged working terriers during the twentieth century, devotees of the longer-legged, square-proportioned fox-hunting type secured formal recognition for the breed in 1990 in Britain and in 1997 in the United States, adopting the distinct name Parson Russell Terrier.
overview.originalPurpose: Trailing mounted foxhound packs across open country and entering underground dens to bay and flush European red foxes without killing them.
currentRoles: Energetic household companion

physical.coatLength: Short to medium depending on whether the coat is smooth, broken, or rough; always displayed in a natural, unclipped outline.
coatColors: Predominantly white with tricolour (black and tan) markings
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate: sheds year-round at a manageable rate, with regular brushing helping remove loose hairs from the dense double coat.
distinctiveFeatures: Nearly square, balanced frame with forelegs slightly longer than chest depth for following hounds across country
Narrow, compressible ribcage behind the elbows that two average-sized hands can span for underground work
Thick, loose skin and laterally flexible back that allow the dog to turn around inside tight burrows
Wedge-shaped head with a flat skull, shallow stop, black nose, and strong scissor bite
Dark, almond-shaped eyes with a keen, intelligent expression and small V-shaped drop ears folding forward toward the outer eye corners
Harsh, weatherproof double coat in smooth, broken, or rough texture kept free of artificial sculpting
Solid white or predominantly white coat with markings preferably restricted to the head and root of the tail

traits: Bold, confident, and fearless when working
Friendly, exuberant, and affectionate with family members
Energetic, athletic, and built for sustained activity
Clever, inquisitive, and independent problem-solver
Tenacious and single-minded when following a scent or quarry
High prey drive toward small mammals and wildlife
Alert and responsive without being quarrelsome toward other dogs
Individual behaviour varies with lineage, early socialisation, training, and daily enrichment

exercise.level: High. Bred to run with horses and hounds across rough terrain, this terrier needs substantial daily physical exercise paired with structured mental work, adjusted for age, fitness, and weather.
activities: Brisk on-leash woodland or countryside walks with abundant sniffing opportunities
Earthdog, barn hunt, and nosework games that channel underground and scenting instincts safely
Agility, flyball, or lure coursing in securely enclosed rings
Interactive fetch, tug, and food-dispensing puzzle toys in a fenced yard
Short, upbeat obedience, trick, and recall drills using positive reinforcement

grooming.level: Low to moderate. Smooth coats need only routine brushing, whereas broken and rough coats require periodic hand-stripping or stripping-knife maintenance to preserve harsh texture and a neat, natural silhouette.
grooming.brushing: Brush weekly with a hound glove or dense bristle brush for smooth coats, or a slicker brush and metal comb for broken and rough coats, removing dead hair and checking the skin for burrs or ticks.
grooming.bathing: Bathe about once a month or whenever the dog gets muddy outdoors, using a mild dog shampoo that preserves the coat's natural weather-resistant oils.
notes: Maintain a natural, unclipped outline on broken and rough coats by plucking dead outer hairs rather than machine-clipping, which softens the texture.
Inspect the forward-folding V-shaped ears weekly for dirt, grass seeds, or wax build-up and clean gently with a veterinary ear cleanser.
Trim nails monthly or as needed so the compact, cat-like feet remain sound and comfortable.
Brush the teeth several times a week using enzymatic canine toothpaste.
Check pads, skin, and coat after field or woodland outings for thorns, abrasions, or external parasites.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for novice handlers. Quick wit and high drive allow rapid learning, but independent problem-solving and intense hunting instincts demand patient, consistent, reward-based guidance and humour.
tips: Keep training sessions brief, varied, and game-oriented so this quick-thinking terrier does not grow bored with repetition.
Use high-value food rewards and play to build reliable engagement and impulse control.
Practice recall inside securely fenced spaces while keeping the dog on a leash or long line in open areas where wildlife may bolt.
Provide designated digging boxes, scent puzzles, or earthdog games so natural digging and hunting behaviours have appropriate outlets.
Teach calm settling on a mat indoors to balance the breed's high outdoor drive.
Prevent rehearsed fence-fighting or sparring with other dogs through proactive management and calm redirection.
training.socialization: Begin structured, positive exposure early with diverse people, well-mannered dogs, household noises, and novel surfaces. Supervise interactions with young children—since these spirited terriers dislike clumsy or heavy-handed treatment from toddlers—and recognize that early socialisation will not erase their innate drive to chase small animals.

climates: Adaptable to temperate climates when given indoor family living and appropriate seasonal care.
In warm weather, schedule strenuous running for cooler morning or evening hours and provide shade and fresh water.
In cold or wet weather, towel-dry the double coat after outings and provide a warm, draft-free indoor bed.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced canine diet formulated for the dog's life stage, activity output, and individual health profile.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed three to four measured meals daily of a complete puppy diet during early growth, tapering to two daily meals as the youngster approaches maturity.
feedingFrequency.adult: Feed two measured meals per day of a complete adult diet, adjusting caloric intake to sustain a lean, hard-muscled working condition.
feedingFrequency.senior: Feed two measured daily meals tailored to senior metabolism, dental condition, and joint or organ health under veterinary guidance.

nutrition.guidelines: Adjust daily food portions using body condition scoring rather than fixed package averages, since energy expenditure differs markedly between active sport or working terriers and household companions. Count training treats within the daily calorie budget to prevent excess weight, introduce food transitions gradually over seven to ten days, and ensure constant access to clean drinking water.
considerations: Maintain a lean, athletic waist and easily palpable ribs so extra weight does not strain the patellas or spine.
Deduct training treats and food-puzzle fillings from the main meal allowance to avoid gradual weight gain.
Keep fresh, clean water available at all times, particularly after vigorous running or earthwork.
Select a life-stage-appropriate diet that meets established veterinary nutritional profiles.
Consult a veterinarian promptly if appetite changes, digestive upset, or dental discomfort occurs.
nutrition.note: Exact calorie and gram targets are intentionally omitted because individual energy needs depend on age, metabolism, neuter status, daily workload, and diet energy density.

health.overview: The Parson Russell Terrier is generally a hardy, long-lived working breed, with most individuals enjoying vigorous health into their teens. However, documented hereditary conditions in the breed include patellar luxation, congenital sensorineural deafness, primary lens luxation and other ocular disorders, two genetically distinct forms of hereditary cerebellar ataxia, and inherited dental enamel hypomineralization. Prospective owners and breeders can reduce risk through clinical evaluations and targeted DNA testing.
commonConditions: Primary lens luxation (PLL), an inherited weakening of the ocular zonular fibres associated with a splice-site mutation (c.1473+1G>A) in the ADAMTS17 gene that can cause painful lens displacement and secondary glaucoma

Spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA), an autosomal-recessive neurodegenerative disorder linked to the KCNJ10 missense variant (c.627C>G; p.Ile209Met), causing progressive cerebellar incoordination, hypermetria, and often myokymia (muscle rippling) or neuromyotonia

Late-onset ataxia (LOA), an autosomal-recessive cerebellar ataxia associated with a missense mutation (c.344G>A; p.Cys115Tyr) in the CAPN1 calpain-1 gene, typically presenting between 6 and 12 months of age with progressive gait incoordination and balance loss
Congenital sensorineural deafness (unilateral or bilateral hearing loss linked to predominantly white piebald pigmentation)
Patellar luxation (intermittent or persistent slippage of the kneecap out of the femoral groove)
Amelogenesis imperfecta (inherited enamel hypomineralization caused by a recessive missense variant, c.716C>T / p.Pro239Leu, in the ENAM gene)
preventiveCare: Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, routine dental assessments, and regionally appropriate vaccination and parasite-control programmes.
Request documented parental health clearances—covering ophthalmologic exams, patellar evaluations, BAER hearing tests, and relevant DNA panels—before acquiring a puppy.
Monitor adult dogs for early signs of ocular pain, redness, cloudiness, or squinting, as lens luxation requires urgent veterinary attention to preserve vision.
Seek veterinary evaluation if a young dog develops hindlimb stiffness, high-stepping gait (hypermetria), balance difficulties, or involuntary muscle twitching.
Keep the dog at a lean working weight to minimize mechanical stress on the stifles and kneecaps.
recommendedScreenings: Orthopedic evaluation of the stifles for patellar luxation.
Comprehensive eye examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist.
Brainstem auditory evoked response (BAER) hearing test to screen for unilateral or bilateral congenital deafness.
DNA testing for the ADAMTS17 primary lens luxation variant, the KCNJ10 spinocerebellar ataxia variant, and the CAPN1 late-onset ataxia variant.
Additional lineage-indicated genetic screening—such as the ENAM amelogenesis imperfecta test—when advised by a veterinarian or genetic counselor.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times weekly with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule professional veterinary dental examinations. In puppies and young dogs, inspect adult teeth as they erupt for rough, pitted, or brownish discoloured enamel that could indicate inherited enamel hypomineralization.
health.earCare: Inspect the V-shaped drop ears weekly for soil, plant awns, redness, or waxy odour—especially after digging or brush work—and clean gently as needed with a dog-specific ear solution.
health.skinCare: Check the thick skin and dense double coat during routine brushing for burrs, ticks, Foxtail awns, or minor scrapes acquired outdoors, and avoid harsh shampoos or clipping that strip natural coat protection.

idealFor: Active individuals and families who enjoy daily woodland hikes, running, or canine sports
Handlers interested in earthdog trials, barn hunt, agility, scent work, or trick training
Households with securely fenced yards and a commitment to leashed or supervised outdoor exercise
Experienced terrier enthusiasts who appreciate a bold, clever, high-drive working companion
notIdealFor: Sedentary households seeking a quiet, low-energy lap dog
Homes with free-roaming small pets or unfenced yards near wildlife and traffic
Owners expecting effortless off-leash obedience around small animals without dedicated training and containment
Households with unsupervised toddlers or rough play styles

funFacts: Reverend John Russell ('The Sporting Parson', 1795–1883) acquired his celebrated foundation female, Trump, from a milkman near Oxford in 1819, establishing the working fox-terrier strain that carries his name.

International conformation guidelines specify separate ideal wither heights of 36 cm for males and 33 cm for females, whereas American guidelines set a 14-inch ideal height for males and a 13-inch ideal for females within an overall 12-to-15-inch window.

Because a working terrier must squeeze into underground fox earths, its ribcage behind the shoulders is designed to be spanned—compressed gently between two average-sized hands with thumbs meeting at the spine and fingers meeting under the sternum.
The predominantly white coat was selected so huntsmen and hounds could immediately distinguish the emerging terrier from the red fox at the mouth of an earth.

faq.question: How tall is a Parson Russell Terrier?
faq.answer: Published height targets depend on the registry: one major tradition specifies a 14-inch male target and a 13-inch female target inside an allowed 12-to-15-inch span, whereas international rules set targets at 36 cm for males and 33 cm for females. Above all, the dog must remain balanced and spannable behind the shoulders.

faq.question: How much does a Parson Russell Terrier weigh?
faq.answer: Adult dogs in lean, hard-muscled working condition typically weigh 13 to 17 pounds. Individual weight should always reflect frame size, bone substance, and overall fitness rather than a rigid number.

faq.question: How does a Parson Russell Terrier differ from a Jack Russell Terrier?
faq.answer: Both trace back to Reverend John Russell's nineteenth-century fox-working terriers, but the Parson Russell Terrier preserves the longer-legged, nearly square outline built to run alongside horses and hounds, whereas the Jack Russell Terrier is bred with a slightly longer-cast body and shorter legs.

faq.question: What coat types and colours are permitted?
faq.answer: The harsh, weatherproof double coat comes in smooth, broken, or rough textures and must appear natural rather than sculpted. The coat is solid white or predominantly white with black, tan, lemon, grizzle, or tricolour markings, ideally concentrated on the head and root of the tail.

faq.question: How long does a Parson Russell Terrier live?
faq.answer: Typical life expectancy is 13 to 15 years, and some reference databases report a slightly broader span of 12 to 16 years. Longevity depends on genetic screening, preventive healthcare, nutrition, and safe containment.

faq.question: What health screenings should prospective puppy buyers request?
faq.answer: Buyers should ask for documented parental clearances for patellar luxation, board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams, and BAER hearing evaluations, along with DNA test results for primary lens luxation (ADAMTS17), spinocerebellar ataxia (KCNJ10), and late-onset ataxia (CAPN1).

faq.question: Can a Parson Russell Terrier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Success in an apartment depends on the owner's commitment rather than floor space alone: because this high-energy hunting terrier can become vocal or destructive when bored, urban owners must provide vigorous daily outdoor exercise, scent or puzzle work, and consistent training.

overview.summary: A tough, compact, and fearless British working earthdog native to the Lake District, renowned for its flexible spannable chest, weatherproof double coat, tenacious drive, and affectionate domestic loyalty.
overview.description: The Patterdale Terrier is an authentic, rugged working earthdog built with a compact, balanced frame designed to pursue quarry into tight underground rock fissures and dens. Characterized by clean, muscular lines and strong bone without coarseness, the terrier possesses an extraordinarily flexible, spannable ribcage that can be encircled by an average pair of human hands directly behind the shoulders. Its dense, weather-resistant double coat appears in smooth, broken, or rough textures, predominantly in solid black, though red, liver, grizzle, and black-and-tan are recognized. The head is strong and trapezoidal with powerful punishing jaws, dark alert eyes, and neat V-shaped drop ears. In the home, it settles into an affectionate, companionable, and quiet pet, but outdoors it reveals boundless stamina, intense focus on scent trails, and game determination.
overview.history: The breed developed in the rocky fells and steep valleys of the Lake District in northern England, descending from hard-bitten northern fell terriers bred to safeguard sheep flocks from red foxes. Unlike southern terriers bred for softer lowland earths, fell terriers required exceptional toughness, flexible chests, and fearless stamina to traverse jagged granite crags. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Joe Bowman, renowned huntsman of the Ullswater Foxhounds, systematically bred these black terriers at his base in Patterdale, establishing the core bloodlines. Subsequent generations of dedicated Cumbria breeders, notably Cyril Breay, Frank Buck, and Brian Nuttall, refined the working strain to maintain its practical earthdog excellence and sound constitution. The breed was later introduced to North America and recognized as a distinct purebred terrier, while remaining an unexaggerated, functional working dog prized by earthdog and sport enthusiasts worldwide.
overview.originalPurpose: Subterranean earthwork, bolting and dispatching foxes from rocky mountain dens, badger and otter control, and farm vermin management across the northern English fells.
currentRoles: Working earthdog and farm pest controller
Competitive earthdog, barn hunt, and terrier trial athlete
Active outdoor companion and hiking partner for experienced handlers
Canine athlete in agility, flyball, and scent tracking
