overview.summary: A large, powerful, and agile mountain livestock guardian from Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, distinguished by its nearly square build, weatherproof parti-coloured double coat, plumed tail carried high in motion, and calm devotion to its family and flocks.
overview.description: The Tornjak—also known as the Bosnian and Herzegovinian-Croatian Shepherd Dog—is a large, strong, and well-proportioned mountain livestock guardian built for endurance and agility rather than excessive heaviness. Its body is almost square, with body length exceeding height at the withers by no more than 8 percent, supported by strong, harmonious bone and a supple, long-reaching trot driven from powerful hindquarters. An elongated head with divergent skull and muzzle planes and a 1:1 skull-to-muzzle ratio carries dark almond-shaped eyes and medium-sized, triangular folded pendant ears held close to the cheeks. Protecting the dog in harsh mountain weather is a long, coarse, straight topcoat over a dense, woolly winter undercoat—short on the face and lower legs but forming a prominent neck mane, forearm feathering, thick thigh breeches, and a richly plumed tail raised above the back line when moving. Calm, affectionate, and steady with its household and the animals in its care, the Tornjak is incorruptible and naturally wary of strangers when guarding, thriving with experienced handlers who provide secure space, early socialization, and patient guidance.
overview.history: Indigenous to the Dinaric mountain ranges and surrounding valleys of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, the Tornjak descends from archaic, genetically homogeneous shepherd and flock-guarding dogs that evolved alongside transhumant pastoralism in the western Balkans (with hypotheses linking early regional livestock guardians to dogs of the Iranian plateau or Tibetan Mastiff lineage). Historical manuscripts from the Catholic Church dated 1067 and 1374 provide detailed written descriptions of this Bosnian-Herzegovinian-Croatian mountain guardian. In its early formal registration history, the breed was initially designated Kanis Montanus ('mountain dog'), while local shepherds and rural communities knew it as the Tornjak—derived from tor, the Croatian and Bosnian word for a fenced sheep and cattle enclosure. As traditional nomadic sheep farming declined in the twentieth century, the native guardian population neared extinction until cynologists launched a coordinated field search and preservation effort simultaneously in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina around 1972, followed by continuous purebred pedigree breeding from 1978. The breed gained provisional international recognition in June 2007, North American registry recognition in August 2011 and foundation-stock recording in May 2012, and definitive international recognition in November 2017.
overview.originalPurpose: Guarding and protecting sheep, cattle, and other livestock against large predators such as wolves and bears on open mountain pastures, as well as guarding farmyards and rural property.
currentRoles: Working livestock guardian protecting sheep, goats, cattle, hogs, and poultry
Farmstead and rural property guardian
Devoted family companion for experienced households with secure outdoor space
Hiking, trekking, and outdoor companion
Participant in obedience, rally, agility, and scent or enrichment activities

physical.coatType: Long, thick, weather-resistant double coat consisting of a long, coarse, straight outer coat (especially long over the upper croup and occasionally slightly wavy over the shoulders and back) and a long, very thick, dense woolly winter undercoat that never parts along the spine. Hair is short on the muzzle, forehead, ears, and fronts of the legs and feet, while forming an abundant neck mane, forearm feathering, thick breeches on the upper thighs, abundant hair on the rear pasterns, and a richly plumed tail.
physical.coatLength: Long
coatColors: Parti-coloured with a dominant white ground colour and distinct patches of various solid colours (such as black, brown, tan, red, yellow, or badger/grey markings)
White with a black mantle covering the body and white markings around the neck, over the head, and along the legs
Almost pure white with small coloured markings on the head, body, or legs (solid-coloured coats and albinism are disqualifications, and a dark facial mask is faulted)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate year-round, with heavy seasonal shedding twice a year in spring and autumn when the dense winter undercoat is blown
distinctiveFeatures: Large, powerful, agile build with a nearly square outline in which body length does not exceed height at the withers by more than 8 percent
Strong, harmonious bone that is neither light nor excessively heavy or coarse, paired with thick, tight-fitting skin
Elongated head with divergent skull and muzzle planes, a 1:1 skull-to-muzzle ratio (shorter muzzle acceptable), flat skull from brows to occiput, slight occipital peak, and slightly pronounced stop

Large nose with dark pigmentation matching the coat (depigmentation / Dudley nose disallowed), rectangular muzzle with straight nasal bridge, tight dark-pigmented lips, and strong jaws with a complete scissor bite
Dark, almond-shaped eyes with close-fitting, darkly pigmented lids and a calm, dignified expression
Medium-sized, triangular, folded pendant ears set rather high, carried close to the cheeks, and covered with short hair
Medium-length, powerful neck carried slightly low with tight skin and a profuse coat forming a distinct mane
Short, taut, straight back, deep oval chest reaching at least to the elbows (never barrel-shaped), and a well-muscled underline sloping gradually upward without a tuck-up
Strong limbs with a ~120° shoulder-blade-to-upper-arm angle, well-bent stifles, arched toes with hard dark-pigmented pads (front feet more developed than hind feet), and optional hind dewclaws
Long, very mobile, richly plumed tail that hangs at rest and is characteristically raised above the level of the back when moving
Balanced, supple, long-reaching trotting gait with strong rear drive and a firm topline

Withers height of 65 to 70 cm (25.5 to 27.5 inches) for males and 60 to 65 cm (23.5 to 25.5 inches) for females with a ±2 cm (±0.75 inch) tolerance (58 to 72 cm / 23 to 28 inches overall), and typical adult weight of 27 to 54 kg (60 to 120 pounds, or 28 to 50 kg / 62 to 110 pounds in some profiles)

traits: Calm, steady, and composed around its owner and household
Deeply affectionate and gentle with family members and charges
Courageous, incorruptible, and resolute when guarding livestock or property
Alert, observant, and suspicious of unfamiliar strangers
Dignified, self-confident, and independent-minded
Intelligent with strong problem-solving ability and long-term memory
Willing to work and responsive to calm, respectful guidance
Peaceful toward people in everyday neutral settings, yet protective against perceived threats to its flock or home
Heightened vigilance and patrol activity around dawn and dusk

exercise.level: Moderate. Primarily focused on calm mental vigilance, steady perimeter patrols or long daily walks, and occasional short bursts of high-speed energy ('zoomies'), with peak alertness around dawn and dusk.
activities: Long, steady daily walks or hikes suited to the dog's age and physical maturity
Supervised perimeter patrolling and free movement in a securely fenced yard or pasture
Working livestock-guardian duties alongside sheep, goats, cattle, or poultry
Short bursts of running and interactive play ('zoomies') in a secure enclosure
Indoor and outdoor mental enrichment, such as hide-and-seek, trick training, and problem-solving games
Obedience, rally, agility, or swimming for mature, well-conditioned dogs

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly about once a week using a slicker brush or undercoat rake to remove loose hair and prevent matting down to the skin. Increase brushing frequency during the two major seasonal coat blows in spring and autumn, paying close attention to the neck mane, forearm feathering, thigh breeches, and tail plume.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally as needed using a mild, dog-safe shampoo. Because the double coat produces natural protective oils that repel dirt and weather, avoid frequent bathing that strips these oils and dries or irritates the skin.
notes: Never shave a Tornjak's double coat unless medically required by a veterinarian; the thick undercoat and coarse topcoat insulate against both winter cold and summer heat.
Expect two heavy seasonal shedding periods each year in spring and autumn when the dense undercoat is released.
Part the coat behind the ears, under the neck mane, in the armpits, along the thigh breeches, and beneath the tail to remove burrs, plant debris, and early tangles.
Because Tornjaks enjoy being outdoors in rain or snow and many like playing in water, inspect and dry the folded pendant ears regularly to prevent moisture buildup and ear infections.
Trim the strong, fast-growing nails regularly with clippers or a grinder to prevent overgrowth, splitting, and cracking.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and accustom puppies early to calm grooming and veterinary handling.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Intelligent, quick to learn, and blessed with a long memory, yet possessing the independent decision-making and territorial instincts of a traditional livestock guardian.
tips: Use calm, patient, reward-based positive reinforcement that builds mutual trust; harsh or forceful corrections are counterproductive with a dignified guardian breed.
Begin foundational obedience, leash manners, and boundary training early in puppyhood before the dog reaches its full adult strength.
Teach clear household rules for greeting welcomed guests so the dog looks to its owner's cues rather than making independent guarding decisions with visitors.
Provide secure physical fencing around yards and pastures, and supervise interactions with unfamiliar dogs, delivery personnel, and visitors.
Keep training sessions purposeful and varied, engaging the dog's natural problem-solving intelligence and strong memory.
Be mindful that guardian instincts and vocal alerting often intensify at maturity and during dawn and dusk when predators are naturally active.
training.socialization: Start structured, positive socialization early in puppyhood, exposing the young Tornjak to diverse people, calm dogs, household routines, veterinary handling, and novel environments outside its home territory. Because the breed is naturally discerning and suspicious of strangers on its property, socialization should foster steady confidence and neutral manners in public rather than expecting indiscriminate friendliness.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality large-breed dog food (commercial or veterinarian-supervised home-prepared diet) appropriate to life stage (puppy, adult, or senior), workload, and body condition.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Several smaller measured meals daily using a large-breed puppy diet to support steady, controlled skeletal growth, adjusted with veterinary guidance.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two or more smaller measured meals daily rather than a single large meal to support safe digestion and help reduce bloat risk.
feedingFrequency.senior: Measured smaller meals tailored to appetite, weight, dental health, mobility, and veterinary advice.

nutrition.guidelines: Historically shaped by harsh mountain conditions with modest food requirements for its size, the Tornjak does well on measured portions of a high-quality diet matched to its age and activity level. To help reduce the risk of life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV or bloat), divide the daily ration into smaller, more frequent meals, restrict vigorous physical activity before and after eating, and avoid feeding from elevated dog bowls (which can encourage gulping air with each bite). Feed a controlled-growth large-breed formula during puppyhood to protect developing hips and elbows, monitor body condition to prevent obesity, and provide clean, fresh water at all times.
considerations: Feed smaller, more frequent meals and restrict strenuous exercise around mealtimes to help lower the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
Feed at floor level rather than from elevated food bowls unless specifically directed otherwise by a veterinarian, as elevated bowls can promote air gulping.
Use an appropriate large-breed puppy diet during growth to avoid rapid weight gain or excessive calcium and calorie intake that stresses developing joints.
Keep adult dogs in lean, muscular body condition and account for training treats within the daily calorie allowance to minimize mechanical strain on the hips and elbows.
Transition between foods gradually over several days and consult a veterinarian before adding dietary or joint supplements.
nutrition.note: Daily caloric needs vary with frame size (ranging from 27 to 54 kg), ambient temperature, and whether the dog works as a pasture guardian or lives as a companion; confirm individual portion sizes with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Tornjak is generally a hardy, resilient mountain breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years and a relatively short list of documented hereditary disorders. The primary orthopaedic and emergency conditions highlighted in veterinary research and breed health guidance are hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, and gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV or bloat). In a peer-reviewed retrospective study of 735 Tornjak hip radiographs evaluated between 2001 and 2016 (median age 18 months), 74.97% were graded healthy (grades A and B) and 25.03% were graded dysplastic (grades C, D, and E; 23.14% dysplastic among the 523 dogs under 24 months of age), with a statistically significant decline in severe grade E dysplasia over the 15-year monitoring period thanks to selective breeding licences. A 2023 veterinary biomarker study of 99 adult Tornjaks (51 non-dysplastic and 48 dysplastic) further demonstrated that serum hyaluronic acid (HA), procollagen II C-terminal propeptide (PIICP), and matrix metallopeptidase 9 (MMP9) activity differentiate dysplastic from normal hips with high sensitivity and specificity. Conformation rules also require breeding stock to be functionally and clinically healthy and penalize or disqualify entropion, ectropion, wall eyes, overshot or undershot bites, cryptorchidism, and albinism.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — a multifactorial developmental malformation of the coxofemoral joint leading to laxity, secondary osteoarthritis, pain, and lameness; in a 15-year retrospective study of 735 screened Tornjaks (2001–2016), 25.03% of evaluated radiographs were graded dysplastic (grades C–E) and 74.97% healthy (grades A–B), reflecting a screened breeding cohort rather than universal population prevalence.
Elbow dysplasia — a developmental joint abnormality affecting large-breed dogs that can cause forelimb lameness, pain, and progressive osteoarthritis, jeopardizing a working guardian's mobility.

Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — an acute, life-threatening emergency in large, deep-chested dogs in which the stomach fills with gas and twists on its axis, cutting off blood flow and requiring immediate emergency veterinary intervention.
preventiveCare: Request documented pre-breeding hip and elbow radiographic clearances for both parents before acquiring a puppy, and breed only functionally sound dogs with healthy joints.
Feed smaller, more frequent meals, restrict physical activity around mealtimes, and avoid elevated food bowls to help reduce the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
Learn the early warning signs of bloat—uncomfortable pacing, restlessness, a tight or painful abdomen, and unproductive retching—and seek emergency veterinary care immediately if suspected.
Support steady, controlled skeletal growth during puppyhood with a balanced large-breed puppy diet and age-appropriate exercise, and maintain a lean adult body weight to protect the hips and elbows.
Inspect and dry the folded pendant ears regularly—especially after rain, snow, or water play—to prevent moisture-related ear canal infections.
Maintain routine veterinary wellness checks, vaccinations, parasite control, dental brushing, and regular nail trimming.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation through an official national or international scoring programme (minimum age 18 to 24 months for definitive large-breed grading).
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation for breeding stock.

Ophthalmic and physical breeding-soundness examination confirming normal eyelid conformation (absence of entropion or ectropion), complete scissor-bite dentition, and normal descended testicles in males.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and schedule periodic veterinary dental assessments. Conformation rules specify very long, strong jaws with full dentition meeting in a complete scissor bite (pincer/even bites and missing premolars are faulted, and overshot or undershot jaws are disqualifying faults).
health.earCare: Check the medium-sized, folded pendant ears weekly—and dry them thoroughly after swimming or wet weather—for trapped moisture, wax buildup, debris, redness, or foul odour. Clean only with a veterinarian-recommended ear cleanser and never insert cotton swabs deep into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: Part the thick double coat down to the tight-fitting skin during weekly brushing to check for tangles, burrs, ticks, or skin irritation. Avoid over-bathing so the coat retains its natural protective oils, and never shave the double coat unless medically necessary.

idealFor: Ranchers, farmers, and rural property owners seeking a steady, devoted livestock and farmyard guardian
Experienced large-dog or guardian-breed handlers who use calm, consistent, reward-based leadership
Households with a securely fenced yard or rural acreage that can provide daily walks and perimeter-patrol space
Active families and outdoor enthusiasts who include their dog in daily life and supervise interactions with visitors
Owners willing to brush a thick double coat weekly and manage heavy spring and autumn coat blows
notIdealFor: First-time or passive dog owners unfamiliar with independent, territorial livestock-guardian breeds
People expecting an indiscriminately outgoing dog that welcomes every stranger onto its property
Households without secure fencing or those unable to manage dawn-and-dusk alerting and patrol behaviour
Fastidious owners unwilling to deal with heavy seasonal shedding twice a year
Sedentary homes unable to provide daily outdoor walks, mental vigilance outlets, and social inclusion

funFacts: The breed's name comes from the Croatian and Bosnian word 'tor', meaning a fenced enclosure or pen for sheep and cattle, reflecting its traditional role guarding livestock in mountain pens and pastures.

Early church manuscripts dated 1067 and 1374 record the Bosnian-Herzegovinian-Croatian shepherd dog in the Dinaric mountains, making the Tornjak one of the few livestock guardians with medieval written documentation.

When modern preservation began in the twentieth century, the breed was initially registered under the Latin-style name 'Kanis Montanus' ('mountain dog') before the traditional local name Tornjak was adopted.

After nearly vanishing by the mid-twentieth century as nomadic sheep herding declined, the Tornjak was saved through a coordinated field expedition launched simultaneously in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina around 1972, with continuous purebred breeding beginning in 1978.
While moving at its characteristic long-reaching trot, a Tornjak always carries its long, richly plumed tail raised high above the line of its back like a banner.

Because wild predators in the Balkan mountains are most active at dawn and dusk, Tornjaks naturally maintain a crepuscular rhythm—resting calmly through much of the day and becoming most alert and active at twilight and daybreak.

Its thick double coat is engineered for mountain extremes: coarse, straight guard hairs shed rain and snow while a dense, woolly winter undercoat insulates against subzero cold and shields the skin from summer heat.

faq.question: Where does the Tornjak originate, and what does its name mean?
faq.answer: The Tornjak originates from the mountain ranges and surrounding valleys of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. In early registries it was called 'Kanis Montanus' ('mountain dog'), but local shepherds named it the Tornjak after 'tor', the regional word for a fenced enclosure or pen for sheep and cattle.

faq.question: What was the Tornjak bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed as a mountain livestock guardian and farmyard protection dog, working independently or in pairs to defend sheep, cattle, and rural property against large predators such as wolves and bears.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Tornjak?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 65 to 70 cm (25.5 to 27.5 inches) at the withers and females stand 60 to 65 cm (23.5 to 25.5 inches), with a tolerance of ±2 cm (±0.75 inches)—giving an overall height range of roughly 58 to 72 cm (23 to 28 inches). Typical adult weights range from 27 to 54 kg (60 to 120 pounds), with some profiles listing 28 to 50 kg (62 to 110 pounds) depending on sex and frame.

faq.question: How long does a Tornjak typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: What is the Tornjak's coat like, and what colours are accepted?
faq.answer: The Tornjak has a long, coarse, straight topcoat over a dense, woolly winter undercoat, with short hair on the face and lower legs and a prominent neck mane, forearm feathering, thigh breeches, and plumed tail. It is almost always parti-coloured with a dominant white base coat and distinct patches of solid colour, though black-mantled dogs with white markings and nearly all-white dogs with small markings also occur. Solid single-coloured dogs are disqualified.

faq.question: Does a Tornjak require a lot of grooming or shaving in summer?
faq.answer: Overall grooming needs are moderate: brushing once a week with a slicker brush or undercoat rake keeps the coat tangle-free, with more frequent brushing needed during heavy spring and autumn shedding seasons. Bathing is needed only occasionally so natural protective skin oils are preserved, and the double coat should never be shaved unless medically necessary because it insulates against both winter cold and summer heat.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Tornjak need?
faq.answer: Tornjaks generally have a moderate energy level shaped by their livestock-guardian heritage. Much of their day is spent in calm, watchful vigilance punctuated by steady perimeter patrols, long daily walks, and short bursts of high-speed energy ('zoomies'), with peak alertness occurring around dawn and dusk.

faq.question: Is a Tornjak a good family companion?
faq.answer: With its own family and familiar people, the Tornjak is calm, gentle, devoted, and affectionate. However, because it is a large, naturally protective guardian that is suspicious of strangers on its territory, it requires an experienced owner, secure fencing, early socialization, and careful supervision around visitors and children.

faq.question: Is the Tornjak easy to train?
faq.answer: Tornjaks are intelligent, learn quickly, and retain lessons in their memory for a long time, willingly performing tasks for a respected handler. Because they also possess the independent judgement of a livestock guardian, they respond best to calm, consistent, reward-based training rather than harsh corrections or repetitive drills.

faq.question: Can a Tornjak live in an apartment?
faq.answer: While short indoor hallway walks and multiple daily outings can help during bad weather, a blanket yes-or-no rating is not established because the Tornjak is a large, vocal, territorial mountain guardian that thrives best in a home with a securely fenced yard or rural acreage.

faq.question: What health problems and screenings are most important in Tornjaks?
faq.answer: The primary health concerns are hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, and gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV or bloat). In a 15-year radiographic study of 735 screened Tornjaks (2001–2016), 74.97% had healthy hips (grades A and B) and 25.03% had hip dysplasia (grades C to E), with selective breeding significantly reducing severe cases over time. Prospective buyers should ask breeders for documented hip and elbow radiographic clearances, and owners should manage bloat risk by feeding smaller meals at floor level (avoiding elevated bowls) and restricting exercise after eating.

overview.summary: A diminutive, athletic American companion dog with a sleek satin coat, erect pointed ears, spirited curiosity, and an enduring terrier drive to investigate its environment.
overview.description: The Toy Fox Terrier harmoniously unites the fearless tenacity of a working ratter with the affectionate charm of a toy lap companion. Its square-proportioned, lithe frame is finely muscled and built for nimble agility, while its short, glossy coat is predominantly pure white with distinct colour patches adorning the head. Large, erect bat-like ears and round, luminous dark eyes give it an intensely keen, animated expression. While deeply devoted to its family and quick to master new tasks, its energetic nature demands regular play, mental enrichment, and clear household guidance. Because of its petite build, careful handling around young children and larger pets is essential to avoid accidental injury.
overview.history: Developed in the United States during the early twentieth century, the breed originated when American breeders crossed diminutive Smooth Fox Terriers with small toy breeds, notably Chihuahuas, Italian Greyhounds, and Manchester Terriers. The resulting dogs preserved the sharp hunting instincts and fearless vermin-control capabilities of larger terriers in a convenient companion size. Valued as efficient farm ratters and entertaining performers in traveling shows, the breed steadily gained national popularity, earning formal recognition as an agile, distinct American toy terrier.
overview.originalPurpose: Hunting rats and small farmyard vermin, alongside serving as an affectionate domestic companion.

Agility, rally, and trick-training competitor

Brush the teeth regularly because dental problems can be significant in small dogs.
Check the ears and keep them clean and dry without inserting cotton buds into the ear canal.

tips: Use short, varied sessions with food rewards, toys, and praise.
Teach recall, leash manners, and calm settling from an early age.
Practise impulse control around birds, rodents, and other small animals.
Reward quiet behaviour and teach an alternative response to alert barking.
Use gentle handling and protect the dog from rough play because of its small size.

training.socialization: Introduce the puppy gradually and positively to people, calm dogs, common sounds, different surfaces, grooming, and veterinary handling. Continue reinforcement through adolescence and adulthood.

nutrition.guidelines: Use the food label as a starting point and adjust portions to maintain a healthy body condition. Measure meals, account for treats, provide fresh water, and consult a veterinarian when choosing a diet for a puppy, senior dog, or dog with a medical condition.

health.overview: Toy Fox Terriers can live active lives, but prospective owners should ask about inherited and breed-associated health risks. Breed and veterinary sources discuss patellar luxation, eye conditions including primary lens luxation, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, von Willebrand disease, and thyroid problems. These are risks to discuss and screen for where appropriate, not diagnoses for an individual dog.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation: displacement of the kneecap that can cause lameness or abnormal gait.
Primary lens luxation (PLL): an inherited eye disorder that can displace the lens and threaten vision.
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease: a disorder affecting the head of the femur and the hip joint.
Von Willebrand disease: an inherited blood-clotting disorder.
Hypothyroidism: reduced thyroid hormone production that requires veterinary assessment.
Spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) — a progressive hereditary neurological condition affecting coordination, identifiable via diagnostic DNA screening.
preventiveCare: Ask the breeder for documented health-test results for both parents.
Discuss patella evaluation and relevant inherited-disease testing with a veterinarian.
Arrange prompt veterinary assessment for limping, persistent pain, unusual bleeding, changes in vision, or altered coordination.
Maintain a healthy body condition with suitable nutrition and regular activity.
Provide routine dental care and veterinary oral examinations.
Keep up with vaccinations, parasite prevention, and routine health checks according to veterinary advice.
recommendedScreenings: Clinical patellar evaluation by a veterinarian.
Clinical thyroid panel evaluation.
Primary Lens Luxation (PLL) genetic testing.
Diagnostic DNA genetic screening for spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) and von Willebrand disease.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental examinations. Small dogs can develop dental disease even when their teeth look clean at a glance.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears regularly for redness, odour, discharge, or discomfort. Clean only with a dog-safe product when needed and follow veterinary advice if signs of inflammation appear.
health.skinCare: Check the short coat and skin during brushing for irritation, parasites, sores, or unusual lumps. Seek veterinary advice for persistent itching or changes in the skin.

notIdealFor: Households seeking a dog that requires no training or daily engagement.

faq.question: Where does the Toy Fox Terrier originate?
faq.answer: The Toy Fox Terrier was developed in the United States from smaller Smooth Fox Terriers and toy-breed influences.

faq.question: How tall is a Toy Fox Terrier?
faq.answer: Accepted height ranges from 8.5 to 11.5 inches at the withers, with the same target span applying to both males and females.

faq.question: What colours does a Toy Fox Terrier come in?
faq.answer: Recognised colour patterns include tri-colour, white and chocolate and tan, white and tan, and white and black. The body is predominantly white, with head markings defined by the pattern.

faq.question: Does a Toy Fox Terrier need a lot of grooming?
faq.answer: No. Its short, smooth coat is relatively easy to maintain with weekly brushing, occasional bathing, and routine nail, ear, and dental care.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Toy Fox Terrier need?
faq.answer: It needs daily walks, play, and mental activity. The exact amount depends on age, fitness, and health, so a fixed daily-minute figure is not given here.

faq.question: What health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Recommended health evaluations include veterinary patella examination, thyroid panel testing, and DNA screening for primary lens luxation (PLL), spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA), and von Willebrand disease.

faq.question: Is a Toy Fox Terrier suitable for a family with children?
faq.answer: It can be affectionate and playful, but its small body needs careful handling. Interactions with young children should be actively supervised, and children should be taught to handle the dog gently.

overview.summary: An ancient, athletic Hungarian hunting hound shaped by the rugged Carpathian wilderness, renowned for its glossy black-and-tan coat with distinct eyebrow points, untiring stamina, calm domestic loyalty, and carrying bell-like bay on the trail.
overview.description: The Transylvanian Hound is an elegant, medium-to-large scent hound developed over centuries to drive and hold quarry across heavily forested and mountainous terrain. Built with an athletic rectangular silhouette, substantial bone, and lean musculature, the hound demonstrates effortless agility and endurance rather than cumbersome mass. Its double coat is short, dense, coarse, and weather-resistant, displaying a jet-black ground accented by clearly delineated tan markings on the muzzle and limbs, characteristic tan spots over the eyes, and occasional white markings on the chest and feet. The head is elongated and noble with a straight bridge, dark expressive eyes radiating calm intelligence, and medium-set pendant ears hanging close to the cheeks. In the home, it is a clean, tranquil, and deeply loyal companion, but in the field it transforms into an impassioned, courageous tracker capable of following trails across difficult wilderness for hours.
overview.history: The roots of the breed trace to the ancient scenthounds that accompanied the Magyar tribes into the Carpathian Basin in the ninth century, which intermingled with indigenous Celtic hounds. Throughout the Middle Ages and Renaissance, the breed was the favored hunting companion of Hungarian royalty and Transylvanian princes, prized for pursuing big game such as wild boar, red deer, European bison, and brown bear across steep, rocky heights. Regional terrain historically fostered two physical strains: a tall, long-legged hound adapted for open woodlands and big game, and a short-legged hound used for hunting hare and fox in dense thickets. Changing forestry laws and political upheavals in the twentieth century caused numbers to decline precipitously, bringing the breed to the brink of extinction. In 1968, dedicated conservationists recovered purebred survivors from isolated mountain valleys, reviving the lineage. Today, the tall variety is preserved as a treasured native breed celebrated for its authentic working qualities.
overview.originalPurpose: Tracking, driving, and baying big game including wild boar, red deer, bear, and lynx across dense mountain woodlands, working either solo or in small matched pairs.
currentRoles: Traditional tracking and driving hunting hound for big game
Field trial and blood-tracking competitor
Active companion for rural sporting households

health.overview: The Transylvanian Hound is an exceptionally robust, hardy hunting dog with a typical life expectancy of 10 to 14 years. Shaped by centuries of natural selection in the demanding Carpathian mountain environment, it has largely escaped the genetic vulnerabilities associated with excessive commercial breeding. Health management focuses on routine orthopedic screening for hip and elbow dysplasia, managing drop ears to prevent otitis externa, avoiding bloat in deep-chested active dogs, and treating field-related injuries.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the coxofemoral joints, monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening programs
Elbow dysplasia — developmental abnormalities of the elbow joints that can cause forelimb lameness and secondary arthritis
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — an acute, life-threatening emergency in deep-chested dogs where the stomach distends with gas and twists on its axis
Otitis externa — bacterial or yeast infections in the ear canal encouraged by folded, pendant ear flaps that reduce air circulation
Field injuries — minor lacerations, pad abrasions, torn nails, or muscle sprains sustained while tracking game through dense brush or across rocky ground
Canine vector-borne infections — tick-borne diseases (such as babesiosis, Lyme disease, and anaplasmosis) encountered in wooded hunting habitats
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have official radiographic hip and elbow evaluation clearances.
Inspect and dry the pendant ears weekly, particularly after wet forest runs or swims.
Maintain strict tick, flea, and internal parasite prevention throughout active tracking seasons.
Check paw pads, toes, and skin after hunting trips for thorns, cuts, burrs, or embedded debris.
Feed two smaller meals daily and avoid vigorous running immediately before or after eating to mitigate bloat risk.
Maintain a lean, athletic body condition to avoid premature joint wear.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine dental care.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia screening through an accredited national screening program prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia screening prior to breeding
Routine clinical veterinary ophthalmic examination
Annual veterinary blood screening for tick-borne diseases in endemic hunting territories
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using dog-specific enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong, well-developed jaws with a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the medium-set pendant ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or foul odor. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather thoroughly without inserting swabs deep into the canal.
health.skinCare: Part the dense short coat weekly to inspect the skin for external parasites, scratches, or hot spots. The close-lying coat naturally sheds dirt and requires minimal skin intervention beyond regular brushing.

funFacts: The breed is one of Hungary's nine indigenous national dog breeds, historically developed in the forested mountains of the Carpathian Basin.

Historically, two distinct varieties of the Erdélyi kopó existed: a long-legged hound used for hunting big game (bear, boar, stag, and lynx) in mountain forests, and a short-legged hound used for hunting small game (hare and fox) in plains and overgrown underbrush.

The breed nearly vanished during the mid-twentieth century when hunting preserves were disrupted and local populations dropped precipitously, but dedicated cynologists located purebred survivors in Transylvania in 1968 and revived the lineage.
In the Middle Ages and Renaissance, the Erdélyi kopó was the prized hunting hound of the Hungarian royal court and Transylvanian princes, celebrated in medieval chronicles and tapestries.
The hound's distinctive hunting voice is high-pitched, resonant, and ringing, echoing off mountain rock faces so handlers can follow its progress several kilometers away.

The tan spots above the eyes are a traditional hound trait colloquially referred to as 'four-eyes', historically believed by mountain huntsmen to provide protective vigilance against forest spirits and predators.
Today, the long-legged variety is officially standardized and flourishing, celebrated as an authentic, versatile hunting partner and cultural treasure.

faq.question: What is a Transylvanian Hound?
faq.answer: The Transylvanian Hound is an ancient medium-to-large Hungarian scenthound bred for trailing big game in mountain forests, known for its sleek black-and-tan coat, athletic build, and resonant voice.

faq.question: Where does the Transylvanian Hound originate?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the Carpathian Basin and historical Transylvania, where it was developed by Hungarian nobility and mountain huntsmen over many centuries.

faq.question: What was the Transylvanian Hound bred to do?
faq.answer: It was bred to track, drive, and hold big game such as wild boar, red deer, bear, and lynx across steep, rocky woodlands, communicating with hunters using a musical ringing bark.

faq.question: What is the difference between the long-legged and short-legged varieties?
faq.answer: Historically, the long-legged variety was used for big game hunting in mountain forests, while the short-legged variety was used for small game like hare and fox in dense underbrush; today, the long-legged hound is the primary officially standardized variety.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Transylvanian Hound?
faq.answer: Adult males and females stand 55 to 65 cm at the withers (with an ideal height between 58 and 62 cm) and weigh 25 to 35 kg, with a minimum required weight of 25 kg.

faq.question: How long does a Transylvanian Hound usually live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, regular exercise, and conscientious preventive veterinary care, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 10 to 14 years.

faq.question: What does the Transylvanian Hound's coat look like?
faq.answer: The coat is short, dense, and coarse with an undercoat, featuring a glossy black base with rich tan markings on the muzzle and legs, distinctive tan spots over the eyes, and small white markings on the chest or feet.

faq.question: Can a Transylvanian Hound live in an apartment?
faq.answer: No. Due to its high exercise requirements, working endurance, and carrying voice, the breed is not suited to apartment living and thrives best in a rural or suburban home with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Is the Transylvanian Hound good with children and other dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. Within its own household, it is gentle, calm, and affectionate with children, and as a traditional pack hound, it coexists harmoniously with other dogs.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Transylvanian Hound need each day?
faq.answer: The breed requires at least 60 to 90 minutes of vigorous daily physical activity, including brisk walks, hiking, and mental scent-tracking enrichment to satisfy its working nature.

faq.question: Does the Transylvanian Hound bark or bay a lot?
faq.answer: In the home, it is calm and composed, but in the field or when tracking quarry it possesses a high-pitched, ringing voice that echoes across great distances.

faq.question: What health problems are known in the Transylvanian Hound?
faq.answer: The breed is remarkably robust with few genetic disorders; primary health considerations include hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, ear infections from drop ears, and occasional field injuries sustained while hunting.

overview.summary: A fast, agile, and athletic American hunting hound known as the people's choice among coonhounds, celebrated for its striking tricolor coat, melodious trailing bugle, and distinct chop bark when game is treed.
overview.description: The Treeing Walker Coonhound is a clean-limbed, powerful, yet graceful medium-to-large scent hound developed for pursuit and treeing of wild game across dense American forests and rough terrain. Characterized by a streamlined, athletic outline with substantial bone and smooth musculature, the hound is built for remarkable speed, agility, and untiring endurance. Its smooth, glossy, and close-fitting short coat traditionally features a bright white ground with black markings and rich tan trim. The head is cleanly chiseled with a broad, slightly rounded skull, expressive dark eyes displaying a soft hound gaze, and medium-length pendant ears that hang gracefully. In the household, it presents an affectionate, calm, and docile temperament, but in the field it transforms into a relentless, competitive tracker with an extraordinary olfactory capacity.
overview.history: The breed traces its heritage to seventeenth- and eighteenth-century English Foxhounds brought to Virginia and Maryland by early American colonists. During the mid-nineteenth century, breeders Thomas Walker and George Washington Maupin in Kentucky crossed these foundation hounds with a stolen hound of mysterious breeding named Tennessee Lead, who possessed extraordinary drive, lightfooted speed, and a natural treeing instinct. These dogs were initially categorized as the Walker strain of the English Coonhound. In 1945, recognizing its distinct conformation, speed, and specialized treeing style, breeders established it as an independent purebred hound. Over the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, it achieved full national and international recognition, cementing its position as the premier competitive coonhound in North American field trials and night hunts.

recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia screening through an accredited national screening program prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia screening prior to breeding
Routine clinical veterinary ophthalmic examination
Annual veterinary blood screening for tick-borne diseases in endemic hunting territories
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using dog-specific enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong, well-developed jaws with a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the pendant ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or foul odor. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather thoroughly without inserting swabs deep into the canal.
health.skinCare: Part the dense short coat weekly to inspect the skin for external parasites, scratches, or hot spots. The close-lying coat naturally sheds dirt and requires minimal skin intervention beyond regular brushing.

funFacts: Known among hunters as 'the people's choice' of coonhounds, it is the most popular and numerous hound in competitive night hunts and field trials across North America.

The breed's lineage traces directly to imported English foxhounds and a famous foundation dog named Tennessee Lead, a hound of unknown ancestry acquired in Tennessee in the 1850s whose speed, drive, and treeing ability revolutionized American hounds.

Two Kentucky breeders, Thomas Walker and George Washington Maupin, were instrumental in selecting and standardizing the breed, which was originally classified alongside the English Coonhound before gaining separate recognition.
The breed is called a 'treeing' hound because upon chasing game up a tree, it places its front paws on the trunk, throws its head back, and bays continuously to alert the hunter.

A skilled hunter can read the hound's distinct vocalizations: a deep, ringing musical bugle while pursuing quarry on the trail, which instantly shifts to an energetic, rapid chop bark the moment the game is treed.
In competitive field trials and water races, the breed's streamlined athletic build makes it one of the fastest and most agile of all six American coonhound breeds.
Despite its fierce drive on the trail, it is famously known for transforming into an affectionate, docile companion the moment it enters the home.

faq.question: What is a Treeing Walker Coonhound?
faq.answer: The Treeing Walker Coonhound is a medium-to-large American hunting hound renowned for its exceptional speed, keen nose, stamina, and ability to track and tree wild game.

faq.question: Where does the Treeing Walker Coonhound originate?
faq.answer: The breed originated in the United States, developed primarily in Virginia and Kentucky from English Foxhounds crossed with a legendary foundation dog named Tennessee Lead.

faq.question: What was the Treeing Walker Coonhound bred to do, and what does 'treeing' mean?
faq.answer: It was bred to trail raccoons, bears, and other game through woodlands. 'Treeing' refers to the hound's instinct to force game up a tree, place its paws against the trunk, and vocalize continuously until the hunter arrives.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Treeing Walker Coonhound?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 22 to 27 inches at the shoulder and weigh 50 to 70 pounds, while females stand 20 to 25 inches and weigh 45 to 65 pounds, presenting an athletic and streamlined build.

faq.question: How long does a Treeing Walker Coonhound usually live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, regular exercise, and conscientious preventive veterinary care, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: What does the Treeing Walker Coonhound's coat look like?
faq.answer: The coat is short, dense, glossy, and close-lying, most often featuring a crisp tricolor pattern of white with black markings and rich tan trim.

faq.question: Can a Treeing Walker Coonhound live in an apartment?
faq.answer: No. Due to its high exercise requirements, working stamina, and carrying voice, the breed is not suited to apartment living and thrives best in a rural or suburban home with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Is the Treeing Walker Coonhound good with children and other dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. It is remarkably gentle, friendly, and affectionate with children, and as a traditional pack hound, it gets along exceptionally well with other dogs.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Treeing Walker Coonhound need each day?
faq.answer: The breed requires at least 60 to 90 minutes of vigorous daily physical activity, including brisk walks, hiking, and mental scent-tracking enrichment to satisfy its working nature.

faq.question: Does the Treeing Walker Coonhound bark or howl a lot?
faq.answer: Yes. It possesses a loud, resonant bay and chop bark that carries over great distances, which it readily uses when excited, bored, or tracking an enticing scent.

faq.question: Is the Treeing Walker Coonhound easy to train?
faq.answer: It is intelligent and eager to please its handler, but strong scenting instincts mean it can be easily distracted outdoors; it responds best to patient, positive reinforcement training and must be kept leashed in unfenced areas.

faq.question: What health problems are known in the Treeing Walker Coonhound?
faq.answer: The breed is remarkably robust with few genetic disorders; primary health considerations include hip dysplasia, ear infections from pendant ears, and occasional field injuries sustained while hunting.

overview.summary: The Tyrolean Hound (Tiroler Bracke) is a weather-hardy, medium-sized Austrian mountain scent hound bred for solo vocal trailing of hare and fox and for tracking wounded game across steep alpine and woodland terrain.
overview.description: Built for stamina and sure-footedness in high mountains and dense forests, the Tyrolean Hound has a long, rectangular silhouette that stands slightly longer than tall on medium-boned, well-muscled, sinewy limbs. A thick double coat with a coarse undercoat, a fully haired belly, feathered breeches on the thighs, and a dense brush on the high-set tail shield the dog from snow and rough brush. The breed comes in two traditional colour types—red (from rich red and deer red to red-fawn) and black-and-tan (a black saddle or mantle with warm tan markings)—either of which may carry white markings on the neck, chest, legs, and feet. Unlike pack hounds kept in kennels, the Tyrolean Hound is a solo worker that needs close daily contact with its handler, combining a resonant trail voice, an unerring sense of direction, and relentless tracking drive in the field with a calm, steady, and affectionate demeanour inside a hunting household.
overview.history: Like other Central European Bracke hounds, the Tyrolean Hound traces its roots to the ancient Celtic Hound (Keltenbracke) and the medieval Eastern Alpine mountain hound known as the Wildbodenhund. Around 1500, Emperor Maximilian I hunted with these alpine hounds in Tyrol and noted in his hunting books that he chose his prized lead tracking hounds (limiers) from them. After wars and economic hardship between 1786 and 1809 sharply reduced local hound numbers, Tyrolean professional hunters and mountain farmers preserved the indigenous strains. Systematic pure breeding of distinct regional lines began in Tyrol around 1860, a formal conformation standard was drafted at the first Innsbruck dog show in 1896, and official recognition followed at the Innsbruck International Dog Show in May 1908. Conservation efforts led by Richard Sauerwein in 1931 and dedicated breeders after the Second World War safeguarded the surviving red and black-and-tan varieties. A dedicated breed club was established in Innsbruck in 1950, definitive international recognition was granted in October 1954, the short-legged variety (Tiroler Niederbracke) was removed in 1994, and North American registry recognition followed in 2006.
overview.originalPurpose: Solo vocal scent-hunting (Brackieren) of hare and fox and blood-tracking (Schweißarbeit) of wounded game across alpine and forest terrain.
currentRoles: Solo vocal scent hound for hare and fox hunting in mountain and woodland districts
Blood-tracking dog (Schweißhund) for recovering wounded ungulate game
Solo flushing and driving hound on driven forest hunts (Bewegungsjagden) for deer, mouflon, and wild boar
Calm stalking partner and household companion for active hunting families

physical.coatType: Thick, weatherproof double coat (Stockhaar) with an undercoat that is coarse rather than fine, covering the belly and forming dense feathering on the hindquarters and tail.
physical.coatLength: Short to medium working coat over the trunk, with fuller feathering along the backs of the thighs and a thick, brush-like coat on the tail.
coatColors: Red (rich red, deer red, or red-fawn; overly pale yellow-fawn is undesirable)
Black and tan (black mantle or saddle with red, usually non-sharply defined tan markings on the legs, chest, belly, and head; tan 'Vieräugl' spots above the eyes are permitted)
Tricolour (red or black-and-tan combined with white markings)
White markings (permitted on both colour varieties as a neck stripe, forechest or lower-chest star, and markings on the feet and legs; absence of white markings is not faulted)
distinctiveFeatures: Medium-sized, rectangularly built mountain hound standing 44 to 50 cm in males and 42 to 48 cm in females, with a typical working weight of 15 to 22 kg
Broad, clean, slightly arched skull with a clearly defined stop, straight moderately deep muzzle, short close-fitting lips, and black nose leather
Strong complete scissor bite of 42 teeth (absence of up to two PM1 or PM2 premolars tolerated)
Large, round dark brown eyes that are not deep-set, with tight-fitting lids and a pigmented third-eyelid margin
Broad, high-set ears with rounded tips that reach the upper canine tooth when moderately drawn forward
Very deep, moderately broad chest with a well-rounded forechest, dry moderately arched neck without dewlap, and broad, heavily muscled thighs
High-set long tail reaching at least to the hock, carried high when excited (sabre curve permitted) with a dense brush
Ground-covering, rapid, and tireless working gait built for steep mountain slopes

traits: Steady, calm, and composed in temperament
Passionate, fine-nosed, and relentless when working a scent trail
Independent solo hunter with a resonant, reliable trail voice (Spurlaut) and keen sense of direction
Closely bonded to its handler and unsuited to isolated kennel or pack keeping
Quiet and pleasant as a stalking partner and affectionate, child-friendly companion inside the hunter's home
Alert and watchful around home and yard without unprovoked aggression or shyness

exercise.level: High. Bred for hours of solo scent work and mountain tracking, this athletic hound requires substantial daily physical activity and purposeful nosework rather than brief neighbourhood strolls.
activities: Practical hunting, vocal trail work (Brackieren), and wounded-game blood tracking (Schweißarbeit)
Long, brisk hikes and hill walks with opportunities for structured sniffing
Laid artificial scent trails (Fährtenschuh), mantrailing, and scent-discrimination games
Reward-based recall and steadiness training in secure or long-line settings
Calm indoor problem-solving and scent-puzzle enrichment

grooming.level: Low to moderate; the coarse double coat is weather-resistant and easy to maintain with weekly brushing, increasing during seasonal coat changes.
grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice a week with a firm bristle brush or hound glove to lift dead hair, stimulate the skin, and clear forest debris from the coarse double coat, thigh breeches, and tail brush.
grooming.bathing: Rinse with clear water after muddy outings and bathe with a mild, dog-formulated shampoo only when necessary so the coat retains its natural weatherproofing.
notes: Inspect the coat, feathered breeches, and belly hair after forest or mountain work for ticks, burrs, needles, and minor scrapes.
Check the broad, high-set hanging ears weekly for trapped moisture, wax, redness, or odour.
Examine the tightly closed, well-arched toes and tough paw pads after rocky terrain work, trimming nails if they do not wear down naturally.
Brush the teeth regularly with canine toothpaste to maintain oral health.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for novice pet owners. Because the breed was selected to search independently and stay on a trail with determination, training requires patience, hunting-hound understanding, and a strong handler bond.
tips: Build a close daily bond indoors; unlike pack hounds, this solo worker thrives on personal connection with its handler and must not be relegated to isolated kennel life.
Use calm, consistent, reward-based methods to channel the dog's natural scenting drive into structured blood-tracking and trail exercises.
Practice recall progressively from an early age and use a leash or long tracking line in unsecured areas where wildlife scents are present.
Condition gun-steadiness, calm waiting at the stand, and dead-game indication systematically for working hounds.
Balance high-focus scent work with quiet settling routines at home.
training.socialization: Expose puppies early and positively to household life, children, visitors, other dogs, and varied woodland and mountain environments so they mature into steady, confident partners.

climates: Well adapted to cold, snowy alpine winters and wet mountain weather thanks to its thick, coarse double coat and fully haired belly
In warm summer weather, schedule strenuous tracking or hiking for cool morning or evening hours and provide ample shade and fresh water
Requires integration into family life inside the home with access to a securely fenced yard or rural grounds rather than pure kennel keeping

nutrition.dietType: Complete, balanced canine diet formulated for active medium-sized working dogs and matched to age, body condition, and seasonal workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Feed a complete puppy ration divided into three to four age-appropriate meals daily, tapering to twice-daily meals as growth matures.
feedingFrequency.adult: Provide two measured meals per day on a consistent schedule, adjusting caloric density to maintain a lean 15 to 22 kg working build.
feedingFrequency.senior: Offer measured meals suited to senior metabolism, joint comfort, and activity level in consultation with a veterinarian.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily rations rather than free-feeding, keep clean drinking water available at all times, and increase energy intake during demanding autumn and winter hunting seasons while preventing excess weight during quieter periods.
considerations: Allow adequate rest before and after strenuous tracking or mountain runs before serving a full meal to protect the deep chest from digestive distress.
Count high-value training rewards used during scent and recall work within the total daily calorie allowance.
Introduce any dietary transitions gradually over several days.
Consult a veterinarian before adding supplements or altering rations for medical needs.
nutrition.note: These guidelines reflect general veterinary nutrition practices for athletic working scent hounds rather than a breed-specific clinical diet.

health.overview: Shaped by generations of rigorous selection for alpine working stamina, the Tyrolean Hound is generally a robust, weather-hardy breed with a typical lifespan of 12 to 14 years. Parent-club breeding regulations mandate pre-breeding radiographic screening for hip dysplasia (HD)—permitting only grades HD A, HD B, and HD C (which may be paired solely with HD A) while barring HD D and HD E from breeding—alongside conformation and field-trial qualification. Because a peer-reviewed pedigree analysis of 1,167 registered Tyrolean Hounds (1992–2004) found a relatively small effective population size (26.5) and an average inbreeding coefficient of 9.5%, breed clubs closely manage mating plans to preserve genetic diversity.
preventiveCare: Schedule routine veterinary wellness examinations and keep vaccinations and parasite prophylaxis current for a hound working in woodland and mountain habitats.
Inspect the coat, ears, eyes, and interdigital spaces after every field or tracking outing to remove ticks, thorns, awns, and debris.
Maintain a lean, muscular body condition and build physical conditioning progressively to match the dog's age and workload.
Request official parent-club hip dysplasia (HD) radiographic clearances for both parents when acquiring a puppy.
Seek prompt veterinary attention for lameness, ear redness or head-shaking, eye irritation, or sudden digestive distress.
recommendedScreenings: Official pre-breeding radiographic hip dysplasia (HD) evaluation (only HD A, HD B, and HD C permitted to breed, with HD C restricted to HD A mates)
Pre-breeding conformation and soundness inspection (Ankörung / Formwert at least 'Very Good' [SG], minimum breeding age 20 months for females and 24 months for males)

Dental, ocular, and reproductive examination verifying a complete scissor bite (at most two PM1 or PM2 premolars absent), taut eyelids with pigmented third-eyelid rims, and two normal descended testicles in males
Pedigree and kinship review prior to mating to limit inbreeding and preserve genetic diversity
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-formulated toothpaste and inspect the scissor dentition for tartar buildup or wear.
health.earCare: Check the broad, high-set drop ears weekly and after wet or snowy field work; clean gently with a veterinarian-approved solution if wax or debris accumulates.
health.skinCare: Part the thick double coat after woodland runs to check the skin and paw pads for ticks, bramble scratches, or soreness.

idealFor: Active mountain and woodland hunters or professional gamekeepers who need a dependable solo scent and blood-tracking hound
Handlers who include their working hound in daily family life indoors while providing regular field or tracking work
Experienced scent-hound enthusiasts prepared to channel strong trailing instincts through mantrailing or scent sports
notIdealFor: Non-hunting or sedentary households unable to satisfy an intense, vocal scent-hunting drive
Note: parent breed clubs in Austria and Germany place puppies exclusively with licensed hunters who hold active hunting grounds
Anyone intending to keep a hound isolated in an outdoor kennel or pack run without close handler contact

funFacts: Around 1500, Emperor Maximilian I hunted with Tyrolean hounds in the Alps and recorded in his hunting diaries that he selected his prized lead tracking hounds (limiers) from this regional stock.

Unlike English pack hounds that hunt in large groups, the Tyrolean Hound works as a solo hunter (Solojäger): it trails hare or fox at a steady pace while giving tongue continuously, prompting the quarry to circle back within 200 to 800 m toward the waiting hunter.

Because professional alpine hunters rely so heavily on its fine nose, trail fidelity, and natural ability to indicate downed game, it is the most widely used hunting dog in Tyrol and is frequently chosen even over specialised bloodhounds for wounded-game recovery.
Parent breed clubs in Austria and Germany maintain strict working preservation rules, placing puppies only with holders of a valid hunting licence and documented hunting access.

From the many local mountain hound strains that once existed across Tyrol, only the red and black-and-tan varieties survived into the modern era, while a short-legged variety (Tiroler Niederbracke) was removed in 1994.

faq.question: Where did the Tyrolean Hound originate?
faq.answer: The breed developed in the Tyrol region of the Austrian Alps from ancient Celtic Hounds and medieval Eastern Alpine mountain hounds, with documented hunting use under Emperor Maximilian I around 1500 and systematic pure breeding beginning around 1860.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Tyrolean Hound?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 44 to 50 cm at the withers and adult females stand 42 to 48 cm, with a typical working weight of 15 to 22 kg.

faq.question: What coat colours and markings are accepted?
faq.answer: Two main colour varieties are accepted—red (red, deer red, or red-fawn, though overly pale yellow-fawn is undesirable) and black-and-tan (a black saddle or mantle with red-tan markings on the head, chest, belly, and legs, optionally including tan spots above the eyes)—either of which may also appear as tricolour with white markings on the neck, chest, legs, and feet. Liver colour and distinctly pied coats are disqualifications.

faq.question: How long does a Tyrolean Hound typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Why is it difficult for non-hunters to acquire a Tyrolean Hound puppy?
faq.answer: To preserve the breed's specialized alpine hunting and blood-tracking instincts, official parent clubs in Austria and Germany allocate puppies exclusively to licensed hunters and gamekeepers who have verified access to hunting grounds.

faq.question: Can a Tyrolean Hound be kept in an outdoor kennel or pack?
faq.answer: No. Unlike pack hounds, the Tyrolean Hound is a solo worker that needs close daily contact with its handler. When properly integrated into the hunter's household, it is a calm, loyal, and child-friendly indoor companion.

faq.question: What health screenings are required before breeding a Tyrolean Hound?
faq.answer: Parent-club breeding rules require official radiographic evaluation for hip dysplasia (HD)—allowing only grades HD A, HD B, and HD C (which may only be paired with HD A)—along with conformation approval (at least 'Very Good'), a complete scissor bite (at most two PM1 or PM2 premolars absent), gun-steadiness, and passing scores in field and trail-voice trials.

overview.summary: A sleek, athletic, and aristocratic German pointing gundog, universally recognized by its striking silver-grey coat, piercing amber or blue-grey eyes, tireless hunting stamina, and shadow-like devotion to its handler.
overview.description: The Weimaraner is a medium-to-large, elegant pointing dog combining lean, sinewy muscular power with graceful, ground-covering athleticism. Built with a clean rectangular silhouette, deep chest, and firm topline, the hound was bred to work closely with huntsmen through demanding forests and fields. Its signature coat appears in two varieties—the classic sleek short coat and a rarer feathered long coat—displaying an unmistakable monochrome palette ranging from shimmering silver-grey to mouse-grey or roe-grey. The head is aristocratically proportioned with a moderate stop, dark flesh-toned or grey nose, long lobular drop ears, and light amber to blue-grey eyes that radiate acute intelligence and focus. Deeply bonded, emotionally sensitive, and energetic, the breed excels as an adaptable field gundog, an enthusiastic canine athlete, and a steadfast household companion that thrives on human companionship.
overview.history: The breed was developed during the early nineteenth century at the royal court of Grand Duke Karl August of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach in Weimar, central Germany. Noble sportsmen crossed historical tracking scenthounds, including the ancient Bloodhound-descended St. Hubert hound and early red Schweisshunde, with versatile German pointing dogs to produce a multi-purpose noble hunting dog capable of tracking big game such as deer, bear, and wild boar. As large game populations dwindled across western Europe, the dogs were redirected toward feathered upland game and hare. In 1897, a dedicated breed club was formed in Germany with strict regulations that permitted breeding stock and puppies to be sold exclusively to certified foresters and active hunters. The breed was introduced to North America and the United Kingdom in the 1920s and 1930s, where its shimmering coat and stealthy field movement earned it the enduring moniker 'The Grey Ghost'.
overview.originalPurpose: Tracking and baying large forest game including red deer, wild boar, and bear, transitioning to versatile pointing, flushing, and water retrieving of upland game birds and hares.
currentRoles: Versatile pointing, flushing, and water-retrieving gundog
Field trial and hunt test competitor

Search, rescue, and tracking detection partner

physical.coatType: Occurs in two distinct varieties: short-haired (short, smooth, very dense, and sleek topcoat with little or no undercoat) and long-haired (soft, long topcoat with or without undercoat, smooth or slightly wavy, with silky feathering on the ears, rear of legs, underside of chest, and a plumed tail).

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice weekly with a rubber curry comb, hound mitt, or soft bristle brush to remove loose dead hairs and maintain skin oils; the long-haired variety requires combing two to three times weekly to keep feathering tangle-free.
grooming.bathing: Bathe every six to eight weeks or when soiled after muddy field hunts, using a gentle canine shampoo.
notes: Inspect the long drop ears weekly for moisture, wax buildup, or debris, especially after swimming or field hunts, drying the canals thoroughly.
Check webbed paws, pads, and toes after running in thick brush or rocky ground for cuts, burrs, or embedded thorns.
Trim fast-growing nails every two to three weeks to maintain correct compact foot structure.
Brush teeth several times weekly using dog-specific enzymatic toothpaste.
Wipe down the short coat with a damp chamois or microfiber cloth after outdoor excursions to remove dust and restore a brilliant sheen.
Provide soft, orthopedic bedding indoors, as the sleek coat and lean frame make pressure points prone to elbow calluses on hard surfaces.

training.difficulty: Moderate; exceptionally intelligent, biddable, and eager to please, but strong-willed, easily bored, and highly energetic, requiring calm, consistent, and reward-based leadership
tips: Use positive reinforcement, high-value food rewards, and enthusiastic praise.
Begin obedience, loose-leash walking, and impulse-control training from early puppyhood.
Keep instructional lessons fast-paced, challenging, and varied to prevent mental boredom.
Avoid harsh verbal reprimands or physical coercion, which cause this sensitive hound to lose trust and become stubborn.
Always exercise within a securely fenced area of at least six feet in height; strong prey drive can prompt sudden pursuit of wildlife.
Practice calm separation routines early to prevent intense velcro attachment from turning into destructive separation anxiety.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy early, gradually, and positively to diverse people, friendly vaccinated dogs of varying sizes, livestock, novel surfaces, and busy environments. Early structured socialization tempers natural protective wariness and fosters an outgoing, self-assured companion.

climates: Temperate climates
Warm climates, provided indoor cooling, shade, fresh water, and exercise during cooler hours are available
Cool climates, provided the dog lives indoors and wears a protective fleece during sub-zero winter weather
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low; intensely bonded to its family and famously nicknamed a 'velcro dog', prone to severe separation anxiety, vocal howling, and destructive chewing if left isolated for long workdays.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for large active sporting or working breeds, adjusted for age, activity level, and seasonal field exertion.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age, transitioning to two meals daily on a large-breed growth diet supporting steady skeletal development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support steady metabolism and minimize digestive discomfort.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic output, joint support, and lean muscle retention.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily rations carefully using a digital kitchen scale or standard measuring cup, adjusting amounts to maintain a lean, athletic body silhouette where the ribs are easily felt. Divide daily food into two distinct meals, restrict vigorous running for at least one hour before and after eating to reduce bloat risk, and provide cool, clean drinking water continuously.
considerations: Maintain a lean, muscular body condition; excess weight places unnecessary mechanical wear on hips and stifles.
Account for training treats within the total daily caloric allowance to avoid creeping weight gain.
Rest the dog before and after meals to mitigate the risk of bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus).
Avoid feeding high-fat table scraps that can trigger digestive upset or acute pancreatitis.
Provide clean drinking water, especially during warm-weather hunting or training excursions.
Transition between diet formulas gradually over five to seven days.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs fluctuate substantially between sedentary home periods and intense autumn hunting seasons. Work with a veterinarian to establish tailored daily feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The Weimaraner is a robust, athletic sporting dog with a typical life expectancy of 11 to 14 years. Developed through strict working standards, it has maintained good constitutional hardiness. Primary health considerations focus on risks associated with deep-chested sporting dogs—notably gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat)—alongside orthopedic screening for hip and elbow dysplasia, hereditary ocular conditions, autoimmune thyroiditis, and rare neurological conditions such as hypomyelination (spinal dysraphism).
commonConditions: Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — an acute, life-threatening emergency in deep-chested breeds where the stomach distends with gas and twists on its mesenteric axis, requiring emergency surgical intervention; preventive prophylactic gastropexy is frequently discussed with veterinarians
Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the coxofemoral joints leading to osteoarthritis and hind-limb lameness, monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening
Elbow dysplasia — developmental abnormalities of the elbow joints causing forelimb lameness and secondary arthritis
Hypomyelination / Spinal Dysraphism ('shaking puppy syndrome') — an inherited neurological disorder causing distinctive tremors and bunny-hopping in young puppies, screenable via DNA testing
Autoimmune thyroiditis — immune-mediated destruction of the thyroid gland causing hypothyroidism, weight gain, lethargy, and coat thinning
Entropion, distichiasis, and corneal dystrophy — eyelid and ocular conditions monitored through regular veterinary ophthalmologist examinations
Chronic otitis externa — bacterial and yeast ear infections promoted by heavy drop ears that trap moisture after swimming
Tricuspid valve dysplasia (TVD) and cardiac murmurs — congenital or acquired cardiac conditions evaluated via veterinary auscultation and echocardiography
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has certified radiographic hip and elbow clearances, DNA clearances, and current specialist eye and thyroid certifications.
Feed two smaller meals daily and avoid vigorous running for at least one hour before and after eating to mitigate bloat risk.
Inspect and thoroughly dry the drop ears after every swim or wet field hunt, wiping canals with an approved veterinary cleanser.
Maintain a lean, muscular body condition throughout life to minimize mechanical wear on joints and ligaments.
Administer consistent year-round parasite prevention against fleas, ticks, and heartworms.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accredited national screening program prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Autoimmune thyroiditis blood panel (free T4, TSH, and autoantibodies) prior to breeding
DNA marker test for Spinal Dysraphism / Hypomyelination
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using dog-specific enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong, wide jaws with a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the long drop ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or redness. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather and canal opening thoroughly after swimming.
health.skinCare: Part the sleek coat weekly during brushing to inspect the skin for external parasites, scratches, or hot spots. Provide thick orthopedic bedding to protect pressure points over elbows and hocks from calluses.
